## 6dy. The rule three screens printed a price for and never sold

**The finding: a scoping sentence that was a claim about this app, and the
claim was false the whole time.** `EffortBurn`'s KDoc justified belonging to
the plain skill roll alone with *"A ritual and a divination keep charging their
own burn, because offering this one as well would charge a single point of
effort twice."* Both halves of that are good rules. The premise was not true of
this codebase:

- `DivinationDialog.kt:186` called `Divination.spiFor(method, spiChoice)` with
  `burned` defaulted; `RitualDialog.kt:229` and `BoonDialog.kt:157` the same.
- No `BurnRow`, no burn chip, and no `burned` identifier in any of the three.
- `Divination.attempt(..., burned)` had **no non-default caller** anywhere in
  `app/`.

So a Beyonder who rolled a ritual was told about the push on one screen
(`RollDialog` has offered it since 6ar) and denied it on the next. This is
6dr's shape a second time — *a refusal whose reason is a claim about the app,
and nothing ever re-reads those* — and it is why that lesson now sits in
`EffortBurn`'s own KDoc rather than only in this log.

**The two halves disagreed in opposite directions, which is the sharper half
of the finding.** `Divination.attempt` added `burned` to the target BEFORE
`SuccessRoll.against`, so its "burn" was a PRE-commitment — a different
decision from the one the book prints, because the whole point of the rule is
that the dice are already on the table. `RitualResolution.attempt` took no
`burned` at all, while `RitualResolution.spiFor(weight, chosen, burned)` would
happily charge for it: **the ritual's charge was implemented and its bonus was
not.** A parameter that only costs is worse than a missing one.

**The book prints this five times and the extraction had all five.** Lines 393
(ch. 2, the general form), 3708 (ch. 6.5), 4105 (Quick Ritual), 4145 (Full
Ritual Phase II) and 4268 (Power Source A). Three of the five are inside
claimed spans. So no coverage number could report this, and no content sweep
could either — it is a rule the engine holds, correctly, and no screen asks
for. 6cf's "every public rules function checked for a UI caller" sweep is one
unit too coarse to see it: the functions HAD callers. **The unit that finds it
is a PARAMETER checked for a non-default argument.** That is a sweep direction
this repo had not run, and it is the deliverable to inherit.

**Boons arrive by referral, not by resemblance.** Chapter 13 prints no burn
sentence — grepped, pages 144-146, and the only SPI it prints is the Effect
Weight row and the Dancer's ability costs. The temptation was to reason from
`Boons.weight()` returning a `RitualWeight`, i.e. from the two screens looking
alike, which is exactly the warrant 6cx returned NO-SHIP on. The real warrant
is a sentence: book line 8933, *"The boon granting ritual uses the standard
Ritualistic Magic system (see Chapter 7)"* — chapter 13's own first line about
the procedure — and ch. 2's SPI row naming **Ritualistic Magic** outright at
line 392. What chapter 13 fixes is the baseline (Heavy complexity, Moderate
weight); it replaces no part of chapter 7 it does not name. **A silence is not
an absence of authority when the chapter has already delegated.**

**`canPush` is arithmetic on both objects, and it is arithmetic in opposite
directions.** A ritual's rolled 17-18 takes `failures.single { it.critical }`
whatever the target and carries no -2 to adjust, so nothing a caster spends
there buys anything — `EffortBurn.canPush`'s own stated reason, applied to a
different sum. A divination's **critical SUCCESS is pushable**, because the
clarity table prints no critical row and grades one by margin like any other;
copying `EffortBurn.canPush` wholesale would have refused it. Same function
name, opposite answer, and the design review caught the copy before it shipped.

**The Critical Failure Table's roll is a second sample, not derived data.**
`RitualOutcome.criticalRoll` is 3d6 taken at resolution and shifted by -2. A
push shrinks the margin, so a severe misfire can leave that table entirely.
Re-rolling on the pushed path would hand the caster a fresh chance at a milder
row the book never offered; keeping it on a result that no longer reaches the
table would leave a GM reading a disaster the caster spent SPI to avoid. So it
is **re-used or dropped, never re-sampled**, and because a push can only
shrink the margin, needing a sample that was never taken is impossible and is
`requireNotNull`-asserted rather than handled. RED-proved by flipping `pushed`
to widen the margin: the guard raised `IllegalArgumentException` at the call
site, read from the message and not from the exit code (6du).

**The deferral of the CoR is the part that needed a design review, and then a
diff review on top.** Charging the critical row's CoR at the roll — where it
used to be, correctly, before this slice — would leave corruption paid for a
consequence the caster then spent SPI to avoid. So it moves to one settlement
point per dialog. The first draft wired that to Close and `onDismissRequest`
and **that was not enough**: `remember` does not survive the dialog leaving
composition, and leaving composition is not a dismiss request, so a rotation
dropped both the pushed SPI and the CoR the roll owed. The CoR half was a
**regression this slice introduced** — the pre-deferral version charged it at
the roll and could not lose it. `DisposableEffect { onDispose { settle() } }`
closes every in-app path; process death still loses it, and loses the outcome
with it, which is where that bound is stated rather than skipped.

**Two taps beat one recomposition.** The push row's callback pushed the
outcome CAPTURED when the row was composed, so two quick taps each started
from the same value: the second overwrote the first, charging 2 SPI for +1,
and the affordability the chips were drawn against was equally stale. Reading
the LIVE state inside the callback fixes both — the `val live = out ?:
return@BurnRow` idiom `RollDialog` has used since 6ar, which is the third time
this repo has needed it and the first time it was found by a reviewer rather
than by a player.

**The SPI is accumulated and charged once, rather than charged per tap.** The
diff review's prescription was an owner-side `trySpendSpi(points): Boolean`
that checks and debits atomically; what ships accumulates in dialog-local state
and settles once, which has no check-then-act window to close because nothing
else spends during the push window. **Take a reviewer's diagnosis over its
prescription** (6cz) — the invariant is theirs, the mechanism is smaller.

**Reviews.** Design review (Codex `gpt-6-astra`, `model_reasoning_effort=xhigh`)
before any code: it supplied the chapter 13 warrant I did not have, returned
NO-SHIP on wiring push buttons into the ritual lifecycle as it stood, and
NO-SHIP on affordability that relies only on rendered chips. Diff review after:
one HIGH (disposal), one MEDIUM (the captured outcome), one LOW (unchecked
`Int` addition on the target — `Math.addExact` now, as `spiFor` already used
for the same wrap) and four LOWs on my own tests, every one of them a name
claiming more than its assertions checked:

- *"refuses one"* asserted the demoted verdict, which a push that HAPPENED also
  satisfies; it asserts the whole outcome comes back unchanged now.
- *"still has a band to improve"* used a fixture already at the top band, so a
  no-op push passed; skill 1 on a Trivial (+2) question is a target of 3, and
  three 1s is a critical success at the MILDEST band.
- *"a rolled 17 or 18"* exercised only the 18, so a threshold slipping to 18
  would have left 17 pushable with the test still green.
- *"improves the success band"* checked inequality, which `null` also satisfies.

That is the thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth and sixteenth vacuous-or-overclaiming
assertion this log has recorded, all four in tests written by an author who
knew about the other twelve. **The class does not go away by being known; it
goes away by being asked about, per test, in the review prompt.**

`--- the census ---`

**Every unclaimed mechanical line in the book is now accounted for, and this is
the list.** `tools/coverage.py` reports 196 across nine chapters. Read as a
work queue it is a lie; read as a proxy it is finished.

**That claim was written before it was true, and the correction is the more
useful half.** The first version of this table covered fourteen candidate
clusters plus three bulk categories — about 155 of the 196 — and the sentence
above it said "every". Ten chapters' worth of lines were outside the corpus it
was written from, including **Appendix C, which reads 0.0%, is claimed by no
content file, and was not in the table at all** — 6db's finding exactly, an
unread chapter filtered out of the sweep that exists to find unread chapters.
6dn's shape in a paragraph written four slices after 6dn. The remaining ~40
were triaged the same way and every one resolves; the table below is the
complete one, and **Appendix C's two lines are the most interesting thing in
it**: they are `(expelled post-1350)` and `(pre-1352)`, so that chapter's 0.0%
is **two dates the `MECHANICAL` filter read as signed numbers.** A political
and ecclesiastical chapter with no rules content in it reads 0.0% forever, and
the number says nothing about whether it was read.

Fourteen candidates
were put to a read-only census (Codex `gpt-6-astra` at `xhigh`, each verdict
required to cite `file:line` or name a grep that returned nothing), and twelve
came back settled before a line was written:

| Book lines | Rule | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 2454 | Parry's cumulative -4 / -2 fencing | implemented, `ParryBlock.kt:115`, applied at `DefenseDialog.kt:523` |
| 2599-2601 | Grappling ST bonus at DX+1 / DX+2 | refused in 6do: it needs an ST-for-grappling path and a trait (`Wrestling Master`) this app does not hold |
| 2861-2895, 2899 | Natural Recovery, First Aid, Regeneration RATES | refused in 6dc under *"track a clock it does not hold"*; the HT roll at 0 HP itself is `VitalRolls`, implemented |
| 4105, 4145, 4268 | the post-roll SPI push | **this slice** |
| 4271 | HP sacrifice, 2 HP = 1 SPI | implemented, `PowerSources.kt:150`, `RitualDialog.kt:864` |
| 4276-4277 | assistants, +1 each capped at +3 | implemented, `PowerSources.kt:172`, offered at `RitualDialog.kt:399` |
| 4289 | catalyst +0 to +2 | implemented, `PowerSources.kt:203`, picked at `RitualDialog.kt:479` |
| 4222 | suspending a ritual, -2 | implemented, `PowerSources.SUSPENSION_PENALTY` |
| 4161 | wrong timing, -1 to -2 | refused at `RitualMode.kt:49` — preparation already prices timing, and charging both charges twice |
| 4398 | reducing ritual CoR by a month's abstinence | refused, the clock again |
| 4642-4670 | Rituals 8 and 9 (offering, union) | recorded in 6dn: they print RANGES, so `extract_worked_rituals.py` reads them as templates and guards them, and executes neither |
| 4730, 4762-4764 | the creature response roll, the Bookworm block | recorded in 6dk: a GM's free roll, and GM content — this app holds one player character |
| ch. 9's nine lines | *"how to read a potion's +N grant"* | prose and worked examples; the rule is `PotionDigestion` |
| ch. 3's 56, App. A's ladder rows | the attribute and skill ladders | arithmetic, so they read unclaimed forever (6cy, 6dp) |
| ch. 8's 19 | four equipment tables | refused in `Equipment.UNMODELLED` (6cx) |
| 9667, 9672, 9723 | facing penalties, the Major Wound summary, SPI recovery | refused in 6da, recorded as a disagreement in 6dl, refused in `Pools.UNMODELLED` in 6dq |
| 234, 266, 273, 350 | *"three six-sided dice (3d6)"*, the Stealth 12 example, the "-2 to Stealth" example | ch. 1-2 prose and worked examples of `SuccessRoll` |
| 2309, 2339 | Spirit Vision's cost printed a second time, and rest recovering 1 SPI | 6dq: the second printing says strictly less, and the rate is `Pools.UNMODELLED` |
| 3548, 3550 | *"Divination Arts costs 1-2 SPI per use"* | prose summarising `divination_methods.json`, which prices each method |
| 2375 | initiative, *"Roll 1d6 — higher goes first"* | refused: no initiative, no map, no turn counter (`HOW-TO-PLAY`'s own list) |
| 2379, 2540-2541, 2598, 2629-2643 | Combat Reflexes' +1, the Brawling and Wrestling defaults and parries, and the Summary: Melee Skill Comparison restating all three | `ActiveDefenses`, `SkillLadder.defaultFor`, `ParryBlock.unarmedParry` |
| 2645-2646 | the ranged prose intro, *"TL5+1 weapons"* | setting prose; the rows are `Ranged` |
| 2695-2696 | the HP ladder in prose, to `-5xHP` | `VitalRolls` and `pool_thresholds.json`, whose last row is *"Dead — no roll required"* |
| 2842-2852 | the FP table's rows | applied in Kotlin since 6h and 6dc (`Pools.isFatigued`, `halvedForFatigue`), which `coverage.py` cannot see |
| 2902, 2917 | the Fright Check's prose and *"3d6 + margin of failure"* | `FrightCheck.against` / `.effectFor` |
| 4360 | the `Critical Failure Table (3d6)` heading | a table heading; its rows are `ritual_critical.json` |
| 4407-4419 | typical maximum SPI by Sequence, and a worked comparison | prose bands ("Seq 9 = 3-6") the sheets settle per character |
| 9953, 10010 | `(expelled post-1350)`, `(pre-1352)` | **dates.** Appendix C's whole 0.0% is the filter reading two years as signed numbers |

**Read that table as a claim with an expiry date, not as a clean bill.** Three
of its rows are refusals whose stated reason is a claim about this app rather
than about the book — the exact shape this very slice overturned — and 6da,
6dj, 6dl, 6dq and 6dr each began by re-running one such reason as a query and
watching it die. The cheap version of that check is one grep per row. What the
table does close is the question *"is there a rule in this book that reaches
nothing and nobody has looked at it"*: there is not one left that a census over
all 196 could see.

**What it cannot see is what found this slice.** A rule can be extracted,
loaded, tested, documented, reachable from a called function, and still be
unreachable by a player, because the call passes a default. Five sweep
directions in this log iterate declarations — fields for a reader (6ai),
functions for a caller (6cf), rows for a consumer (6ci), files for a loader
(6dg), strings a screen types (6cq) — and every one of them is blind to a
**parameter with no non-default argument**. That query is:

**two** steps, and the grep alone is not it — recording only the grep would be
a count without its query (6df), in the paragraph naming that lesson:

```bash
# 1. ENUMERATE the optional parameters. This is the candidate list, not the
#    finding list: 369 in core/rules + core/model on the run this slice made.
grep -rnoE '\b[a-z][A-Za-z]*: [A-Za-z<>?]+ = [^,)]+' \
  core/rules/src/main/kotlin core/model/src/main/kotlin --include=*.kt

# 2. For each, look for a call site passing a NON-default value, in
#    app/src/main (the only UI) and core/rules/src/main (internal composition
#    counts as production). A call in src/test does NOT count as reachable.
```

**with three exclusions, which are the difference between 369 and the 194 that
were actually checked**, and without which a re-run cannot reproduce 36 or 5:

- a parameter whose default is a `ContentLoader` call, and every `RandomSource`
  — those are injection seams this repo builds on purpose;
- a parameter on a function with no production caller at all, which belongs to
  6cf's sweep rather than this one.

It is the one sweep this repo has now run exactly once.

**1701 Kotlin** (1215 `core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and **347
Python**, all green, counted from the JUnit XML after a full unfiltered run.
Build warnings: none.

**Device-verified on an SM-T570, on both screens, and the arithmetic is the
proof.** Apothecary drinking Hermit Sequence 9 (Ritualistic Magic 14,
Divination Arts 20, SPI 18). Divination, Extreme question and Complex scope,
target 10: *"3d6: 12 vs 10 — Failure by 1-4 — Murky"*, then **+2** gives
*"3d6: 12 vs 12 — Success by 0-2 — Vague"*. **The total did not move and the
target did**, which is the whole rule, and the band was re-read with it. Ritual,
Light weight, target 14: *"3d6: 11 vs 14"*, then **+1** gives *"11 vs 15"*.
The pool tells the rest: SPI went 18 → 15 (1 Pendulum fuel + 2 pushed) → 12
(2 ritual fuel + 1 pushed). **Each push charged exactly once, at close, on top
of a fuel cost it never touched.** The push row prints its own chapter's note
on each screen (*"Separate from the method's cost"* / *"the ritual's fuel"*).

**The third screen and the rotation path were verified afterwards, and the
rotation is the one that mattered.** `BoonDialog` got the same treatment and
had never been rendered — *"The prayer fails — 3d6: 13 vs 12"* became **"The
boon is granted — 3d6: 13 vs 13"** on a +1, with the title, the verdict and
the consequence block all re-derived, and SPI went 6 → 1 (4 fuel + 1 push). It
offered **only +1 and +2**, because 2 SPI was all the caster had left: the
pool bound `EffortBurn.affordable` applies reaches a third screen.

**Rotation settles.** With a ritual result on screen and +2 pushed but
uncharged, rotating to landscape and back destroys the activity and takes the
dialog's `remember` with it — and SPI came back 10 → 6, which is that ritual's
2 fuel plus the 2 pushed, charged exactly once through
`DisposableEffect { onDispose { settle() } }`. Without it those 2 were simply
lost, and so was the CoR a critical failure would have owed. **The stale-
capture worry does not bite**: the closure captures composition #1's callbacks,
and those are `BeyonderSession` methods on an object that outlives the
activity, not inline lambdas over dead state.

What is still unverified on a device: the divination backlash disappearing
when a push clears a critical failure, which needs a state a 3d6 roll reaches
rarely.

**And the device taught the scale lesson again.** The `+2` chip's `uiautomator`
bounds times 4/3 — the factor that is correct for the activity window — put the
tap 200px low, on nothing, three times in a row, which is indistinguishable
from a chip that does not respond. **The dialog window's factor is about
1.126**, and the way through is the one the memory already records: take the
coordinate off the SCREENCAP, never off the dump.

## 6dx. The refusal that never needed writing, and the citation that wrapped

6dw named three things. Two of them are this slice: **run the sweep it argued
for**, and **rule on `Shaken`**, which had been carried unchecked from 6dk
through 6dw — thirteen slices of "likely a refusal; nobody has looked".

### The sweep, in four shapes, clean

6dw's unit: *every composable gated on a state, checked for a block that does
not depend on that state.* Its own defect was a gear reference sitting below a
`return@Column`, so the instrument has to see more than one shape.

| shape | sites | finding |
|---|---|---|
| `return@` inside a composable | 4 | none — three partition post-roll from pre-roll correctly, the fourth is 6dw's own fix |
| `if (x != null) { }` whose body never names `x` | 9 reported | none — destructured lambda params and gate-as-affordance (`HubAction` gated on `ritualLevel`, which the dialog reads) |
| `if (x == null) { }` same test | 19 reported | none — every one is a picker branch, pre-roll by rule |
| `when (x) { }` same test | 17 scanned, 16 reported | **this shape cannot find anything by construction**: an exhaustive `when` names its subject in the BRANCH LABELS (`Pool.HP`), never in the bodies |
| bare `when { cond -> }` | 10, read by eye | none — the automated test above does NOT cover these, and they CAN carry 6dw's shape; every one is a value selector rather than a block placement |

Plus a census that is not this sweep and was worth one grep: eight sites guard
a roll button with `if (result != null) return@TextButton`, and
`DefenseDialog`, `DamageDialog` and `AttackDialog` appear in none of them. All
three are guarded another way — `AttackDialog` partitions on
`outcomes.isNotEmpty()` in a `when`, `DamageDialog` returns before the button
when `shock != null`, and the Acrobatic Dodge deliberately says **"Roll
again"** beside a Clear, which is a re-roll affordance and not a missing guard.

**The discriminator matters more than the query.** 6dw's defect was not "the
block does not name the state" — it was "and its purpose requires the other
state". Without the second clause every literal `Text(…)` in a gated branch is
a hit, which is what the 45 reported sites above are.

### `Shaken` is not a special case, and a query says so

Book line 8030, the Werewolf's Sequence 7 upgrade: *"on a successful hit, the
target must roll HT or be Shaken (see GURPS p. B360) for 1 turn."* Every
predecessor read this as a rule whose definition is in a book this one does not
reprint, and therefore as a refusal wanting a record of its own.

It is not. Its carrier is `reinforcedAbilities` prose, and
**`PotionDigestion.UNPARSED` already records that prose** — as a GAP, in the
KDoc's own words *"unbuilt work, and it must not be inherited as settled"*.
Filing an UNPAYABLE-standard refusal beside a GAP is a category error twice
over: it says the clause is settled, and it invites the next reader to treat
the prose around it the same way.

And the instance is not even distinctive. **Seven lines in this book defer to a
GURPS Basic Set rule it does not reprint** (2723; 3653-3654; 6553; 7348; 8030;
8059; 8062, whose clause opens at 8061). Two sit outside the ability prose, are
claimed by a content file, and have a verdict already:

- **2723** is `spirit_damage.json`'s threshold list, whose `HP ≤ 0` row points
  at rules chapter 5 prints for itself and `VitalRolls` applies (6de).
- **3653-3654** is `divination_methods.json`, and its specialisation technique
  is refused in `Divination.UNAPPLIED` (6cs).

Of the five inside it, **three name a term this book prints elsewhere and this
app models** — `grappled` (the Wrestling table, 6do) and `mentally Stunned`
twice (chapter 5's Major Wound row, `StunRecovery`) — **and TWO name a term
printed exactly once in the whole book: `Shaken`, and 7348's `suffocates`.** A
refusal filed against `Shaken` alone would have been a blocklist of one with
its twin a chapter away, which is the move CLAUDE.md's own rules forbid.

So what ships is a paragraph on the object that owns the prose, and two guards.

### What the review found, and it is the older lesson

`task --effort high`, scoped to three questions with *"do not read CLAUDE.md or
docs/SLICE-LOG.md"*. One HIGH and one MEDIUM, both taken.

**The HIGH: my census read one line at a time and the book wraps.** Line 3653
ends *"(see GURPS Techniques, p."* and 3654 opens *"B229)"*, so a `p\. B\d+`
search over single lines returns seven sites and drops that one **silently** —
6ba's rule, which this repo wrote down for claimed SPANS and had not applied to
a regex over lines. The scan now joins each line to the next and attributes a
match to the line it STARTS on. RED-proved by restoring the line-local version:
it returns the census with `3653` missing and `6553` in its place.

That correction is also what reconciles this slice with 6dr, whose hand census
listed `p. B229` and which my first query had quietly dropped: **the fixed
query reproduces the predecessor's membership exactly.**

**The MEDIUM: one of the four "names its effect inline" claims was weaker than
I wrote.** 8062 prints only *"stun rules, p. B420"* plus a Will recovery; the
term `mentally Stunned` is on 8061 and the `-4 to active defenses` gloss
belongs to 8059's separate clause. The discriminator moved off "does the
sentence gloss it" and onto **"does the book print this term anywhere else"**,
which is a query rather than a reading — and running it is what found
`suffocates`, the twin that killed the instance refusal.

### Guards

`test_the_gurps_deferrals_outside_the_ability_prose_are_all_ruled_on` pins the
eight-site census, the two outside claimants, and that the five inside really
are inside a Sequence block's prose.
`test_shaken_is_one_of_two_deferred_terms_the_book_prints_once` pins both
single printings and the case-insensitive count of three (*"shaken awake"*,
6521; *"damaged, shaken, or a loud noise"*, 8602), so a re-extraction that
turns either into the game term reddens rather than widening the reason in
silence. Three mutations, one at a time, restored from a copy: a second
printing of the term, the loss of a sibling's gloss, and the line-local scan.

**1691 Kotlin** unchanged and **347 Python** (from 345). Nothing renders, so
there is nothing to device-verify — stated rather than skipped.

### The next slice

- **A direction this slice earned: every census in this repo that scans book
  lines one at a time.** The wrap that hid `p. B229` is not specific to
  citations, and `coverage.py`'s filter, the `MECHANICAL` sweeps and every
  ad-hoc grep in these notes read one line at a time. One of them has already
  been shown to have false negatives twice (6db, 6di) without anyone looking at
  the line boundary.
- **The grapple-state surface** (6do) is still the biggest named thing, and
  still a milestone rather than a slice.
- Still unrun, inherited: catalogue → fixture, and extractor → `sourceLines`.

## 6dw. Reference after the dice, and the one-line early return that put it there

6dv's device pass found this and left it: `RollDialog`'s pre-roll state ends
with **`return@Column`**, so every block below it composed only once a result
existed. Three blocks sit there and only one was misplaced.

| Block | Belongs post-roll? |
|---|---|
| the burn row | **Yes.** "You may use this after seeing the result", and `EffortBurn.canPush` takes a non-null outcome |
| the conditional-burn note | **Yes**, same gate, so post-roll by construction |
| chapter 8's gear reference | **No.** It has no dependency on the outcome at all |

So the rows that name a skill reached the GM *after* the dice, when the one
thing they are for is choosing a modifier *before* them. It moves into the
pre-roll branch, after `CircumstanceRow`, and no longer renders post-roll —
which is the deliberate half of the change, not an oversight: the roll is
over, the reference can inform nothing, and leaving it there mainly invites
re-reading a modifier that can no longer be applied.

**The `return@Column` is not the defect and was left alone.** Removing it to
let the block stay at the bottom and render in both states is a ~40-line
indentation diff and a deeper nest for behaviour this screen does not need;
a local composable called from both branches is two call sites for a list
whose only purpose is pre-roll. Both were considered and are recorded here
rather than in a commit message.

**Below the chips, against the reviewer's preference.** The design review
called reference-before-picker "slightly stronger" and named the case for the
other side itself: these rows print numbers (`+1 to First Aid`), and a
numbered line directly above a row of tappable modifier chips reads as another
selectable one. This app has already returned NO-SHIP on a design that blurred
an applied chip into a shown reference (6cx), so that precedent breaks the tie
and the reviewer's own counter-case is what ships. Its other two answers were
taken as given: losing the post-roll appearance is acceptable, and the gear
list is the only block that return misplaces.

### Verified the only way it can be

**Nothing in this repo can assert a Compose label**, so the check is the
device and there is no test to write — which is exactly why the defect
survived from 6cx to now with `Equipment.referenceFor` wired to a caller the
whole time. Three cases on an SM-T570, all pre-roll:

- **`Savoir-Faire (High Society)`** (Fortune Teller) — `Gear that names this
  skill (not applied):` / `Fine clothes (quality) (£1 10s) — +1 to
  Savoir-Faire (High Society); status marker`. 6dv's own join, now visible
  when it is useful.
- **`Psychology`** — `Crystal ball (glass) (£2) — Fortune-telling prop; +1 to
  Fortune-Telling or Psychology`. A join that has existed since 6cx, so the
  fix is not specific to 6dv's rows.
- **`Occultism`** — no section at all, the null case.

And post-roll the same dialog prints the result with no gear line, which is
the change's other half confirmed rather than assumed.

**1691 Kotlin** and **345 Python**, unchanged: this slice adds no test,
because the only assertion available would restate the source.

### The next slice

- **`Shaken`** (line 8030), still unchecked, unchanged from 6dt through 6dv:
  whether one clause of one pathway ability deserves a recorded refusal when
  no pathway ability mechanic is modelled at all.
- **The grapple-state surface** (6do) — still the biggest named thing, still a
  milestone with its own decomposition rather than a slice.
- **A direction this slice argues for**: every composable gated on a state,
  checked for a block that does not depend on that state. This one was found
  by device verification of an unrelated rules fix, not by a sweep, and the
  sweep that would find the next one iterates `if` conditions in the app
  module rather than anything in `core:rules` — a unit no sweep here has ever
  taken.

## 6dv. The same predicate, taught on one side of the join

6du named a sweep with evidence: nine extractors read a content JSON they do
not write, and the question was which of them **DERIVE an output row** from it
rather than merely verify against it. Ten sites, and **nine are verify-only** —
`extract_appearance`, `extract_appendix`, `extract_blessings`,
`extract_common_modifiers`, `extract_core_rules`, `extract_defense_refusals`,
`extract_detection`, `extract_languages` and `extract_non_standard` all read a
sibling to assert something and never to build a row. That is the house style
and it stays.

The tenth is `extract_equipment.skill_index()`, whose return value goes into
`parse(tagged, index)` and decides the `skills` field on all 77 equipment
rows. And what it decided was wrong.

### Chapter 3 leaves two rows OPEN, and that is what makes an instance a match

| | |
|---|---|
| `Connoisseur` | printed once, `specialization: null`, `specializable: true`, *"Expert knowledge... in a specific field"* |
| `Savoir-Faire` | printed once, `specialization: null`, `specializable: true`, *"Social graces (specify class)"* |

Chapter 8 prices instances of both — *"+1 to Connoisseur (Books) when
appraising tomes"*, *"+1 to Savoir-Faire (High Society); status marker"*. The
join was a strict `(name, spec) in index`, so both read as skills chapter 3
never printed and both bonuses were dropped. **Four of 23 fixtures buy
Savoir-Faire and one buys exactly High Society**, so the Fortune Teller's own
roll was offered nothing.

**This is 6cz's defect on the WRITING side of the same join.** 6cz taught
`Equipment.forSkill` that an open row is matched by its instance — its
`isTemplate` reads `skills.json`'s `specializable` flag — and the extractor,
which reads the same flag from the same file, was never taught. Not "a finding
on the reader never run against the writer": it is **one predicate answered at
two sites**, which is this repo's own recorded defect shape, and it says what
to look for next — the two should agree by construction, not by both having
been edited. The flag is now the single source both read, and
`skill_index()` returns `{(name, spec): specializable}` so `key in index`
still answers the old question with the new fact beside it.

**The widening stops at the book's own line.** Navigation is printed three
times — bare, `(Sea)`, `(Land)` — and marked NOT specializable, so the list
enumerates its own instances and `Navigation (Air)` is a skill this book does
not have. `joins()` asks the catalogue, never the parenthesis.

### A committed test asserted the defect, quoting the fact that disproves it

`test_a_specialization_is_part_of_the_identity` has pinned

```python
# The two the book writes the same way and chapter 3 leaves open.
assert equipment_named("Rare book catalogue")["skills"] == []
assert equipment_named("Fine clothes (quality)")["skills"] == []
```

since 6cx. **"chapter 3 leaves open" is the template condition**, written into
the comment beside an assertion that the openness means no match. Another
instance of 6do's shape — a test encoding a reason, expiring with it — and the
inverse of this repo's usual "the tests knew and production did not".

### The guard that ran one way

`verify()` checked that no recorded exclusion RESOLVED, and never that every
unresolved target is RECORDED. So a new clause naming a skill under a spelling
chapter 3 does not print would be dropped in silence with `EXPECTED_ROWS`, the
`PINNED_JOINS` and `JOINED_CLAUSES` all green — 6dh's blind-side class, in an
extractor otherwise guarded to the teeth. `RECORDED_UNJOINED` closes it as one
set built from three: rolls the book never prints as skills (`spot`, `fool
officials`, `infection-resistance rolls`, `ritual effects`, and now
`reaction`, the Velvet shawl's), skills chapter 3 omits (`Forced Entry`,
`Gather Information`), and one it spells differently (`Fortune-Telling`).

**The hyphenation seam is recorded, not resolved.** Naming it in a set is what
lets the unresolved set be closed; the authority on the FACT stays the spelling
pair already asserted at the bottom of `verify()`, so there is one check on one
fact. Overturning that disagreement needs its own warrant and did not get one
here — no fixture carries `Fortune Telling` at all.

**The RED proof had to be an ADDITION, and the first attempt proved nothing.**
The failure mode is a new drop appearing, not an old one going away, so the
mutation appends a clause. The first one appended `+1 to Cryptography` — which
IS in chapter 3's list, so it resolved and the guard never spoke. **A mutation
has to land where the guard looks.**

### Reachability, checked in three corpora rather than one

- `Savoir-Faire (High Society)`: **live**. The Fortune Teller holds exactly
  that instance and now sees the row; the Barmaid (Servant), the Foreman
  (Worker) and the Librarian (Academic) correctly do not, which is the book's
  own scoping and is asserted per sheet.
- `Connoisseur (Books)`: correct, and **no carrier**. No fixture buys it, and
  **the builder cannot produce a specialized instance at all** — its picker
  passes `definition.specialization`, which is null for an open row, and prints
  *"needs a specialization"* beside it. A missing producer (6cf, 6dp), not a
  reachable row, and 6de's verdict died within the hour for claiming otherwise.

### The review, and the device

One LOW, taken, and it is the vacuity class again in a test written to be
careful about it: `ABSENT_FROM_CHAPTER_3 <= unresolved` is forced by the
equality two lines above, because `RECORDED_UNJOINED` is built from that set.
What the union cannot see is a name recorded in TWO of the three sets — two
records of one fact — so the assertion is now disjointness, RED-proved by
putting `Fortune-Telling` in both.

**Device-verified** on an SM-T570. The Fortune Teller's `Savoir-Faire (High
Society)` roll prints:

```
Gear that names this skill (not applied):
Fine clothes (quality) (£1 10s) — +1 to Savoir-Faire (High Society); status marker
```

### And the device found something the tests cannot

Getting that line on screen took four wrong hypotheses, and the answer is
**`MainActivity.kt:2195` — a `return@Column`** in `RollDialog`. Everything below
it composes only once a result exists: the burn row (deliberately, "you may use
this after seeing the result"), the conditional-burn note, and **the gear
reference**. So chapter 8's rows are shown to the GM *after* the dice, when the
one thing they are for is deciding a modifier *before* it. Recorded, not
repaired: moving the block changes the reading order of a screen and the early
return is load-bearing for the burn's own semantics, so it wants its own design
review. **A rule can be applied, tested, wired to a caller, and still be shown
at the wrong moment** — no test in this repo reaches a composable, and the
first three hypotheses (stale APK, a failed content load, a key mismatch) were
all disproved by one temporary `Log.w` that printed `rows=77 withSkills=34
ref=1` while the screen showed nothing.

**And the dump's scale is per WINDOW, which corrects yesterday's note.** 6du
recorded that a `uiautomator dump` reports this device's sheet in a 900x1440
space against a physical 1200x1920. True — and the DIALOG window is not the
same: the sheet's Roll button at dump `(848,549)` is tapped at `(1130,732)`,
a clean 4/3, while the dialog's Roll at dump `(787,1146)` is at roughly
`(1024,1356)` and the 4/3 point `(1049,1528)` lands on the scrim and dismisses
it. **One scale cannot drive both windows**, so a tap inside a dialog comes
from a screenshot and is confirmed by the state it produces, never by
arithmetic on the dump.

**1691 Kotlin** (+1) and **345 Python** (+4), no compile warnings.

### The next slice

- **The `return@Column` above.** It is the sharpest thing this slice found and
  it is a UI decomposition question, not a rules one: which of the three blocks
  below that return belong to the pre-roll state, and where does a reference
  list sit on a screen whose top half is the modifier picker.
- **`Shaken`** (line 8030), still unchecked, unchanged from 6dt and 6du.
- **The grapple-state surface** (6do), still the biggest named thing and still
  a milestone rather than a slice.
- The sibling-derivation sweep is **closed**: one derivation in ten, fixed, and
  the other nine recorded as verify-only so the direction does not need
  re-running.

## 6du. The one duration the table computes, and two sweeps that came back clean

6dt named four things and this builds the second. Before it, the sweep 6dt
left unrun was run in a sharper form than the one it describes, and it is the
larger half of what this slice is worth.

### The sweep: numbers, not words

6dt ran *lines a file CLAIMS whose WORDS appear nowhere in it* — 76 hits, no
defect, and recorded as a measurement of the instrument, because a cell storing
`+1` and a line reading "+1 to reaction rolls" share no word by construction.
The sharper query is the same shape over **numbers**: for every claimed line
`coverage.py` calls mechanical, do any of that line's mechanical tokens' digits
appear anywhere in the file claiming it? A rules line's number is exactly what
a content file would have had to store.

**26 hits across 7 files, and 18 of them were the instrument.** Three content
files share one span (`languages.json`, `language_proficiency.json`,
`language_notes.json` are written from one `source` variable), so each was
being asked to hold its siblings' numbers. Unioning the files that claim a line
before comparing drops it to **8, in 5 files** — and all 8 are accounted for:

- **`3559-3560`, `3580`, `4028`** — the cross-skill default and the two
  support-skill caps. Each lives in Kotlin (`Divination.CROSS_DEFAULT_PENALTY`,
  `CROSS_DEFAULT_THRESHOLD`, and the two `supportBonus` ceilings), pinned
  against the book in Python by `verify_cross_default`. 6dt chased the two caps
  to the end already.
- **`4087`, `4090`** — the Effect Weight table's FIRST printing, inside
  `ritual_success.json`'s span. `ritual_weights.json` claims the second
  printing (4318-4345) and the numbers agree; `verify_step_four` records why
  only the success half of Step 4's table is adopted.
- **`4104`** — "1 SPI = +1 ... There is no cap", which is chapter 2's universal
  burn. `effort_burn.json` holds it, and `EffortBurn`'s KDoc records that this
  chapter is one of the two agreeing printings that let the general form ship.
- **`2231`** — a worked example.

So the sweep is clean, and it discriminates: 8 hits out of roughly two thousand
claimed mechanical lines, against 76 for the word version.

### The inverse direction, which had not been run either

*Numbers a content file STORES that appear nowhere in the span it claims* — a
fabrication check rather than a coverage one. Six files, and five are the
instrument again (`pathways.json` and `non_standard_pathways.json` store each
block's own line numbers as fields; three `0`s are defaults).

The sixth is worth writing down and is **not a defect**: `spirit_vision.json`
stores two grants at Sequence 8 (Mother, Red Priest) and its span is chapter
7.6's alone. Those two rows never came from 7.6 — 6dh's whole finding was that
section C is wrong in both directions, so `grants()` reads each pathway's OWN
block out of `pathways.json` instead. The provenance is one hop away and
`pathways.json` claims those lines, so no coverage number moves.
**`sourceLines` says "which source lines it consumed", and a file deriving rows
from a sibling content file consumes lines it cannot name.** Recorded, not
repaired: naming chapter 9-12 spans there would double-claim lines another file
already owns.

### The slice: row 12

| Band | Fright | Awe | Confusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4-9 | Stunned **1 sec** | Stunned 1 sec | Stunned 1 sec |
| 10-11 | Stunned **1d-2d sec** | Stunned 1d-2d sec | Stunned 1d-2d sec |
| 12 | Retching for **(25 − HT)** sec | Ecstasy for **(25 − Will)** sec | Dazed for **(25 − IQ)** sec |

6ds structured the recovery ROLL of those three bands and left the duration in
prose. The dialog printed the cell verbatim, so a player read the parenthetical
and did the subtraction by hand.

**The boundary is the table's own, not a list of the cases I wanted.** A
duration with a STAT OPERAND is the only kind this app can work out: "1 sec" is
already resolved in the cell, and "1d-2d sec" is a range the GM rolls. That
came out of the design review, along with the field name — `frightDuration`
would read as "the table's duration is structured" when eight of nine bands
answer null, so the fields are `frightComputedDuration` and its two siblings
and the type is `ComputedDuration`. **A name is where a scope decision either
survives or gets misread.**

**The operand is not the attribute the same cell ROLLS**, which is the whole
reason this could not ride on `FrightRecovery`: the fright cell counts down
from HT and rolls Will. So `DurationAttribute` is a third member wider than
`RecoveryAttribute` — HT is named by no recovery roll in the table, and
widening the existing enum would have put a value in `FrightCheck.levelFor`'s
exhaustive `when` that no recovery can ever take. The extractor anchors on the
printed parenthetical (6do's rule, applied before the bad parse rather than
after it), and `verify()` **fails the day the two anchors answer alike** — that
disagreement exists in exactly one cell of the nine, and it is the only
evidence they did not collapse.

Both extractor guards were RED-proved separately, and the second proof is the
one that mattered: the first mutation (the duration reading the recovery's
phrase) was caught by the BAND-set check before the attribute check could
speak, so the equality guard was still unproved. A second mutation that keeps
the band set at `['12']` and only flips the attribute is what fired it.
**A guard caught by its neighbour is a guard not yet proved.**

### The floor is this app's

`25 − HT` runs negative above HT 25 and the book prints none. Zero ships,
because a negative duration is not a duration — and the screen prints the
subtraction beside the answer (`0 sec (25 − HT 27)`), so the reading is visible
rather than swallowed. `FrightCheck.durationLine` composes that sentence in the
rules object for `Divination.sourceLine`'s reason: the screen would otherwise
need the attribute's NAME and its LEVEL, which is the attribute-to-level
mapping asked a second time somewhere no test can reach it.

### The reviews

The design review ran before any code, took all three questions, and answered
them the way this ships — correcting the field name and asking for the clamp's
working to stay on screen. The diff review returned **no findings** on its own
terms: no vacuous assertion, and it named the production edit that fails each
of the eight new tests. Its one design opinion — that `durationLine` is
presentation copy and a `durationBreakdown` struct would be the better boundary
— is refused as an abstraction with one consumer, and it said itself it would
not block.

**1690 Kotlin** (+7) and **341 Python** (+4), no compile warnings.

### Device-verified, all three columns

On an SM-T570, Church Healer (HT 9, Will 11, IQ 11), driven through the real
dialog until the effect roll landed on 12:

| Column | The cell | The line the app adds |
|---|---|---|
| fright | `Retching for (25 − HT) sec; roll vs. Will to recover.` | `16 sec (25 − HT 9)`, over `Roll WILL 11 to recover now` |
| awe | `Ecstasy for (25 − Will) sec; roll vs. Will to recover.` | `14 sec (25 − Will 11)` |
| confusion | `Dazed for (25 − IQ) sec; roll vs. IQ to recover.` | `14 sec (25 − IQ 11)`, over `Roll IQ 11 to recover now` |

The fright row is the one worth having on a screenshot: **sixteen seconds off
HT beside a recovery roll against Will**, on one cell. Band 4-9 came up during
the runs (`Stunned 1 sec`) and printed no duration line, which is the null
case.

**Getting there cost more than the slice did, and two things are worth
keeping.** Band 12 is a single value on a 3d6-plus-margin table, so it cannot
be navigated to — at a target of 7 the chance per attempt is
`Σ P(3d6 = 7+m)·P(3d6 = 12−m) = 3195/46656`, about 6.9%, and it took 5, 10
and 1 attempts for the three columns. And **the taps have to come from
screencap, not from the dump**: `uiautomator dump` reports this device's sheet
in a 900x1440 space against a physical 1200x1920, and deriving the scale from
the largest node in the dump gives `(1.386, 1.576)` when a dialog is up,
because no node spans the window then. That put one tap 400 px low, onto the
scrim, which dismissed the dialog — **indistinguishable from the control not
responding**, and it cost about twenty minutes of a loop that looked like it
was working. Screencap pixels are physical; four fixed coordinates read off a
screenshot drove 30 attempts without a miss, and one shell round trip per
attempt (four taps and the dump in a single `adb shell`) took it from ~75 s to
6 s.

### Three follow-ups the reviews were never asked for

The new `init` require on `FrightEffect` was **the slice's one unproved
branch** — every other guard had a mutation behind it — and neutering it is
its RED proof. The extractor's 0-or-3 check was reading the FRIGHT column
alone, so a parse emitting two of three durations passed it and then hit
`TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` three lines later; the
shape check runs over both field families in one loop now, and both halves
were RED-proved (without the loop the parse `TypeError`s; with it, the band
names the columns it dropped). And `docs/HOW-TO-PLAY.md` was **a slice behind
before this one touched it** — it never got 6ds's recovery roll either, so
the guide CLAUDE.md calls "verified against the labels in source" had been
describing a two-line screen for two slices. **A doc's staleness is not
reported by the slice that caused it.**

### And the heredoc ate an escape again

Writing the new regex through a Python heredoc produced
`re.compile(r"\((\d+)\s*[" + MINUS + "–—]\s*([A-Za-z]+)\)")` — the second
fragment is not raw, so `\s` and `\)` are unknown escapes. **This time it was
visible**: Python printed `SyntaxWarning: invalid escape sequence` on import,
where 6ds's `\b` became a backspace byte in silence. Same class as the
`sed a/i/c` rule; the pattern was checked with `repr()` before anything read
it, and both mutation restores were verified by reading the diff's REMOVED
lines rather than by re-running the suite.

### The next slice

- **`Shaken`** (line 8030) is still unchecked, unchanged from 6dt: whether one
  clause of one pathway ability deserves a recorded refusal when no pathway
  ability mechanic is modelled at all.
- **The grapple-state surface** (6do) is still the biggest named thing, and it
  is a milestone with its own decomposition rather than a slice.
- **A sweep direction now named with evidence**: `spirit_vision.json` is not
  the only content file whose rows may be derived from a SIBLING content file
  rather than from the book — `extract_appearance`, `extract_appendix`,
  `extract_common_modifiers`, `extract_core_rules`, `extract_defense_refusals`,
  `extract_detection`, `extract_equipment`, `extract_languages` and
  `extract_non_standard` all read a JSON they do not write. Most only VERIFY
  against it, which is the house style; the question is which of them DERIVE an
  output row from it, because that is the case where `sourceLines` cannot name
  what was consumed and where a stale sibling changes an answer in silence
  (6dk: a failing extractor never rewrites its JSON).

## 6dt. The row printed directly below the one that was applied

Three sweeps ran this slice and two returned nothing. The third found a trait
that **quotes the HP table's own words back at it** and reached nothing, in the
object built one slice ago to distinguish exactly the roll it names.

| | |
|---|---|
| `Hard to Kill` | 2 pts/level, *"+1/level to HT rolls **to avoid death**; 1-5 levels"* — applied since 6de |
| `Hard to Subdue` | 2 pts/level, *"+1/level **to remain conscious** when reduced to 0 or negative HP"* — reached nothing |

Adjacent rows, same price, same shape, and between them they partition the two
rolls chapter 5's HP table prints. The `0 HP` row reads *"Roll 3d6 ≤ HT or fall
unconscious; **roll each turn to remain conscious**"* — the second trait's cell
is not an inference from that row, it is a quotation of it.

### Why every sweep was blind to it

`VitalRolls`' own KDoc said *"Three traits name an HT roll and they do not
agree on which"* and enumerated Fit / Very Fit / Unfit, Hard to Kill, High Pain
Threshold. There were four, and the fourth's cell **never contains the words
"HT roll"**. Every census that would have found it filtered on that phrase —
including 6de's, which was written specifically to sort the traits that name
these two rolls.

That is 6bu's finding on a fourth mechanic: **a roll the book NAMES rather than
describes.** A Fright Check, a morale roll, a death roll, a knockdown roll —
and now "remain conscious". The census test guarding that class searches for
those four literal strings, and this cell contains none of them.

### The second gap, which cancelled the first

Found alongside it, and only because the sweep's own instrument was checked
before its output was read: **`TraitEffects.known()` omitted two traits it
applies.** That function says in its KDoc it is *"every trait this object knows
about, applied or not"*, and it is what the catalogue guard uses as its handled
set. It is built out of the collections — and `Hard to Kill` and `High Pain
Threshold` are applied by single-trait functions belonging to no collection.
Both return non-zero, both `reported()` empty, both absent.

**The two gaps cancel, which is why nothing ever went red.** The census filter
cannot see the phrasing `High Pain Threshold` uses ("HT rolls to avoid
knockdown" against a filter looking for "knockdown roll"), and if the filter
were widened the handled set would report a correctly-applied trait as dropped.
Either gap alone produces a wrong answer; together they produce silence.

`known()`'s KDoc already records this same failure **twice** — Outdoorsman,
then the HT-roll map — and both fixes were "add the collection". These three
had none, so the declaration IS the collection now: `BespokeBonus` is a private
enum whose entries carry the trait name and an optional flat value, each bonus
function reads its own entry, and `known()` reads the enum. **A fourth bespoke
bonus cannot be written without an entry**, which is what stops a fourth
instance.

### The scope, and the clause that names its own condition

`Hard to Subdue` reaches `CONSCIOUSNESS` and not `SURVIVAL`, and the
interesting part is that it names *"0 **or negative** HP"* — where both checks
are due, because `Pools` sets both flags below `-HP` and the dying row does not
withdraw the consciousness roll above it. **Two rolls falling in one moment
does not merge their scopes**: the survival row's own words are "or die", and
widening a clause that names its own condition is 6ck's refused move. The
design review took the same reading and named the case against it.

No cap, because its cell prints none where its sibling's prints "1-5 levels" —
a ceiling here would be app-authored (4.1).

### Three sweeps, two clean, and what that is worth

- **Every content span against its chapter's own bounds**: 81 files, all
  inside. Clean.
- **Lines a file CLAIMS whose words appear nowhere in it**: 76 hits and no
  defect. The instrument is too blunt — a cell storing `+1` and a line reading
  "+1 to reaction rolls" share no word by construction — so this is a
  measurement of the instrument, not a bill of health. Two candidates were
  chased to the end anyway: the two support-skill caps (`+2` for divination,
  `+3` for rituals) are each correct against their own printing, and both
  dedupe.
- **Catalogue rows with a signed clause reaching nothing**: the one that paid.

### The review

One LOW, taken, and it is the vacuity class in a test written to be careful
about exactly that. My "no cap" guard asserted the catalogue text lacks the
word "levels" — **a claim about the data**, which a mistaken cap of 5 in
production satisfies along with every level below it. It asserts `Hard to
Subdue 6` gives +6 now, above the sibling's ceiling, and that is RED-proved by
capping the registry at 5.

Two other mutations RED-proved the slice: widening the clause to reach
`SURVIVAL` fails 1, emptying the registry's contribution to `known()` fails 1.

**And the restore from that second mutation corrupted an unrelated line.** I
patched `emptyList()` back with a first-occurrence replace and hit a different
function 600 lines up. CLAUDE.md's own rule — `cp` the file first, restore from
the copy — written down and not followed, in the same session that wrote a
memory about a related hazard. The repair was checked by reading the diff's
REMOVED lines rather than by re-running the suite, because the suite was green
under the corruption.

**1683 Kotlin** (+3) and **337 Python**, no compile warnings. Test-only on the
UI side: a Hard to Subdue carrier's consciousness-roll target and its "from
traits" line move, and nothing else does — checked against every caller of
`VitalRolls.bonusFor`.

### The next slice

- **`Shaken`** (line 8030) is still unchecked, and the earlier assumption about
  it is already dead: I expected the book to quote its GURPS deferrals inline
  and it does that in **one of six** places (the B420 stun, twice). So the
  contrast that would have justified a refusal does not exist, and the honest
  question is narrower — whether one clause of one pathway ability deserves a
  recorded refusal when no pathway ability mechanic is modelled at all.
- **Row 12's computed durations** (6ds), which need the duration parsed as
  structure.
- **The grapple-state surface** (6do) is still the biggest named thing.
- Still unrun: extractor → `sourceLines` in its sharp form (does each
  extractor's declared RANGE match what it parses, rather than what it claims).

## 6ds. Nine cells, and the attribute belongs to the column

6dr left this as a stated gap with its blocker named: the Fright Effects table
prints a recovery roll nine times, the attribute is carried in prose, and
structuring prose is the extractor's job. This builds it.

| band | Fright | Awe | Confusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4-9 | Stunned, **Will** | Stunned, **Will** | Stunned, **IQ** |
| 10-11 | Stunned, Will | Stunned, Will | Stunned, IQ |
| 12 | Retching, Will | Ecstasy, Will | Dazed, IQ |

The other six bands print an outcome and no way out of it — a quirk, a
disadvantage, a permanent loss — so nothing is offered there. **Offering a roll
where the table prints none would be granting a way back the book withholds**,
which is the same class as offering a defence it does not grant.

### The anchor was the whole parsing problem

The obvious parse is to find an attribute name in the cell. Row 12 is where
that dies, and it dies twice in one row:

> **Retching for (25 − HT) sec; roll vs. Will to recover.**
> Ecstasy for (25 − **Will**) sec; roll vs. **Will** to recover.

The fright cell names HT and rolls Will. The awe cell prints `Will` twice in
two different roles. So the anchor is the cell's own `roll vs. X` — 6do's rule
that a candidate anchor colliding with another column's values is not an
anchor, applied before the bad parse rather than after it. **Mutation-proved**:
swapping the regex for a bare attribute search reddens the anchor test, and the
mutation was verified to have landed before the result was read (6db's rule
that a mutation reporting success is not a mutation that happened).

A third case is neither of the two: a cell that says `roll vs.` and then
something this book does not roll. That **raises** rather than returning None —
silently treating it as "no recovery here" would turn a drifted parse into a
row the screen quietly never offers.

### The state is the book's word, decoded not matched

Combat Reflexes' "+6 to recover from stun" reaches rows 4-9 and 10-11 and none
of row 12. The discriminator could have been a boolean from the extractor, and
the design review rejected that: it would make the extractor decide what a stun
IS rather than structure what the cell printed. So the state ships as a decoded
enum — `STUNNED`, `RETCHING`, `ECSTASY`, `DAZED` — and `StunRecovery.isStun`
answers, because that object already holds which Major Wound row is the stun
and **two sites deciding what a stun is would be the defect** (6cr).

### The Will clauses, and a gap that is the book's

The recovery roll is a bare Will roll a second after the check in two columns
of three, so the clauses 6df wired to bare Will rolls reach it — but the rows
scoped to the Fright Check itself do not, because that check is over. The
Confusion column gets nothing, and **that is a gap rather than a choice**: this
book prints no trait clause naming IQ rolls, so there is no list to offer.
Recorded in `FrightCheck.takesWillClauses`' KDoc, where a sweep finds it.

### The review found the same defect in last slice's panel

Three findings, all taken. The sharpest is one **6dr shipped and this slice
copied**: both panels stored a `RollResult` and then re-judged it against a
RECOMPUTED target, so a clause chip or a tracker moving under an open dialog
reprints an old roll against a number it never faced. `RollResult` carries its
own `target` and `outcome`; both panels use them now, and `Outcome.isSuccess`
replaces a two-branch comparison three sites were making. **A finding on new
code is a finding on the code it was modelled on** — worth running backwards
one slice, every time.

The second was mine at two call sites: `attribute == "IQ"` decided the number
AND which clause list applied, with every non-IQ silently read as Will. The
attribute is a typed enum now and both questions are answered once, in
`FrightCheck`.

The third was a **data-shape assertion** in my own test — `twelve.fright
.contains("HT")`, which restates the book instead of exercising production, and
whose real guard is the extractor's mutation-proved anchor test. Deleted, and
what replaced it asserts the number a screen would roll against.

### What shipped

- `extract_fright.py`: `recovery_of`, the anchor, and two `verify()` guards —
  a band offers a way out in all three columns or none, and exactly three
  bands do.
- `FrightRecovery` + `RecoveryState` + `RecoveryAttribute` in the content
  model; `FrightCheck.recoveryFor` / `.recoveryBonus` / `.levelFor` /
  `.takesWillClauses`; `StunRecovery.isStun`.
- `FrightDialog` takes `iq`, the Will-only clause list and the resolved stun
  bonus; `FrightRecoveryPanel` renders one roll, keyed on the check (6cp).
- **1680 Kotlin** (+7) and **337 Python** (+4), no compile warnings. **Not
  device-verified.**

### An editing hazard worth the line

Writing a regex through a Python heredoc's replacement string **ate `\b` as a
backspace byte**: the pattern still compiled, matched nothing, and the
extractor reported no recovery rows at all. Exit 0, no error. Same class as
this repo's `sed a/i/c` rule — a payload reparsed as program text — and the
tell was a `search()` returning None on a string that plainly contains the
phrase. Verify a written pattern by printing `repr()` of the line, not by
re-reading it through a tool that renders control characters invisibly.

### The next slice

- **`Shaken`** (line 8030) is the last GURPS deferral with no verdict.
- **Row 12's computed durations** — "(25 − HT)", "(25 − Will)", "(25 − IQ)" —
  are deliberately unread, and the design review's own case against that is
  worth keeping: two of the three subtract an attribute the column does not
  roll, which is exactly the sort of thing a player misreads. Printing them
  needs the duration parsed as structure and `ht` threaded, and it is a
  separate slice.
- **The grapple-state surface** (6do) is still the biggest named thing.
- Still unrun: catalogue → fixture, and extractor → `sourceLines`.

## 6dr. The roll a refusal said did not exist

6dq's finding was a refusal whose SUBJECT was wrong. This one is the harder
version: a refusal whose subject was right, whose reason was a claim about the
app, and whose claim was **false when it was written down and false every day
since**.

`TraitEffects.PARTLY_APPLIED` reported Combat Reflexes' printed clause:

> **+6 to recover from stun** — *not applied here: this app models no stun
> recovery roll to make.*

The Major Wound table's Failure row is

> Stunned for 1d6 seconds (**roll HT each turn to recover early**)

and `DamageDialog`'s `MajorWoundPanel` has rendered that sentence since 6n.
**Military Police carries Combat Reflexes.** So a GM who rolled a Major Wound,
failed it, and read the row telling them to roll HT was looking at a screen
that also told them the trait moving that roll did nothing.

### The sweep that found it, and the one it started as

The direction was **every place the book explicitly defers to a rule it does
not reprint** — a census this repo had not run, with one instance already
recorded by accident (`Divination.UNAPPLIED`'s GURPS technique, 6cs). Six
sites: `p. B360` (Shaken), `p. B420` twice, `p. B229`, "per GURPS grappling
rules", "per normal GURPS rules" (suffocation), plus `HP ≤ 0: Standard GURPS
death/dying rules`.

**The census found nothing and the walk to it found this.** Both `B420` lines
quote the effect inline, and one of them prints a recovery roll — which sent
the query back into chapter 5, where the same roll is printed in a table this
app extracts, loads and displays. The GURPS-deferral census remains a real
direction with a real yield of zero: every one of the six is prose in a block
whose surrounding rules are already claimed, and none reaches a control.

### Five printings, and the attribute is never the stun's

| where | attribute |
|---|---|
| Major Wound, Failure row (p. 42) | **HT** |
| Fright Effects 4-9 and 10-11, Fright column | Will |
| the same rows, Awe column | Will |
| the same rows, Confusion column | **IQ** |
| Interrogator, Psychic Piercing (p. 128) | HT |
| Interrogator, Whip of Pain (p. 128) | **Will** |

The last two are the same book, the same page, the same ability block and the
same GURPS citation, disagreeing about which attribute recovers from the stun
they both inflict. **Recorded, never repaired.** What it settles is the design
question: *recover from stun* is not one roll, and any object answering for all
of them would have to take the attribute from the source.

That is why `StunRecovery` answers for **one** of the six and says so. Its
`bonusFor` composes `TraitEffects.htRollBonus` unconditionally — correct only
because this row's roll is HT — and **a KDoc saying so cannot fail**, so the
claim is read off the row itself in the test that pins the composition. The
fright rows are a **GAP, not a refusal**: their recovery attribute is in prose,
and structuring prose is the extractor's job (6dh), which is a slice of its own.

### The scope is two clauses, one each way

- **Combat Reflexes reaches this roll and not the table's own.** "+6 to recover
  from stun" names the CONDITION and no attribute — so it would reach the Will
  and IQ rolls too, if they were offered.
- **High Pain Threshold reaches the table's roll and not this one.** "+3 on **HT
  rolls** to avoid knockdown" names both, and the fail-by-5 row is a knockdown;
  recovering from the stun one row above avoids no knockdown, so widening it is
  6ck's refused move.

The two scopes crossing is why the credit is a second function rather than
`majorWoundHt` with a flag — a flag would be one predicate answering two
questions.

### Two committed tests asserted the expired reason

Second instance of 6do's shape in three slices, and this time the tests said
so in their own comments — *"which is the roll this app has no clock for"* and
*"What is left is the RECOVERY roll, which needs a clock"*. Both were rewritten
to assert the OPPOSITE, which is what they were actually for:
`ActiveDefensesTest`'s seam test exists to catch a GM being told a trait does
nothing on a screen that applies it, and it was enforcing exactly that defect
in the other direction.

**Its own reason was half right and that half survives.** The clock refusal
holds for the DURATION: `Rapid Recovery`'s "Stun durations halved" stays
refused, one roll is offered rather than one a turn, and the button reads
**"Roll HT n to recover now"** — 6cn's rule that an unnamed label gets picked by
whoever writes the screen, and a bare "Recover" would promise a rule the book
does not print.

### The review

Design review before any code: approved the shape, narrowed it twice (row 12 of
the fright table — Retching / Ecstasy / Dazed — is a different state and out of
Combat Reflexes' scope; the control must be GM-gated in its wording). Diff
review returned a **MEDIUM and a LOW, both taken**:

- **The recovery roll omitted an active shock.** `Shock.appliesTo` refuses only
  `MAJOR_WOUND_HT` — because that roll CREATES the shock — and reaches every
  other kind, so a character already shocked from an earlier wound should
  recover at -4. `DamageDialog` took only the Major Wound's `hurt`. The fix is
  a separate parameter, never folded into `hurt`, because the two rolls answer
  differently. `shockOnAttribute` already existed at the call site.
- **A KDoc is not a guard** — the LOW above, and its fix is the test that reads
  the row.

Q1 came back with **no vacuous assertion**, which is worth stating as the
weaker claim it is: the reviewer named one weak pin (the credit compared
against `bonusFor`, so a shared wrong `bonusFor` satisfies both) and that is
the honest ceiling on it.

`recovery` is `remember(shock)` — keyed on the wound roll rather than cleared
at the five sites that clear it, because adding a sixth line to each is how one
gets missed (6cp: the key IS the guard).

Both mutations RED-proved: the row name `Failure` → `Success` fails 2, dropping
`htRollBonus` from the composition fails 1. **1673 Kotlin** (+8) and **333
Python**, no compile warnings (6dl). **Not device-verified** — read this as
compiles, unit-tested, not rendered.

### The next slice

- **The Fright Effects table's own recovery rolls**, with the blocker stated:

  in prose. `extract_fright.py` must emit the attribute as structure before any
  engine reads it, and `FrightDialog` takes `will` and would need `iq`. Combat
  Reflexes reaches all of them on the warrant already argued here.
- **`Shaken`** (line 8030) is still unchecked and is now the last GURPS
  deferral with no verdict — one occurrence, and the book never prints what it
  does.
- **The grapple-state surface** (6do) is still the biggest named thing.
- Still unrun: catalogue → fixture, and extractor → `sourceLines`.

## 6dq. A refusal recorded against the summary, not the rule

Chapter 4 was the smallest thing left with anything in it — **80.0%, two
unclaimed mechanical lines** — and the finding is not the count. It is the
SUBJECT of a refusal that has been correct the whole time.

### The two lines

| line | what it is |
|---|---|
| 2309-2310 | Spirit Vision priced a second time: *"Cost: 1 SPI per minute."* |
| 2339-2341 | Spirituality Recovery: 1 SPI per hour of rest |

Neither is a gap. What made the second worth a slice is where its reason
lived.

### The refusal named the quick-reference table

`Study.kt`'s KDoc explains why a downtime planner is stateless, and cites two
siblings on the way past:

> this app holds no clock — the reason **Appendix A's SPI recovery** (6ad) and
> a technique's duration (6ah) are both unmodelled.

Appendix A is the SUMMARY. Its row (9718-9724) is three cells — `Rest` /
`1 SPI per hour` / `No strenuous physical or spiritual activity`. The rule is
printed at p. 34, and it carries two clauses that row drops:

> A character who rests … recovers 1 SPI per hour. **This is the standard and
> only recovery rate.** Combat, ritual casting, or heavy physical exertion
> **interrupts rest and halts recovery.**

So the recorded reason named a printing that says less than the one that
governs, and never mentioned the chapter at all. **Claim status was never the
same question as which printing governs (6dl), and neither is being handy to
quote.** This is 6cj on top of it: the reason was a parenthetical in an object
about downtime STUDY, so a sweep for what `Pools` refuses could not find it —
and `Pools` is the object that owns `spi()`.

The reason itself never expired. Only its subject and its address were wrong,
which is the half of a refusal nothing ever re-reads.

### The exclusivity clause is not enforceable and says so

*"the standard and only recovery rate"* is contradicted in the letter by a
printed pathway ability: p. 88's Sequence 9 Bard picks one Singing buff and
option (d) is *"Spiritual Recovery — allies recover 1 SPI at the song's
end"*, doubled at p. 100. **The reading that ships is specific-beats-general,
and it is recorded AS this repo's reading rather than as the book's** — the
design review's call, and the diff review then caught the first draft
asserting it as fact. The book states no priority between them. Nothing turns
on it while both are unmodelled, and the parenthetical *"(Bard cannot benefit
from this effect)"* is the evidence the ability's scope is deliberate.

### What a content file would have cost

The obvious way to close chapter 4 is an `spi_recovery.json`. **It is the
defect 6dg found and 6dh closed** — data no Kotlin loads, and this repo has
exactly one measurement of what that produces (a chapter reporting 100% off a
file nothing read). So the refusal is Kotlin, the pins are Python, and
**chapter 4 stays at 80.0%.** That is the third measurement of claiming being
orthogonal to the percentage (6di, 6dk), and the first where the honest move
was to claim nothing at all.

### What shipped

- `Pools.UNMODELLED`, one entry, at the `Equipment.UNMODELLED` /
  `ActiveDefenses.UNPAYABLE` / `Divination.UNAPPLIED` standard, with the
  book's sentence, the reason, and the Bard exception inside it.
- `Study.kt`'s parenthetical corrected to name ch. 4 and point at it.
- `SpiritVision`'s KDoc: ch. 4 prices it a second time and **says strictly
  less** — no activation charge — so 7.6 governs and the dialog's price is
  undisputed. 6da's bar, applied to a line rather than to a modifier.
- Three Python pins, each RED-proved by mutating its line in `lines.json`.
  **No Kotlin test**: a census over a one-entry map written in the same
  commit asserts the compiler compiled a string. The design review named that
  before it was written, which is cheaper than the eleven this repo shipped
  and had a reviewer find.
- **1665 Kotlin** (unchanged) and **333 Python** (+3). No compile warnings
  (6dl).

  GURPS p. B360) for 1 turn"*, on the Werewolf's improvised-weapon upgrade.

## 6dp. The constant the summary box could not see

Chapter 3 was the largest block left — **56 unclaimed mechanical lines at
87.9%** — and 6cy's warning held: read one at a time, all 56 are accounted for.

| lines | what they are |
|---|---|
| 475-501 | the attribute cost ladder, 10/20/40/80/160 per rung — `AttributeCosts` computes it, so it reads unclaimed forever (6cy) |
| 508-525 | the p.11 Character Creation budget table |
| 456, 1120-1122 | the -40 disadvantage cap and the quirk allowance |
| 1577-1579 | the skill point ladder in prose; `skill_ladder.json` claims the table at 1580-1658 |
| 2206-2230 | the STUDY points ladder, **compared cell by cell rather than inherited** — see below |
| 2238-2244 | the Character Creation Summary box |
| 505-506 | how much SPI a pathway grants, prose |

**That is the third chapter this session whose unclaimed count is a coverage
proxy rather than a gap** (7's `PowerSources` constants, 9's reading
instructions, and now 3's ladders). What the sweep found instead was in the
guard that reads the last row of that table.

### The one restatement that was checked instead of believed

Line 2204 says study points *"follow the same exponential ladder as normal
character points"* — which is **the book asserting its two printings agree, not
a comparison of them**, and three findings this session were exactly a summary
saying something true about itself while disagreeing with the table it
summarised (6dl's Major Wound, 6dn's nine costs, 6do's damage cell). So the
grid at 2211-2230 is compared with `skill_ladder.json` cell by cell: four
cumulative CP values against four difficulties, **16 of 16 agree**. That
comparison is a test now rather than a sentence, RED-proved by drifting Hard's
2-CP offset from -1 to 0.

### One of three constants had no tie to a printed line

`GoldenStudyPointsTest` has carried a test since 6v — *"the Character Creation
Summary agrees with the constants it summarises"* — pinning
`PointBudget.STARTING_TOTAL` and `MAX_DISADVANTAGES` against the summary box's
bullets. **`MAX_QUIRKS` is not in it**, and the reason is 6dn's shape a second
time in three slices: the box prints *"Disadvantages: 0 to -40 pts maximum"*
and says nothing about quirks at all, so the guard's corpus excluded the one
constant it could not see. A grep confirms it: `MAX_QUIRKS` was asserted
nowhere in 1665 tests.

Its printing wraps across lines 1121-1122:

> Up to 5 **additional** points of quirks (minor personality traits at -1 pt
> each) are allowed.

**`additional` is the load-bearing word.** It is what makes
`70 + min(dis, 40) + min(quirks, 5)` right rather than quirks coming out of the
-40 — and I read the paragraph the other way first, on line 1120 alone, before
1121 settled it. That is the assertion whose failure mode is real, so it is
pinned in `test_tools.py`, which can read the book, and the Kotlin constant is
asserted inside the EXISTING guard rather than a new one beside it (the same
predicate at two sites is the defect).

The second assertion is the finding itself made checkable: the summary box
contains `40` and does not contain `quirk`. A corpus that cannot see a constant
is a fact about the corpus, and now it reddens if the box ever gains the row.

### What the quirk term actually is

Nothing this app ships produces one. Checked against three corpora rather than
one, because 6de's reachability verdict failed within the hour for naming a
single one:

- no Kotlin under any `src/main` constructs `TraitKind.QUIRK` — the enum has
  one reader, `PointBudget`, and no producer;
- none of the 23 fixtures carries a trait of that kind;
- no row of `disadvantages.json` costs 1, so `PurchasableTraits` cannot offer
  one either.

`extract_sheets.py` reads the sheets' own block named **"DISADVANTAGES AND
QUIRKS"** and files all of it as `DISADVANTAGE` — a block NAME, not evidence a
sheet holds a quirk; none does, and the two lists were checked rather than
inferred from the heading.

**And the consequence is smaller than it looks, which is worth saying rather
than dressing up.** A quirk filed as a disadvantage credits the same point
unless the character is at the -40 cap, and no fixture is within five points of
it. So this is a producer that does not exist, not a miscount — the 6cf class,
not a defect.

The review corrected the word: the first draft called the term **unreachable**,
and `report` takes any `List<Trait>`, so a caller or a deserialized character
can hand it a quirk and the branch answers correctly. *No producer in the
bundled corpus* is the true claim; unreachable is not. The term stays for that
reason — the book prints the rule and the engine answers it.

### What shipped

- `PointBudget`'s KDoc: the printing, the word `additional`, the three corpora
  and what each was checked against.
- `MAX_QUIRKS` asserted in the existing Kotlin guard, renamed to *"the printed
  budget agrees with the constants it is built from"* because its subject is no
  longer the summary box alone.
- One Python test comparing the study grid with the ladder, 16 cells.
- One Python test pinning lines 1121-1122 and the box's silence. Keyed by each
  line's own `n` rather than sliced positionally — the review's other finding,
  and a real one: **a positional slice proves nothing about the line number it
  claims to cite.**
- **1665 Kotlin** (unchanged: the assertion joined a test rather than adding
  one) and **330 Python** (+2).

- **Appendix A: 35 unclaimed at 25.5%.** 6da read 32 one at a time and 6dl

- **`Shaken`** (line 8030) — one occurrence in the whole book, which never

- **Available, and deliberately not built here:** the p.11 table's two advisory
