## 6do. The table a true reason about one column kept out whole

`AttackDialog.kt:113` read *"Null for every skill with no attack table --
Wrestling included, which the book gives 'None (grapple only)'"*, and
`extract_unarmed.py`'s docstring gave the same reason at length: Wrestling
*"deals no damage at all ... so parsing it as a damage table would invent
damage the book does not print."*

**Both sentences are true, and both are about the DAMAGE column.** Book lines
2602-2621 print a four-row Wrestling table with different columns —
**Maneuver / Roll / Opposed Roll / Notes** — claimed by no content file and
modelled nowhere:

```
Grapple  | Wrestling   | DX or Escape    | Initiate grapple; both roll DX
Takedown | Wrestling-1 | DX or Wrestling | Knock down; target falls prone
Pin      | Wrestling-2 | DX or Wrestling | Immobilize; target cannot act
Escape   | Escape-2    | DX or Wrestling | Break free from grapple or pin
```

**And the counter-example is in the file the reason is written in.** `Shove`
has been a row of `unarmed_attacks.json` since M0 with `damage: "Special"` and
no damage parts at all — its own KDoc argues *"an attack that knocks down
instead of wounding deals no damage, which is not the same as dealing zero."*
So "no damage, therefore no row" was refuted by the table's own contents before
it was ever written down. Third instance running of 6dl's shape, and the
sharpest: the sentence stayed true while answering a question the decision did
not ask.

**Reachable, checked before the slice was named.** `Wrestling` and `Escape` are
both in `skills.json`, and **five of the 23 fixtures carry one** — Barmaid
Brawler, Dock Foreman and Docks Bouncer have Wrestling; Pickpocket and Street
Acrobat have Escape. A Docks Bouncer picked Wrestling in the attack screen and
was offered nothing at all.

**And the reason was not inherited blindly — it was read SELECTIVELY.** The
same summary row's third cell reads *"No default; ST bonus for grappling; parry
at -3"*, and `parry at -3` is applied, through `ParryBlock`. One cell of that
row governed the whole table and the cell beside it was taken. That is a
narrower finding than "nobody read it" and a truer one.

### The subject is what decides the shape, not the column count

I had weighed reuse-vs-new-table on the columns. The discriminator is the
**subject**: Grapple, Takedown and Pin are the GRAPPLER's, and `Escape-2` is
rolled by the person being HELD. `unarmed_attacks.json` is keyed by the acting
character's skill and read by an attack picker, so storing the fourth row would
offer anyone with Escape a way out of a grapple they are not in. It is left out
as a **GAP** — this app holds no grappled state and has no screen for the
acted-upon character — not as a refusal (6by's distinction). The design review
agreed and named the strongest case against, which is that it leaves an
Escape-trained character with no path to a printed row: *that argues for a
grapple-state surface, not for putting it in this table.*

The filter is drawn from the table's own definition — keep the rows whose roll
is the table's own skill — rather than from a blocklist of the one row that
went wrong; `GRAPPLED_ROW` exists only so `verify_grappling` can assert that
exactly that one was dropped.

### The parse: an anchor that matched a maneuver name

The two damage tables are cut on the **Roll** column, *"always the table's own
skill with an optional penalty ... a closed shape per table"*. That does not
hold here, and the guard is what said so rather than a silent bad parse:

```
ValueError: the grappling table now prints ['Grapple', 'Takedown', 'Pin',
'Immobilize; target cannot act', 'Escape'], not [...]
```

**The maneuver named `Escape` is spelled exactly like the skill named
`Escape`**, so the roll pattern matched a row's NAME and read the note above it
as a maneuver. The anchor moved to the **Opposed Roll** column
(`^DX or (Wrestling|Escape)$`), which is the closed shape this table actually
has. A column whose values collide with another column's is not an anchor.

`damage` stays non-null and carries the summary's own cell, `"None (grapple
only)"`, **read from line 2640 rather than typed** — the design review's
alternative to making the field nullable, which would have weakened the type
for the ten rows that do print a damage cell. `opposedRoll` is the book's third
column, and it is RENDERED (*"Rolls no damage. The target rolls DX or
Wrestling."*), because a column with no reader is 6di's finding waiting to
happen.

### Two committed tests asserted the expired half

```
DamageTest > wrestling has no attack rows, brawling and boxing do  FAILED
GoldenMeleeSummaryTest > Wrestling prints no attacks, so it can roll no damage  FAILED
```

The second's own comment states the mistake exactly: *"its table is Maneuver /
Roll / Opposed Roll and parsing it beside the other two would invent damage
(6j)"* — right about damage, and it concluded *no attacks*. Both were rewritten
to assert the half that survives: three maneuvers, none of which rolls damage,
each carrying the summary's cell. **A test can encode a reason, and then it
expires with the reason** — which is the inverse of this repo's usual "the
tests knew and production did not".

The diff review's second finding is about exactly that rewrite: the old
assertion caught **any** Wrestling row appearing, and the new pair checks
count, damage and opposed roll but not row identity — which the new
`AttacksTest` case does. The identity guard survived by moving file, so those
two tests have to be read together. Its third finding asked `verify_grappling`
to also assert the offered set is exactly the three; refused, because `verify()`
already owns that for all three tables through `EXPECTED`, and the refusal is
recorded in the function's own docstring.

### What shipped

- `tools/extract_unarmed.py` — `parse_grappling`, `verify_grappling`,
  `GRAPPLING_*`, `SUMMARY_DAMAGE`, the new spans, and a docstring that no
  longer stops at the damage column.
- `UnarmedAttack.opposedRoll`, its KDoc, and `AttackDialog`'s render of it —
  which names the contest ONLY, because a grappling row's own damage cell two
  lines above already reads "None (grapple only)". Shove keeps the "rolls no
  damage" sentence, because its cell reads "Special" and does not say it.
- The Kotlin guard asserts the three rows share ONE damage cell rather than
  naming the string: `extract_unarmed.SUMMARY_DAMAGE` ties it to book line
  2640, and typing it in a Kotlin test would be a guard comparing the extractor
  against a literal in the test file (6dl's twelfth vacuity, avoided). **The
  tie exists one language over, which is worth knowing before trusting it.**
- Six tests (three Python, three Kotlin) and two rewritten.
- **1665 Kotlin** (+2) and **328 Python** (+3), all green. Chapter 5:
  **74.4% → 76.3%**, unclaimed mechanical lines 40 → 37 — a percentage that
  moved, unlike 6di's.

## 6dn. Nine costs, seven counted — and the corpus stopped one line short

`tools/coverage.py`, re-run: chapters 1, 2, 4, 6.5, 7, 9 and C between them hold
**44 unclaimed mechanical lines**, and every one was read. The verdict is that
44 of 44 are already accounted for — which is the deliverable a sweep that
finds nothing still owes (6de) — except that reading them turned up a claimed
span that stops one line before the rows that would contradict its own
assertion.

### What the seven chapters actually hold

| ch | lines | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 234 | prose defining 3d6 |
| 2 | 266, 273, 350 | worked examples of the roll procedure |
| 4 | 2309, 2339 | Spirit Vision's cost, said with strictly less than 7.6's printing; SPI recovery on its **third** printing, refused for a clock since 6ad |
| 6.5 | 3548, 3550 | prose restating the method table's own 1-2 SPI |
| 7 | 25 lines | `PowerSources` constants (4271, 4276-7, 4289, 4222), recorded refusals (4161 timing in `RitualMode.kt:49`, 4398 CoR-by-rest), prose, and the ritual templates below |
| 9 | 9 lines | how to read a potion's `+N` grant. Checked, not assumed: 5458-5462's *"if you already have the skill"* rule, including its **name AND difficulty must match exactly** condition, is cited by line and applied in `PotionDigestion`'s KDoc |
| C | 9953, 10010 | `(pre-1352)` and `(expelled post-1350)`: dates the widened filter matches and nothing prices |

**Chapter 7's constants are the interesting half of that table.** `PowerSources`
holds `HP_PER_SPI`, `PARTICIPANT_BONUS`/`CAP`, `SENTIENT_BONUS`,
`CATALYST_LOWEST`/`HIGHEST` and `SUSPENSION_PENALTY`, and its KDoc says why they
are constants rather than content: *"a column for +1-per-assistant or +0-to-+2
for a catalyst would make the book look like it printed a table it never did."*
So those lines read unclaimed forever, by design — 6cy's *"a table implemented
as arithmetic reads 0% forever"* at line resolution.

### The finding: a count taken with the wrong filter

`extract_worked_rituals.py` claims **4422-4638**, and Section VIII's list runs to
Ritual 10 at ~4717. Its stated exclusion:

> Rituals 8-10's templates: they print ranges rather than a worked total, so
> there is no arithmetic to check an engine against.

**True, and about the ORACLE.** It says nothing about whether the lines are
READ — and the file itself proves that, because it already reads Ritual 8's
template through a second range for two pinned disagreements. **Ritual 9 got
group membership and nothing else**: inside the sentence that excludes it, and
outside every range the file reads. Ritual 10 at least got a named deferral
with its own reason.

So the docstring's other claim was worth re-running as a query — *"Rechecked
against all seven costed rituals"*, the evidence CLAUDE.md 6aa's two-axis SPI
decision rests on, with `verify()` asserting it *"so the evidence the decision
rests on cannot quietly change"*. Every `SPI Cost:` line in 4415-4725:

```
R1 Luck Enhancement       4      rung: Moderate
R2 Divination             3      rung: Light
R3 Summoning              7      rung: Heavy
R4 Curse                  7      rung: Heavy
R5 Oath-Sealing           5      rung: Moderate
R6 Fabrication            6      rung: Moderate
R7 Binding                9      rung: Heavy
R8 Sacrificial          2-4      rung: NONE
R9 Dualistic            4-8      rung: NONE
```

**The section prints nine costs, not seven.** "All seven costed rituals" was
taken with the filter *has a worked total*, and the two it drops are the only
two that fall outside the ladder — R8 straddles Light (2-3) and Moderate (4-6),
R9 straddles Moderate and Heavy (7-10). Neither is inside a weight-table row
either (Light 2, Moderate 4-6, Heavy 8+). **An assertion whose corpus excludes
the only rows that could contradict it**, and the exclusion and the assertion
were written in the same docstring.

### And it is not a disagreement to repair

A template prices a CLASS of ritual across scopes; a rung prices one ritual.
That is exactly why the seven single values each sit in a rung and these two
sit in none — so this is recorded, in the 4.2 shape: `verify()` now reads both
templates and **fails the day a printed row contains a template range whole**,
because that is the day the two axes have merged. RED-proved by handing
`verify()` a rung spanning 2-20.

Ritual 10 stays deferred on its own reason (its 17-row pathway/material table
has no caller — nothing in this app creates charms) with one fact added: **it
prints no SPI cost at all**, which is why the count is nine and not ten.

### The review found a scope the widening had broken

Codex answered on `task --effort high`. Q1 and Q2 came back clean — the new
branch is reachable, and the `pytest.raises(match=...)` proves the NEW branch
raised rather than an earlier check. Q3 was the finding, and it is one the
widening itself created: `TEMPLATE_TIERS` and `TEMPLATE_SHIFT` are **Ritual
8's** facts and they search the joined blob, which now contains Ritual 9. Lose
the fact from Ritual 8, have Ritual 9 print matching text, and **a guard about
one ritual passes on its neighbour's line.** Cut at the book's own `Ritual 9:`
title before those two are searched — and the absence of that title is a
stated failure rather than a silent fallback to the whole blob. RED-proved by
moving the tiers sentence from Ritual 8's half into Ritual 9's.

**A widened range is a widened scope for every predicate reading it.**

- Three Python tests. **325 Python** (+3), **1663 Kotlin** unchanged — no Kotlin

## 6dm. The control that did not name its price — and the caller it still has not got

6dl named this next with its query, and the query holds: `grep -rn "spiFor"
--include=*.kt app/src/main` returns `Boons`, `Divination` and `PowerSources`,
never `AntiDivinationTechniques`. Its two siblings both have callers —
`penaltyTotal` at `DivinationDialog.kt:153`, `detectionBonus` inside
`Detection.modifierTotal` — so the object is called and one function of it is
not.

### The number had three possible sources and only one of them is `spiFor`

`DetectionDialog` offered a `Spiritual Warding +2` chip under a caption reading
*"The SPI a technique costs is spent on the tracker"*, with no number anywhere
on the screen. Three things could have printed it:

| | |
|---|---|
| `row.spi` | the parsed `2`, which makes the screen type the unit `SPI` itself — 6cq's defect class |
| `row.bullet("Cost")` | the book's own `"2 SPI"`, which is 6dj's `printedCost` shape |
| `spiFor(pickedWards)` | the SUM of what is picked |

And the third is the same number as the first two, on today's content. `wards`
is filtered on `detectionBonus != null`, and **3A is the only one of the six
rows that prints one** — measured from the JSON, which is a claim about the
file as it stands and not a promise about a re-extraction — so the chip price
and the total are one value, and printing both is 6cr exactly (*"`+1 each` was a third copy of a value the chips beneath
it already print"*). The chip prints `bullet("Cost")` and nothing prints a
total.

### So this slice does NOT close what 6dl named, and that is the finding

`spiFor` still has no production caller. Calling it on a one-element list to
retire a sweep hit would be the sweep answering itself — and the function's own
shape is evidence about the caller it is waiting for: `distinctBy { it.id }`,
`sumOf`, and a throw for the one row priced in prose only make sense for a
caller that can be handed more than one technique. **The dialog's filter is not
that caller and never will be.** The wider slice — the target declaring any
technique they pay for, whether or not it moves this roll — is named at the
bottom with the two questions it has to answer first.

### The offered set moved out of the screen

The guard had to not copy the dialog's predicate, or a widening would move the
chips and leave the guard checking the set they used to be — this repo's *"the
same predicate at two call sites is the defect, not the drift it produces"*. So
`AntiDivinationTechniques.onDetectionRoll()` resolves it once and both read it.
The test asserts every row it returns prints a `Cost` the chip can show, plus
the non-emptiness that keeps the `forEach` from passing vacuously.

RED-proved against the real file rather than argued: `cp` the content file
aside, delete 3A's `Cost` bullet, and exactly that test reddens — no other test
in the class notices, which is what makes it the guard rather than a duplicate
of the duration check three lines above it. Restored from the copy, never with
`git checkout`, because the implementation was uncommitted (6dl hit that live).

### The review's three findings, all refused, one of them for a rule

Codex answered on `task --effort high` with the target list and the
*"do not read CLAUDE.md or docs/SLICE-LOG.md"* instruction (6dd/6df).

- **MEDIUM: the test does not exercise the chip label**, so a dialog regression
  that stops appending the Cost still passes. True, and it asks for the Compose
  test this repo cannot write (6cq, and 6dh refused two LOWs of the same shape).
  Its alternative — extract the label into a testable function — is an
  abstraction with one implementation.
- **MEDIUM: `onDetectionRoll()` can offer a row `spiFor` cannot price.** The
  strongest of the three, and its prescription is the wrong half. A ward that
  helps you notice AND prices itself in prose belongs on the screen: withdrawing
  a printed rule for being unsummable is the 4.1 sin, and it is the failure 6cz
  shipped in the concrete. **Take the diagnosis over the prescription** (6cz
  again). What ships is the seam written down: `onDetectionRoll` answers which
  rows move the roll, `spiFor` answers what a set costs, and a caller that sums
  this set has to answer the second question again.
- **LOW: a null `Cost` renders a chip with no price, silently.** It cannot
  print `"null"` (the `?.let` sees to that), and the guard makes real content
  fail in the suite rather than on the screen. Refused.

### What shipped

- `AntiDivinationTechniques.onDetectionRoll()` and its KDoc seam.
- `DetectionDialog` — the chip's price, and a caption that no longer claims the
  number is somewhere it is not.
- One Kotlin test, carrying two assertions with separate failure modes: that
  every offered ward prints a `Cost` at all, and that 3A's reads exactly
  `"2 SPI"`. The second is not redundant — `spi` is parsed off the FRONT of
  that string, so a line that grew a clause (`"2 SPI, or 1 if already
  warded"`) leaves `spi == 2` and every existing pin green while the chip
  prints the clause whole. RED-proved with exactly that edit: the price test
  reddens, `SPI costs add` does not. **The chip prints the string, so the
  string is what needs pinning.**
- **1663 Kotlin** (+1) and **322 Python**, all green.

### The next slice

- **The wider `spiFor` caller: a target declaring any technique they pay for.**

## 6dl. A reason that stayed true and stopped being relevant

6dk named the cross-reference sweep next and it was run deliberately: **35
claimed lines carry a cross-reference**, and every target resolves to a claimed
file — the Critical Failure Table, the Entity Response Table, Step 1's
difficulty table, ch. 2's burning mechanic. A clean sweep. What it found on the
way past was a line in the corpus it was reading, and the finding is about a
REASON rather than a rule.

### Two printings of one row, fifteen minutes against six hours

Appendix A line 9672, unclaimed:

> Major Wound: Hit > ½ HP -> HT or stunned 1d6 sec | **Fail by 5+ -> down 15 min**

Chapter 5's own table, extracted into `major_wound.json` since M0:

> Fail by 5+ — **Knocked down and unconscious for 1d hours**

Fifteen minutes against one-to-six hours. Chapter 5 governs — a summary may
define but not overrule, which is line 9667's own principle in the other
direction — so this is RECORDED and never repaired (4.1), and
`major_wound.json` is untouched.

**It is not a rule nobody reads.** `DamageDialog` renders
`"${row.result} — ${row.effect}"` on every Major Wound, so the app has been
printing one of the two printings to the player with nothing recording that
the other exists. That check was run first, because it decides the size of the
slice: 6di found `HitLocation.effect` stored on nine rows and read by nothing,
and the sibling column here could have been the same.

### The reason that failed twice, in two different ways

`extract_appendix.py` skipped the rest of the page for a stated reason: **"a
summary of chapters already claimed"**. That sentence does two jobs at once —
the lines restate claimed content, THEREFORE nothing is lost — and both halves
have now failed, separately:

| | |
|---|---|
| 6da, line 9667 | killed the FIRST job: a line that is not a summary of a claimed chapter at all (the facing rule, which nothing extracts) |
| 6dl, line 9672 | kills the SECOND: it **is** a summary of claimed content **and it disagrees with it** |

The second is the worse failure, because **the reason stays TRUE while becoming
irrelevant.** A stated reason that fails by being falsified is one a re-run
catches; one that fails by answering a different question than the decision
needs is invisible to any re-run of itself. Claim status was never the same
question as agreement.

**And 6da read this line.** Its pass went through Appendix A's 32 unclaimed
mechanical lines one at a time and returned "31 are faithful restatements and
one is not". 9672 carries `1d6`, so it was visible under the pre-6db filter,
and both its neighbours' claims (`damage_abbreviations` on 9671,
`success_ladder` on 9673-9676) landed on 2026-08-04 and 2026-08-06 against
6da's 2026-08-16 — checked with `git log -S`, because the accusation is a claim
about a corpus and 6ci and 6cj were both burned by asserting one without its
query.

Its docstring is not silent about disagreements either: it already records two,
the hit-location line's flat "Vitals -3 ×3" dropping chapter 5's "(imp/pi
only)" scope, and its "Hand/Foot" where chapter 5 has only Hand. **Both are in
prose, which no sweep over this repo can read (6cj)** — and a third, which
changes a number the app displays, sat between them unrecorded.

### So the method is a guard rather than a sentence

`verify_major_wound` compares the summary with the rows it summarises, clause
by clause, and `SUMMARY_DISAGREEMENTS` names **both printings** of the one that
differs — in the 4.2 shape, so the day they agree the extraction FAILS rather
than a repair going unnoticed. RED-proved against the real file: editing
`major_wound.json`'s third row to match the appendix makes the extractor exit
with *"the appendix and chapter 5 no longer disagree"*.

The other clause is checked in the same pass rather than assumed, and `> ½ HP`
against chapter 5's "more than half your HP (round up)" is **not** counted as a
second disagreement: it says strictly less, which is 6da's own NO-SHIP standard.

### The review's three findings, all taken, and one is 6dh's lesson again

- **MEDIUM: a one-way check with a blind side.** The agreement clause was
  compared against the APPENDIX's wording alone, so chapter 5's row could drift
  to anything while the guard kept passing. Both sides now. The tests above did
  not find it; the reviewer did.
- **MEDIUM: reading another extractor's output made the guard order-dependent.**
  It read `major_wound.json` off disk — a file this extractor does not write —
  so the answer depended on which extractor ran last, which is the staleness
  family 6dk had just been bitten by. It reads chapter 5's own LINES now
  (2826, 2830), addressed by number the way `WOUNDING_LINE` already is. **This
  is a question about two printings, and the book is the authority for both.**
- **LOW:** `SUMMARISES` was partitioned by `AGREES_ON` and
  `SUMMARY_DISAGREEMENTS` only implicitly, so a clause in neither fell through
  to a `KeyError`. Now a stated failure.

**No vacuous assertion in what the reviewer read.** That is a weaker claim
than "the first slice in eleven with none", and the difference matters: the
tests were RESTRUCTURED after the review to take chapter 5's lines instead of
`major_wound.json`, so the reviewed tests and the shipped tests are not the
same tests. The restructuring introduced one — `CHAPTER_5_MAJOR_WOUND` is a
hand-typed literal of two book lines, and nothing tied it to them, so the
guard would have been checking the appendix against strings typed in the test
file. One loop over `SUMMARISES` closes it, RED-proved by corrupting the
literal. **A review's verdict expires when the diff moves under it.**

And restoring the file after that proof with `git checkout` **discarded the
fix**, which was uncommitted at the time — this repo's own recorded lesson,
hit live rather than read. `cp` aside first.

### What shipped

- `tools/extract_appendix.py` — `parse_major_wound`, `verify_major_wound`,
  `SUMMARISES` / `AGREES_ON` / `SUMMARY_DISAGREEMENTS`, wired into `main()`,
  and the docstring's stated reason rewritten from the sentence that failed to
  the guard that replaces it.
- Four Python tests. Nothing in Kotlin, and nothing in `content/`: the app
  already applies the printing that governs.

**1662 Kotlin** (unchanged) and **322 Python**, all green.

### A twelfth vacuous assertion, and the compiler had been reporting it

Found while verifying the tree before handover, not by a reviewer.
`PoolsTest.kt:183` read:

```kotlin
assertTrue(Pools.spi(0, 9).penalty != null || Pools.spi(0, 9).corGained == 0)
```

`PoolStatus.penalty` is `Int = 0`, **non-nullable**, so `penalty != null` is
always true, the `||` short-circuits, and the assertion cannot fail. **Kotlin
had been printing `Condition is always 'true'` on every single build** — the
eleven found before this one were found by reviewers reading a diff, and this
one was free, in the build output, for however many slices.

Replaced by the boundary the test's own name is about: at exactly 0 SPI the
Exhaustion row still reports (`abilitiesOffline`) and Soul Debt has NOT
started, because the book charges "+1 CoR per 1 point **below** 0". RED-proved
by mutating `corGained`'s comparison to `<= 0` — two tests redden, where the
old assertion stayed green.

**Read the build's own warnings before asking a reviewer for findings.**

### One non-reproducible test failure, stated rather than hidden

The first verification run after committing reported `:core:rules:test FAILED`.
**Six subsequent full `--rerun-tasks` runs were green**, exit 0, and no
`failures` or `errors` attribute in any of the 1662 tests' JUnit XML. Not
diagnosed and not reproduced; this machine has a recorded history of Gradle
daemons surviving `--stop` and starving the box. Recorded because an
unexplained red that goes away is worth a sentence in the log rather than
silence.

Named with its query, because a closing paragraph is the one part of a slice
log nothing verifies (6cp):

- **`AntiDivinationTechniques.spiFor` has no production caller.** `grep -rn

## 6dk. The reference a claimed sentence pointed at

6dj named chapter 7.5 next — the last rules chapter claimed by nothing,
reading 0.0%. **It was right to name it and wrong about what was in it**, and
finding that out took four checks that each cost a grep.

### 7.5's ritual is already in the app, and was before anyone read the chapter

| 7.5 prints | where it already lives |
|---|---|
| "performing a ritual" to summon | `RitualResolution`, reachable today |
| its weight | `ritual_weights.json` prints **Summoning** as the first Heavy category, and `RitualDialog` renders `weight.categories` |
| Full vs Quick | p. 61: "Full Ritual is for consequential magic (curses, binding, **summoning**, cleansing)" |
| "supplicating a higher being" | ch. 7 IV.F, `Invocation` + `entity_response.json` |
| a mystical language | `RitualDialog`'s proficiency picker |

So a player can roll a summoning today: Heavy, -4, 8+ SPI. **The join was
checked from 7.5's own side rather than from the shared word**, which is the
`pts/level` trap 6cy paid for — p. 61 naming summoning among the Full
Ritual's own examples is the warrant, not the fact that two chapters use one
noun.

Three things in 7.5 are refused with their reasons, and one is a GAP rather
than a refusal — 6by's distinction, because calling a gap a refusal is how
this repo shipped four milestones of unreachable rules:

- **The 3d creature-response roll is NOT the Entity Response Table.** That
  table sits under "F. Invocation (Deity or Hidden Existence)" and a spiritual
  creature is neither. Better: the book **names that table by its proper name
  four times** (4046, 4144, 4295, 4506) and line 4730 does not — and the output
  axis differs, a modifier to the ritual roll against "the higher the chance
  they will peacefully arrive". A GM's free roll.
- **The creature format and the Bookworm** are GM content: this app holds one
  player character.
- **The ancient/regular mystical-language partition is a GAP.** 7.5 splits the
  six mystical languages into ancient (Ancient Hermes, Jotun, Dragonese,
  Elvish) and regular (Hermes, Ancient Feysac) — a complete partition of
  `languages.json` — and requires one of each. It reaches nothing because the
  app records a proficiency TIER and never which language. **7.5 is the first
  rule in the book that would need language identity**, and that names what
  unblocks it.

### What the chapter did have, and where it led

7.5's one player-facing rule is its **three-line summoning incantation**. And
chasing that found the slice, one chapter over.

Book line 4141 — **inside `ritual_preparation.json`'s claimed span 4120-4143** —
reads:

> The player narrates the incantation (**4-part Hermes structure — see
> reference below**). The GM may award a Flourish Bonus (+1) for good
> in-character delivery.

`RitualDialog` renders a "Flourish +1" chip and quotes that sentence — its
SECOND half. The parenthetical was read past, and the reference it points at
(4195-4204) was **claimed by no content file and modelled nowhere**. So the app
awarded a bonus for narrating a structure it never showed.

That is a sweep direction this repo had not run: **a CLAIMED line whose
cross-reference target is unclaimed.** `divination_modifiers.json`'s "See Step
1 table" row is the same shape and its target IS claimed, which is why nothing
had noticed the class. And every line involved is **filter-invisible** — none
carries a number — so 6di's finding holds a second time: not reported
unclaimed, not reported claimed, not reported at all.

The test suite knew. `test_the_flourish_bonus_is_read_across_the_line_it_wraps_on`
has quoted the whole sentence, parenthetical included, since the Flourish
slice. **Fourth instance of the suite knowing what production does not**, and
the third found by accident after 6bz ran that sweep deliberately and closed it.

### Three structures, and why they are three rows

| structure | scope | printed at |
|---|---|---|
| Four-part Hermes | Invocation | 4195-4204 |
| Three-line self-description | Praying to Oneself | 3992-3996 |
| Three-line summoning incantation | Summoning a spiritual creature | 4718-4720 |

The design review settled the two questions that decide the shape. **The two
three-line forms are two rows, not one**: one identifies the CASTER's spiritual
location within the Wall of Spirituality, the other identifies a creature by
realm and descriptors. Merging them on the shared shape would print a rule the
book does not.

And **the first two are SELECTED, the third is shown.** The book's own sentence
does the selecting — "For Praying to Oneself, replace the four-part structure
with the three-line self-description" — and it keys on a two-state chip pair
`RitualDialog` has had all along, `invoked`, whose "Personal SPI" label p. 62
spells "Personal SPI (Praying to Oneself)". A caster burning HP, leading
assistants or feeding a catalyst is still praying to oneself: IV.B-E are fuel
and bonuses stacked ON a source. The summoning row is `referenceOnly` because
**nothing here can say a ritual IS a summoning** — the weight is picked and its
category list is display text, and gating on Heavy would claim it of binding,
affliction and four others.

`verify_incantations` pins the replacement sentence for that reason: without
it the two structures are unrelated printings and the branch is invented.

### The review found a stale file, and I had hidden the failure that made it

**MEDIUM, and it is this repo's own recorded trap.** I split `text` from `note`
in the extractor, re-ran it as `py extract_ritual.py >/dev/null 2>&1`, and ran
the suite: 318 green. The extractor had **crashed on its own new guard** —
`verify_incantations` was still looking for a phrase that had just moved — and
**a failing extractor never rewrites its JSON** (6cx). The stale file kept the
old shape, the Python tests build their entries in memory so they could not
see it, and my Kotlin test asserted `structure` and `parts`, which were both
still right. Only `note` was missing, and nothing read `note`.

Two fixes, and the second is the one that matters: re-run visibly, and **pin
the field from the committed FILE** — the Kotlin test now asserts `note`, so a
crashed extractor reddens. **Never redirect an extractor's stderr.**

Its other three findings, all taken:

- **MEDIUM: a guard that hid its own input error.** `parse_parts` joins every
  non-bullet line onto the part above it, so a `HERMES_PARTS_RANGE` running
  past the last bullet would swallow the note into Part 4 with the count and
  the order both still right. Now the note's own opening words are checked for
  inside the parts, RED-proved by widening the range to 4204 (it fires).
- **LOW: the ninth vacuous assertion in nine slices.** The scope list was
  compared against `INCANTATION_SCOPES`, the same constant `build_incantations`
  writes them from. Literal strings now.
- **LOW:** the committed span said 4717 and the extractor said 4718 — the
  stale file's second face, invisible while the file was old.

### What shipped

- `tools/extract_ritual.py` — `parse_parts` (bullet-anchored, wrap-joining),

- `incantations.json` — three structures, claiming ch. 7 3992-3996 and
  4195-4204 and ch. 7.5 4718-4720, **the first line of that chapter anything

- `Incantation`, `ContentLoader.incantations()`, `Incantations.all()` /

- `RitualDialog`'s "Incantation (Phase II)" block, rendered after the power
  source that selects it rather than beside the chip that points at it.
- Four Python tests, three Kotlin.

**A Boolean, not the two-value enum the review proposed.** The book's sentence
is binary, the control is a two-chip pair with no third state, and an enum
whose only job is to rename `true` is the abstraction 6df refused. Recorded in
the KDoc with the condition that would revive it.

**1662 Kotlin** (1176 `core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and **318
Python**, all green. **Not device-verified.**

## 6dj. Two minus fours, agreeing by coincidence

6di named its own successor: **28 of the 29 newly-visible unclaimed lines are
still unread, and the honest first question about each is not "build it" but
"is it already implemented as arithmetic".** Running that list one line at a
time is what found this — but not where 6di pointed. Four of the 29 sit in
chapter 6.5's Section I, and reading them led to six lines no content file
claimed, one of which carries a number this app had **deliberately refused,
for a reason that does not survive being re-run as a query.**

### The seam, which is 6da's shape a second time

Book lines 3553-3558, chapter 6.5 Section I:

> The two skills overlap at the following boundaries:
> • **Simple** divination (yes/no, vague direction, basic insight): Divination Arts is sufficient. Cost: 1–2 SPI.
> • **Moderate** divination (find a person, glimpse a scene, interpret a dream): Either skill works. Divination Arts is faster (minutes vs. ritual setup) but may receive less detail. Cost: 2 SPI.
> • **Complex** divination (long-range, multiple questions, resisting countermeasures): Requires Ritualistic Magic or a very high Divination Arts roll (**-4 penalty**). Cost: 2 SPI.

`divination_support.json` claims **3559-3560** and **3563-3580**. The claims
BRACKET this table and skip it — the seam sweep's shape (6ay, 6ba), and the
second time after 6da that two careful claims have left a rule between them.

### The refusal, and the half of it that died

`tools/extract_divination.py` did not overlook the -4. It read it and refused
it, in its module docstring:

> it is prose for the SAME axis the Question Difficulty table already prices,
> whose "Hard — well-guarded, future, abstract" row is exactly -4 … applying
> both would charge one hard question twice

and `verify_cross_default` guarded that refusal by asserting the two numbers
still agree — its own message calling that agreement **"the only evidence"**.

Re-run as a query, the evidence does not survive. **The two tables' descriptors
are disjoint, and they cross:**

| The complex bullet says | which band owns that word |
|---|---|
| long-range | **Moderate** — "impersonal, **distant**, vague" (**-2**, not -4) |
| multiple questions | no band at all |
| resisting countermeasures | not a band: Sec. 4-6's Sequence Immunity and the target's techniques, which `AntiDivination` already prices |

and neither of the Hard band's own distinctive words — *future*, *abstract* —
appears in the bullet. A question can be Complex in scope at any band ("where
is my own key, 500 km away" is personal and concrete, and long-range), and
Hard at any scope ("will the Church raid this hideout" is one yes/no question).
**The two -4s price different facts and agree by coincidence.** The axis the
scope table actually names is which SKILL suffices, which is why its other two
rows carry no number: "Divination Arts is sufficient" and "Either skill works"
are the book saying the substitution is free.

**Half the reason survives and is honoured.** It really is not a sixth row of
the Step 3 modifier table — that table is enumerated under "Roll Divination
Arts, adding all applicable modifiers" and this bullet is not in it. So the
rule ships as **Section I's own table**, `divination_scope.json`, and
`divination_modifiers.json` is left alone. 6cp's lesson again, on a different
document: a refusal can survive its author's stated reason and die of a fact
none of its words mention — and here the author had already written down that
the evidence was thin.

### Three things the design review settled before any code

Scoped to three questions and four files through `task --effort high`, since
`adversarial-review` refuses this repo's input length and `review` no longer
takes focus text (6df).

- **The composition is additive**, and the boundary that stops a reversal is
  that the two arrive through different parameters: `targetFor(skill,
  difficulty, extras)` takes the band on its own. A later reader who made them
  exclusive would satisfy every assertion that checks one alone; what fails is
  the total, so the test pins `targetFor(14, Hard, complex) == 6`. The strongest
  case against, recorded: -8 is harsh, and "well-guarded" does partly overlap
  "resisting countermeasures" — but this app already adds the band and the
  anti-divination penalty side by side on the same screen, so overlapping
  descriptors have not collapsed those axes either.
- **"Very high" is not a gate.** The cross-skill default one line BELOW prints
  its threshold ("a character with one skill at 12+") and this sentence prints
  none, so any cutoff would be app-authored. The enforceable rule is the -4.
  The tell was stated in advance: *if you find yourself inventing a threshold
  for "very high", that is the tell.*
- **The cost column is not a second charge.** Step 2 reads "Select a divination
  method (see Section II). Pay the SPI cost", which names the method table —
  what `Divination.spiFor` already charges. Note the tiers print 1–2 / 2 / 2
  against methods costing 1..2, so a tier cost read as authoritative would
  make a Pendulum cost 2 on a moderate question. It is stored as **prose**
  (`printedCost: "2 SPI"`), which is the type-level version of "shown, never
  applied" — an Int there is 6bx's live double count.

### The guard, and what a guard on a dead reason must become

The old `verify_cross_default` asserted the two numbers agree. That guard was
protecting the refusal, so it cannot simply be deleted: what replaces it is
`verify_scope`, asserting the evidence the refusal DIED on, in the direction
that can disagree — **no difficulty band's descriptor may appear in a priced
scope row's**. If a re-extraction ever puts *future* or *abstract* into that
bullet the two really are one axis, and the reading has to be made again
rather than inherited. Both corpora are asserted non-empty first, because a
disjointness check over an empty side is the guard that cannot fire (6cz).

### The parse: the bullet is the row, and two rows wrap

Two of the three rows wrap onto a second line, and the wrapped half carries
the payload **both times** — Moderate's cost and Complex's penalty. A
line-at-a-time read returns two rows with no number, which is
indistinguishable from a table that prints none. RED-proved by deleting the
join: two Python tests redden.

### The picker, and a default that must not charge

Three chips rather than one, because the book distinguishes three scopes and
the existing difficulty picker renders straight from its rows — the loop is
LESS bespoke code than one hand-labelled chip (6cn, on which side "the rule
shapes the control" falls this time). The two free rows show no modifier,
because `+0` would print a number the book does not. It defaults to Simple:
the same first-row default the band above it takes, and also the row that
prices nothing — **a default that charges is a rule nobody declared.**

### The diff review, and the vacuity I caught first

Codex returned **one LOW and two explicit no-findings** (the dialog's
`scopePenalty` reaches the target, the breakdown and `attempt`'s `extras`, and
the breakdown still sums to the target; `printedCost` is safe as a String). The
LOW: `assertEquals(-4, hard.modifier)` inside the composition test duplicates
a guard the difficulty test above already carries, and the input the test
actually composes — the scope penalty — was unpinned. Now `assertEquals(-4,
scope)`.

Before sending the diff I had already deleted a third test of my own for the
opposite failure: `the scope rows print a cost and hold no number to charge`
asserted a string and a method cost, and **neither assertion could check what
the name claimed**. What enforces it is the TYPE. An intent with no independent
failure mode is a comment, not a test (6dg) — so it is one, on
`DivinationScope`.

### What shipped

- `tools/extract_divination.py` — `parse_scope` (bullet-anchored, wrap-joining),
  `verify_scope` (the disjointness guard), the docstring section rewritten from
  the dead reason to the live one, and `verify_cross_default` trimmed to the
  rule it is named for: one predicate, one home.
- `divination_scope.json` — three rows claiming 3553-3558.
- `DivinationScope`, `ContentLoader.divinationScopes()`, `Divination.scopes()`
  / `.scopeNamed()` / `.penaltyFor()`.
- `DivinationDialog`'s Scope picker, its guidance line, and the breakdown's
  named term.
- Three Python tests, two Kotlin.

Chapter 6.5: **92.3% → 96.9%**, unclaimed 5 → 2. **1659 Kotlin** (1173
`core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and **314 Python**, all green. Two
mutations RED-proved: the wrap-join deleted (2 Python fail) and `penaltyFor`
returning 0 (2 Kotlin fail). **Not device-verified** — no test in this repo
reaches a composable, and the picker has not been rendered.

### The next slice

The two lines left unclaimed in 6.5 are 3548 and 3550, and they stay that way
on purpose: both restate the method table's 1–2 SPI range, and claiming lines
a file did not consume would make `sourceLines` a lie. 6da left Appendix A's
31 restatements unclaimed for the same reason, so **a chapter's last few
percent may be restatement rather than work** — the honest reading of a
coverage number that will not reach 100.

What is genuinely outstanding, in order of evidence:

- **Chapter 7.5, Summoning Spiritual Creatures, reads 0.0% and is claimed by
  NO content file** — the last wholly unstarted rules chapter, and it has been
  at 0.0% in plain sight the whole time, because `main()` sets `failed` only
  for a chapter that HAS claims. Measured, not assumed: line 4730's `3d`
  matches the PRE-6db filter, so 7.5 read 0.0% with one unclaimed line before
  the widening and 0.0% with four after — it was never invisible the way 7.6
  was. 6cw's census missed 7.6 because the instrument said 100%; it missed 7.5
  for the OPPOSITE reason, that 0.0% reads as "not started yet" rather than as
  a defect. **Both directions of a coverage number can hide a chapter.** **Read it before building it**: its
  four visible lines are an example creature's stat block and a GM's 3d roll
  for a summoned creature's response, and that roll is NOT the Entity Response
  Table `Invocation` already models — that table sits under "F. Invocation
  (Deity or Hidden Existence)" and a spiritual creature is neither. An app
  holding one player character may have no consumer for a GM procedure at all,
  and saying so with the evidence is a deliverable.
- The remaining 25 of 6di's 29 lines. The HP/FP recovery block (2842-2899) and
  the CoR abstinence rule (4398) are RATES, which `docs/HOW-TO-PLAY.md` refuses
  under "Track a clock it does not hold" — 6dc confirmed that refusal has a
  mechanism reason. 3548/3550 are settled above. That leaves 4646 and 4660,
  two ritual EXAMPLES' SPI costs, and 2309's Spirit Vision maintenance cost.
- The unrun sweep directions 6di named: catalogue → fixture, and extractor →
  `sourceLines`.

## 6di. The rule no coverage number could ever have reported

6dh named a method rather than a target: **a check that reconciles two
printings runs one way, and the reverse is a separate sweep.** Running the
reverse of `coverage.py` — content files' claims back against the book, rather
than book lines forward against the claims — found four overlapping spans (all
sibling files splitting one printed table, legitimate) and then something
better by a different route.

### 6db widened the filter after 6da had already read the chapter

`coverage.py`'s `MECHANICAL` filter decides which lines COUNT. 6db widened it
from three alternatives to five, making 286 lines newly visible. **6da had read
Appendix A's unclaimed lines one at a time BEFORE that**, under the narrow
filter, which is exactly what 6db's own warning says not to compare across.

So: which lines became mechanical only after 6db, and are claimed by nobody?
**29.** Most are rules already implemented as Kotlin arithmetic — the FP
thresholds, the 2 HP → 1 SPI ritual burn — which 6cy already established read
0% forever. The genuinely unread cluster is chapter 5's Healing & Recovery
table, and 6dc's refusal covers most of it (the recovery and Regeneration
RATES need a clock this app does not hold).

**The first run of that query filed glossary lines 10185 and 10203 under
Appendix C and reported them unclaimed.** They are claimed, under `G`. My
partition used `chapters.json`'s raw page ranges, which `coverage.py`'s own
comment says disagree with the boundaries it measures by. Re-run
chapter-agnostically — *is this line claimed by ANY content file* — the false
positives vanished. **A sweep that re-derives the instrument's partition
inherits none of its corrections** (6dg's 79 false positives, one slice later,
by a different mechanism).

### What the neighbourhood held

Reading around the cluster reached book lines 2785-2787:

> **Crippling:** A limb or extremity struck for more than ½ its HP is crippled
> — unusable until healed. Arm/leg crippling: drop held items or reduce Move
> to 1. Recovers when the limb returns to positive HP. First Aid (skill 12+)
> removes permanent damage risk.

Three lines. Claimed by nothing. They sit in the **three-line seam** between
`hit_locations.json` (2743-2784) and `wounding_multipliers.json` (2789+) —
6ba's gap. And they match **neither the old `MECHANICAL` filter nor the widened
one**, so they were never in any denominator, in either era: the numbers are a
fraction glyph, a bare `1`, and a `12+` whose sign comes last where the
filter's signed-number rule wants it first.

**A line invisible to the filter is not reported as unclaimed and is not
reported as claimed. It is not reported.** 6db found a chapter reading 100%
because its lines were filtered out of the sweep for unread chapters; this is
the same shape at line resolution, and it survived 6db's widening.

### And the column it governs had no reader at all

`HitLocation.effect` is stored on all nine rows and read by **nothing** —
checked in production and in the test suite. `DamageDialog` picks a pool and
applies a number; `AttackDialog` picks a location and prints its to-hit
penalty and wounding multiplier. Neither reads the effect column, which prices
five outcomes against damage:

| Row | Cell | Computable |
|---|---|---|
| Arm | `Drop held item if damage >= 3; crippled at > ½ HP of limb (~ HP/3)` | both |
| Leg | `Knock prone if damage >= 3; crippled at > HP/3` | both |
| Hand | `Drop held item; crippled easily (> HP/6)` | both |
| Neck | `Knockdown roll at -5; choke possible if damage > HP/2` | the choke |
| Eye | `Blind at > HP/10; bypasses head DR` | the blinding |

**Two of the four refusals were already recorded in production source**, and
citing them beat re-deriving them: `Shock.kt` says the hit-location knockdown
cells "print no attribute to roll against", and `Equipment.UNMODELLED["Armour"]`
says nothing here models DR. The other two — "risk of blindness or
disfigurement", "bleeding risk" — price nothing at all.

### The design review, and the distinction it saved

**Arm and Leg print TWO numbers and only one is the rule.** The governing
threshold is "> ½ HP of **limb**"; `~ HP/3` is the BOOK's own approximation of
it in character HP, tilde and all. Hand, Neck and Eye print character-HP
thresholds outright. Storing one `hpDivisor` for both shapes would let a test
bless the approximation as the rule, so `approximate` travels with it and the
KDoc says which is which. That is the finding I would not have made.

Its other two: a `List<String>` return makes UI copy into engine identity, so a
small record ships instead — and a sealed hierarchy for five cells would be the
one-implementation abstraction the repo forbids. And the UI must report a
**trigger**, never an applied state: "unusable until healed" is duration this
app does not track, so nothing marks a limb, starts a clock, or changes a
character.

### Where the picker had to go, which was not where the table is

`AttackDialog` has the location and the damage EXPRESSION; `DamageDialog` has
the damage AMOUNT and the target's HP. **Neither screen had all three**, which
is `DetectionDialog`'s problem again — this app holds one character, and an
attack is aimed at somebody else. The picker went where the character actually
takes the hit, and it does **not** re-price the damage: the wounding multiplier
is the attacker's business and `AttackDialog` already prints it, so the number
typed in is the injury that got through. Saying that on screen was necessary,
because a player choosing "Skull" would otherwise expect ×4.

### The diff review: four findings, four taken

**A prefix match can name the wrong outcome and silence its own guard.**
`clause.lower().startswith("blind")` reads `Blindness or disfigurement at >
HP/10` — the Face cell's wording one re-extraction away — as the Eye's definite
`Blind`, prices it, fires it, and leaves the raise-guard quiet because it had
found a name. Not a crash, not a dropped clause: a confident wrong effect. The
keys are anchored regexes closed at a word boundary now, and the reviewer's
exact case is a test. (`Knock prone` and `Knockdown` share five letters and are
the only pair in the column that do.)

**The eighth vacuous assertion in eight slices, and mine again.** `assertEquals(
location.thresholds.isNotEmpty(), effectsAt(damage = 99).isNotEmpty())` cannot
fail: `effectsAt` FILTERS that same list, so a row silently losing its
thresholds makes both sides `false`. Replaced by the named set — which five
rows, and how many clauses each.

**A selection survived out of sight.** `landed` persisted while the HP-only
picker was hidden, so picking Eye, switching to FP, changing the amount and
switching back showed an effect fired for a hit nobody described. It clears
with the pool now, beside the shock, for the same stated reason: moving the
damage to another pool makes it a different hit.

**And a KDoc my own edit orphaned** — inserting `HitLocationFile` between the
threshold type's KDoc and its class left the comment describing the wrong
declaration. Third instance of a block inheriting where it landed.

### Two things worth inheriting

**Claiming these lines moved no number.** Chapter 5 reads 74.4% before and
after, because the filter cannot see what was claimed. A slice whose whole
subject is invisible to the metric produces no metric movement, and a coverage
percentage is therefore not a measure of whether the chapter has been read.

**A `\b` written through a heredoc collapsed to a literal backspace byte
(0x08).** The extractor then failed loudly on its own guard — the right
failure, from the wrong cause — and `cat -A` is what showed `^H` where `\b`
should be. A regex assembled through two layers of quoting needs its bytes
checked, not its source read.

### What shipped

- `tools/extract_wounds.py` — `OUTCOMES` as anchored regexes, `parse_thresholds`,
  the `CRIPPLING_RANGE` claim, and the governing paragraph STORED rather than
  merely claimed (a span with nothing behind it says the lines were read and
  leaves nothing that can disagree when they change).
- `hit_locations.json` — `thresholds` per row, `cripplingRule` whole.
- `HitLocationThreshold`, `HitLocationFile`, `ContentLoader.cripplingRule()`,
  and `Wounds.thresholdFor` / `.effectsAt` / `.cripplingRule`, with
  `WoundEffectsTest` (7 tests). Mutating the `+1` off the fraction reddens two.
- `DamageDialog`'s "Where it landed", HP only, reporting triggers.
- Four Python tests: the invisibility, the parsed set, the word boundary, the
  closed seam.

1657 Kotlin (1171 `core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and 312 Python, all
green. **Not device-verified**; no test here reaches a composable.

### The next slice

The reverse-sweep method still has unrun directions — catalogue → fixture (6ct
ran fixture → Kotlin), and extractor → `sourceLines`. But the sharper lead is
the one this slice opened and did not take: **28 of the 29 newly-visible
unclaimed lines are still unread**, and the honest first question about each is
not "build it" but "is it already implemented as arithmetic". The FP rows and
the 2 HP → 1 SPI burn are; chapter 6.5's `1–2 SPI per use` and chapter 7's
ritual SPI costs need checking one at a time. And **`coverage.py`'s filter has
now been shown to have false negatives twice** — the fraction glyph and the
trailing-sign form are two shapes it cannot see, and neither was found by
looking at the filter.

## 6dh. The summary was wrong in both directions at once

6dg's sweep named this: of 79 content files, exactly one had no `ContentLoader`
function — `spirit_vision.json` — and it was also the **sole claimant of
chapter 7.6**, so `coverage.py` reported that chapter 100.0% off a file no
Kotlin read. Its extractor had shipped deliberately without a consumer,
recording *"a loader with no caller is 6cf's defect, and this slice would ship
one"*, and deferring the model together with the question of which screen shows
it.

### The finding: section C is not four-right-and-one-wrong

Chapter 7.6's section C is a five-row summary of which Sequence 9 pathways see
what. The extractor already pinned one disagreement in it: the **Spectator**
row files a power under Spirit Vision that the Spectator's own chapter 9 block
prices in FP as `Body Language Analysis` and never names Spirit Vision at all.

That check runs **row → block**: for each row in C, does the pathway's block
agree? It cannot see the opposite question. Running **block → row** finds
**Moon's Apothecary**, whose block prints `Spirit Vision — Ether Body` and
which section C does not list.

So the table is the right SIZE and the wrong MEMBERSHIP:

| | |
|---|---|
| Section C lists | Fool, Hermit, **Visionary**, Darkness, Death |
| Blocks grant at Seq 9 | Fool, Hermit, **Moon**, Darkness, Death |

Five against five. **A magnitude check passes, a count check passes, and a
one-directional check finds half of it.** A screen gated on C would have
refused the ability to the one premade pathway in the corpus that has it and
offered it to one that does not. Both halves are asserted, in the extractor and
in Python, because repairing either alone leaves the other standing.

### 21 blocks say "Spirit Vision" and mean three things

The gate reads each pathway's own block. A substring match over those blocks is
wrong in a way that only shows up on three characters:

| Class | Count | Example |
|---|---|---|
| GRANT | 9 | `Spirit Vision:` / `Eyes of Mystery Prying (` |
| UPGRADE | 7 | the same label inside `reinforcedAbilities` |
| NEITHER | 5 | a DEFENCE against someone else's, or a mention of other pathways' |

The five non-grants are the interesting ones. The **Werewolf** (Chained 7)
"reveals only a figure covered in black hair" to it; the **Hypnotist**
(Visionary 6) has an illusion that "works even against Spirit Vision"; the
**Monster** (Wheel of Fortune 9) perceives what "Pathways with strong Spirit
Vision abilities cannot". Three characters the book gives no part of the
ability, and a bare match hands it to all three.

The discriminator comes from how the book WRITES a power rather than from the
cases that went wrong: a granted ability is a **label opening its own clause**,
so the name is followed by `:`, `(` or an em dash. Every non-grant says the
words mid-sentence. The mutation is in `test_tools.py`.

**And the common name is not enough.** The Mystery Pryer's block never writes
"Spirit Vision" — it writes `Eyes of Mystery Prying`, which section C and the
chapter's Special Forms sentence both confirm is the same ability. Matching only
the common name silently loses one grant of seven, so the pattern carries both
names and the tile is labelled with the pathway's own.

**Two pathways grant it at Sequence 8, not 9** — Mother's Doctor and Red
Priest's Provoker — which is why a Sequence 9 table is right to omit them, and
why "the five rows are the five pathways" was never a safe reading.

### The design review moved the parser out of the engine

Its Q1 answer is the one that changed the shape: matching prose inside
`SpiritVision.grantedTo` would make the rules engine *"another authority
surface"*, competing with the content files, and typography would become part
of rules logic. Taken whole. `GRANT` and the classification now live in
`tools/extract_spirit_vision.py`, which writes a `grants` block of
`{pathway, sequence, form}`; Kotlin consumes structure and parses nothing.

Its Q2 answer killed a branch I had proposed: **`reinforcedAbilities` is not
read.** Every upgrade in the book sits on a pathway granted the ability at a
higher rung, so reading it cannot change an answer — and a branch no data can
reach is one a later reader trusts as though it meant something. What ships
instead is the invariant, asserted: every `reinforcedAbilities` mention has an
earlier grant on the same pathway, and `verify()` fails loudly if the book ever
upgrades an ability it never granted. It also named the asymmetry that decides
the default: a **false grant fabricates a rule-backed action, an SPI cost and a
roll**, where a false omission is only an omission.

Its Q3 answer shaped the screen. This table prints a **FAILURE row** —
"Incorrect reading" — where chapter 4's sibling tables print none, and
`SpiritualSenses.rowFor` returns null on a failure by documented design. A
failed Spirit Vision is not the absence of an answer, it is a confident WRONG
one. So `rowForOutcome` returns the row rather than null, and the dialog
**renders the row's own words with no "Failure" label beside them**: a screen
that prints the verdict has modelled the die and not the rule, and hands the
player information their character does not have. `isMisleading` exists so a
caller can tell the two apart without matching on the text.

### The gate, RED-proved

The whole slice rests on `grantedTo` reading the grants and not section C, so
that is the mutation: point it at `pathwayDifferences()` and **four tests
redden**, including the one named for it. Restored from a `cp` copy, never
`git checkout` — the file held uncommitted work.

Four extractor mutations also fire: a bare-substring `GRANT` (grants Moon and
Wheel of Fortune wrongly), dropping the Hermit alias, removing Moon from
`grants()`, and moving Mother and Red Priest to Sequence 9.

### The diff review: one MEDIUM refused with the lines that disprove it

It reported that `Look again` rolls with stale inputs, that `spiAvailable`
never recomposes, and that the button stays enabled after the pool empties.
All three are wrong, and the code says so:

- `spiAvailable` is `vitals.maxSpi - session.spiSpent` read at
  `MainActivity.kt:1092`, in the caller's composable scope, and `spiSpent` is
  `mutableIntStateOf` (`BeyonderSession.kt:74`). Spending recomposes the caller
  and the dialog is handed the new figure — the same wiring `RitualDialog`
  already ships.
- **Nothing about spending SPI can make the target stale**:
  `SpiritVision.targetFor` is `per + shock + hurt`, and those read the
  ATTRIBUTE and the HP/FP pools. There is no SPI term. Passing a remaining pool
  is the defect `DetectionDialog` already records having made once.
- Re-roll-and-recharge is `ArtifactDialog`'s `"Use again"` exactly.

What the finding was worth: the button did not SAY the second press costs
another point. It now reads `Look again (1 SPI)`, and the warrant for all three
refusals is in the dialog's KDoc rather than in this file alone.

Its two LOWs asked for Compose tests, which this repo cannot write. The
survivable half is that both test NAMES overclaimed: `section C is reference and
is never the gate` asserted no such thing, and its last line duplicated an
assertion from the test above it — the forced-assertion pattern for the seventh
time. It is now `section C and the grants are the same size and disagree both
ways`, asserting the set difference in each direction, which nothing else in
Kotlin does.

### One decision worth inheriting

`grantedTo` **throws** on a pathway no content file prints, rather than
answering false. This app walks 22 pathways plus the non-standard ones, and a
typo silently withdrawing a character's ability is the failure that refuses to
be had. The reviewer checked whether that crashes the sheet screen and found it
cannot: `formFor` short-circuits first.

### What shipped

- `tools/extract_spirit_vision.py` — `GRANT`, `grants()`, and a `verify()` that
  pins the swap in both directions, the seven grants verbatim, the Hermit's
  alias, the three non-grants, and the upgrade invariant.
- `spirit_vision.json` — a `grants` block; the file now has a loader.
- `SpiritVision` + six content types + `ContentLoader.spiritVision()`
  (`loadWhole`, six sibling sections rather than `entries`), with
  `SpiritVisionTest` (15 tests).
- `SpiritVisionDialog` and one BEYONDER hub tile, gated on the character's own
  block and labelled with the pathway's own name for the ability.
- Two Python tests: the swap, and the three-class predicate.

Chapter 7.6 now reads 100.0% because something reads it. **Every content file
has a loader: 79 of 79.** 1650 Kotlin (1164 `core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20
`core:model`) and 308 Python, all green.

**Not device-verified.** The tile and the dialog compile and the rules beneath
them have 15 tests; no test in this repo reaches a composable.

### The next slice, and the sweep that names it

The file-for-loader sweep is now clean and stays worth re-running, but it will
not find the next thing. What this slice suggests instead is the direction that
found its own defect: **a check that runs one way over two printings has a
blind side, and the reverse query is a separate sweep.** Section C had been
checked row → block since it was extracted; block → row was never run, and it
is where Moon was. Candidates with the same shape: the fixtures against the
catalogue (6ct ran fixture → Kotlin; catalogue → fixture is unrun), and
`sourceLines` claims against the extractors that write them.

## 6dg. A guard that could not pass, and the surface it was waiting for

`tools/extract_glossary.py` was sitting untracked in the tree, fully written,
with a docstring arguing its own case. It had never run. `glossary.json` did
not exist, no `ContentLoader` function named it, and nothing in the app could
show a player what CoR is.

### Two assertions that cannot both hold

`verify()` asserted `len(ent) == 26` and, eleven lines further down, that
`"Examples"` is not among the terms. With the `NOT_TERMS` exclusion in force
the parse yields **25**; without it, 26 — *including* `Examples`. There is no
state in which both assertions pass, so `verify()` had never reached its end,
and the missing output file is the corroboration.

The glossary is 25 entries. The docstring said 28, the assertion said 26, and
the book says 25. **Three numbers, no query between them** — 6df's lesson
arriving from a different direction: 6df's count was right and unreproducible,
this one was simply wrong, and the same fix covers both. `TERMS` is now a named
ordered list and `verify()` asserts equality against it, so the file states the
set rather than its size.

### What the broken count was hiding

The closing note wraps onto a second line — *"Characters (4th Edition)."* —
which starts with neither the note nor a term. `entries()` skipped the note
with `continue`, so the second line fell through to the fold-into-the-previous
branch and landed in the last entry. `Will` read:

> Mental fortitude and resistance to influence. = IQ at character creation.
> Used to resist intimidation, mind control, and CoR. **Characters (4th
> Edition).**

The closing note is now a `break`. Nothing about that defect is visible in a
term list: all 25 terms are present, correctly spelled, in the book's order,
and one definition carries a sentence the book prints somewhere else.

### The guard that replaced the count, and the guard's own vacuity

A term list cannot see a continuation line that stops being emitted — the
definition just gets shorter. So `verify()` now also asserts **conservation**:
the entries, rendered back to `Term: definition` and joined, must EQUAL the
lines they were built from. Nothing dropped, nothing added, nothing attached
to the wrong entry.

The first version of that assertion was **vacuous**, and the mutation suite is
what said so. It built its expected value by calling `stream()` — the same
function the parse uses — so widening `FURNITURE` to swallow a continuation
line dropped that line from the output *and* from the expectation, and the
check stayed green. It now reads the raw lines from `lines.json` and drops
page furniture by NAME (`FURNITURE_IN_RANGE`), which is the only version that
can disagree with the parser.

Naming the furniture then **caught its own author**: the list shipped with four
entries, two page breaks' worth, and the baseline went red. Only ONE page break
is inside the range — p.167 → p.168, falling between the second and third lines
of the SPI entry. The p.166 → p.167 break sits two lines *above* the heading and
so is out of range. The assertion written to catch a future page-break move
caught a present miscount instead.

Seven mutations, all fired, all restored: drop a continuation line, neuter the
closing-note stop, allow a full stop in a term, remove the `Examples`
exclusion, run the range into the back cover, shorten `TERMS`, and move a
furniture line to the wrong number. An eighth — removing the apostrophe from
the character class — stays GREEN, correctly: no *term* contains one, only
definitions do.

### A comment crediting the wrong condition, again

`TERM`'s comment said *"The length bound is what keeps a mid-sentence colon
out"*, and named `Examples` as a line that *"never matches at the start"*. Both
false, and the second is contradicted by the paragraph above it — `Examples`
matches at the start of line 10193, which is precisely why `NOT_TERMS` exists.

Measured, one condition at a time:

| Mutation | Terms |
|---|---|
| baseline | 25 |
| add `.` to the class | **26** — `Disadvantages give points back. Starting budget` |
| add `,` to the class | 25 |
| relax the bound 58 → 200 | 25 |

The **full stop** is load-bearing; the bound is slack (the longest real term is
31 characters). Line 10172 ends *"...Starting budget: 70 points."* and would
have parsed as a term named for the prose in front of its colon, stealing
`Character Points`' continuation. 6cb's pattern for the third time: a safety
rationale is a hypothesis about which condition does the work, and the
hypothesis was wrong. The mutation now runs in `test_tools.py`, because a
comment is not a pin.

### The design review: one finding taken whole, two refused with their own warrants

`task --effort high`, three questions, four files, with the audit paragraph and
the `UNPAYABLE`/`UNMODELLED` precedent quoted **inline** — the reviewer is told
not to read `CLAUDE.md` or this file, so a precedent it cannot see is a
precedent it cannot weigh (6df).

**Q3 taken whole.** Its answer is the conservation check above: a set assertion
cannot see order, duplicates, or a stray line folded into a valid neighbour. It
named `Will` as the entry a stray line would lengthen. It was right, and the
stray line was already there.

**Q1 refused, and the refusal fixed the warrant rather than the code.** The
reviewer called the gallery top bar a weak host: `ThemePicker` sits there
because it MUTATES a preference the whole app reads, and a static reference
sheet does not inherit that reason — 6cx's "a precedent travels by ROLE, not by
shape", correctly applied to a decomposition that had cited exactly that
resemblance. The control stays where it is on a reason of its own: `SHEET`,
`PATHWAY` and `BUILDER` all require a selected character, and *"what is CoR"*
is not a question about one. The gallery is the only character-independent
screen this app has. The reviewer's alternative — a row in the body list beside
"Start from a blank sheet" — was declined because that list is the roster, and
a reference surface below a scroll of 23 characters is reachable the way
`Divination.UNAPPLIED` is reachable.

**Q2 refused.** The reviewer argued the surface is scope talked into existence,
and that the honest slice is extractor + JSON with a recorded refusal. Against
it: `docs/AUDIT-2026-08-19.md:75` records *"nothing in the app browses the
book"* as **the dominant term in the 58% parity figure**, so the surface closes
a gap this repo has already written down rather than inventing one. And a
loader with no caller is 6cf exactly.

### G moved to 100.0%, and the number is nearly weightless

Chapter G went 0.0% → 100.0%. **Do not quote that without its denominator.**
`coverage.py`'s `MECHANICAL` filter matches **three lines** in the whole
chapter — the `HP`, `Spirit Vision` and `3d6` entries, the only ones carrying a
number it recognises. The other 55 lines of glossary are prose, and so are the
39 lines of back matter below the closing note (blurb, credits, and a full
table-of-contents reprint), which are inside G's declared page range, claimed
by nothing, and **invisible to the metric because not one of them is
mechanical**. 6db in the other direction: there an unread chapter reported
100%, here a read one reports 100% for a reason almost unrelated to having been
read. `sourceLines` — 10156-10213 — is the honest statement of what was read,
and a test pins the denominator so the next sweep cannot mistake the percentage
for completion.

### One line I nearly typed into a screen

The sheet's first draft carried a subtitle: *"Terms unique to this book. For
full GURPS terminology, see the GURPS Basic Set: Characters (4th Edition)."*
That is book text — lines 10212-10213, the closing note the extractor
deliberately drops — hand-retyped into a composable. 6cq's defect class,
authored rather than inherited. The sheet shows its title and nothing else.

### The sweep, and the next slice it names

A direction this repo had not run: **every content FILE checked for a loader.**
Previous sweeps ran fields-for-readers (6ai), functions-for-callers (6cf) and
rows-for-consumers (6ci); none of them can see a file that `ContentLoader`
never names. 79 files, and exactly **one** is unloaded:

```bash
LOADER=core/rules/src/main/kotlin/com/pathways/rules/content/ContentLoader.kt
for f in core/rules/src/main/resources/content/*.json; do
  grep -q "\"$(basename "$f")\"" "$LOADER" || echo "NO LOADER: $(basename "$f")"
done
```

`spirit_vision.json`. And it is worse than unloaded: it is the **sole claimant
of chapter 7.6**, which `coverage.py` therefore reports at 100.0%. A grep for
`spirit_vision` across Kotlin returns nothing. So 7.6's completion rests on a
file no code reads — the same shape 6db found when an unread chapter reported
100%, except this one has content extracted and stranded rather than missing.
**That is the named next slice, and the query above is what checks it.**

The first run of that sweep also produced 79 false positives: a relative path
put the loader out of reach, every `grep` failed, and a failed command read as
a finding — so the query above resolves the loader once and asserts it exists.

### What shipped

- `tools/extract_glossary.py` — the count replaced by `TERMS`, the closing note
  a stop rather than a skip, `FURNITURE_IN_RANGE` named, conservation asserted
  against the raw lines.
- `content/glossary.json` — 25 entries, `sourceLines` `{"G": [[10156, 10213]]}`.
- `GlossaryEntry` + `ContentLoader.glossary()`, with `GlossaryContentTest`
  (3 tests) pinning the ordered set, whole-sentence definitions, and the folded
  continuations.
- `app/GlossarySheet.kt` and one icon in `PremadeGallery`'s existing `actions`.
- Four Python tests: the typography the exclusion rests on, the full-stop
  mutation, the conservation guard's own vacuity, and G's denominator.

1635 Kotlin (1149 `core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and 306 Python,
all green.

**Both counts in `CLAUDE.md` needed re-deriving, and one was wrong.** The
Python row read 300 against a `HEAD` that carried 302, so adding this slice's
delta to the recorded number would have shipped 304. And counting Kotlin
straight after a filtered run gives **489**: `--tests '*GlossaryContentTest*'`
leaves the results directory holding only the three files it wrote, and Gradle
then reports the unfiltered `test` task UP-TO-DATE and does not repopulate it.
`--rerun-tasks` is what makes the directory mean what the row claims.

### The diff review: three LOWs, all three taken

`task --effort high` again, target list named. All three findings were about
assertions rather than behaviour, and all three were right.

**Five assertions were forced by the canonical term list.** The exact ordered
`assertEquals` at the top of `GlossaryContentTest` already fixes the order, so
a separate "is not alphabetical" test, an `Examples`-is-not-a-term check, and a
`containsAll` over the five terms the engine implements could not fail on their
own — and `definition.isNotBlank()` is forced by the assertion one line above
it that the definition ends in a full stop. Two tests deleted, two assertions
removed, and what they were *saying* moved into the canonical list's KDoc,
which is where an intent with no independent failure mode belongs. Five in five
slices now; the reviewer found this set in a file written to be careful about
exactly this.

**`FURNITURE_IN_RANGE` was consumed by text and is now keyed by line number.**
The ledger popped its head whenever a raw line equalled it, so a line that came
to read exactly like the page header could be dropped in the header's place
while the real header went unnoticed and conservation still passed. The
reviewer's concrete case needed two simultaneous changes and is remote; the fix
is four lines and makes each drop exact, which is the whole point of a guard
built to disagree with the parser. It also bought the seventh mutation above.

**Q3 returned no finding**, asked plainly: `remember { ContentLoader.glossary() }`
on a 25-entry classpath resource is the pattern `DefenseDialog.kt:252` and
`PathwayScreen.kt:104` already use, and no coroutine was proposed.

### What is NOT verified, and the risk that was removed instead of tested

**The sheet has never been rendered.** Compile plus three unit tests prove
`ContentLoader.glossary()` returns the right 25 rows in the right order; nothing
here proves the control opens. Every app-level defect in this repo's history has
landed in wiring rather than rules, so read this slice as *compiles,
unit-tested, not device-verified*.

One specific risk was removed rather than left untested. The sheet first shipped
a `LazyColumn` inside `ModalBottomSheet`, which puts the list's vertical scroll
and the sheet's drag-to-dismiss on the same gesture — the usual symptom is a
list that will not scroll or a sheet that dismisses when you try. `ThemePicker`
is NOT precedent for that: it uses a plain `Column`. Twenty-five short rows do
not need lazy layout, so the list is now a `Column` with `verticalScroll`,
matching the file one directory over. **The cheapest answer to an interaction
question no test in this repo can reach is not to create the interaction.**

## 6df. Three clauses, no join — and a count that could not be checked

6de named this next: the Will rolls, and the corpus its own sweep should have
used. Both halves survived. What did not survive is the shape of the answer.

### The census, and why 6de's number was unfalsifiable

6de recorded "four rows name Will rolls, all four CONDITIONAL". The number is
right and it was **unreproducible**, because the sentence states no query.
Three queries, three numbers:

| Query | Rows |
|---|---|
| `to all Will rolls` — the shape 6de's own sweep says it ran | 1 |
| `Will roll` | 5 |
| `Will rolls` (plural) | **4** |

The plural query is the one that returns four, and what it drops is
`Compulsive Gambling`: "requires Will **roll** at -2", singular, and already
read as a self-control check through the catalogue's own `selfControl` field.
So the recorded count was correct under a filter nobody could recover from the
words. **A count without its query cannot be checked**, and the fix is a test
that asserts the set and names the filter, not a paragraph that asserts the
number.

Of the four the plural query returns, two are already read (`Compulsive
Gambling` at -2, `Reluctant Killer` at 0 — a row NAMING a roll is not a row
MODIFYING one). Three carry a modifier and reached nothing:

| Row | Cost | Clause |
|---|---|---|
| `Incorruptible Will` | 10 | "+3 to all Will rolls **to resist Beyonder abilities, evil god whispers, and ritual compulsion**. Does not apply to mundane social pressure." |
| `Grief-Stricken` | 5 | "**In situations that echo a specific loss**, Will rolls **to act clearly** are at -2." |
| `Evil Eye Fear` | 5 | "**If interrupted from a warding routine**, -1 to Will rolls for the day." |

None is carried by a fixture, and all three are buyable today —
`PurchasableTraits.offered()` takes the whole advantages and disadvantages
catalogue minus Wealth, which is 6de's own correction to its own reachability
verdict, applied.

### The scope, which is where the slice was nearly wrong

The obvious split was two rows applied and `Grief-Stricken` refused: its cell
adds "to act clearly" on top of its circumstance, which looked like `Hard to
Kill`'s "HT rolls **to avoid death**" — the shape 6de refused the consciousness
roll one slice earlier. A design review agreed there was a problem and returned
**NO-SHIP**, and the reviewer's own answer was a per-row scope enum
(`allWill` / `fright` / `selfControl` / `concentrate` / `unsupported`).

Both were wrong, and one line of the repo settled it. **The discriminator is
not whether the cell adds a qualifier — it is whether the qualifier names a
roll this book PRINTS.** `Hard to Kill`'s "to avoid death" picks one of a
printed pair, which is what made scoping available at all; `High Pain
Threshold`'s "to avoid knockdown" names a printed roll this app does not make,
which is why it reached neither. "To act clearly" names no printed roll, and
