neither does "to resist Beyonder abilities". So all three name a
**circumstance**, all three are declarations, and the roll each reaches is
whichever bare Will roll is happening when the GM says the circumstance holds.

That answers the reviewer's second finding by removing it: with no row
qualified by roll, its enum has **one inhabitant** — an abstraction with one
implementation, which this repo's own rules name as a prohibition. **Take a
reviewer's diagnosis over its prescription** (6cz), and note the reviewer was
working from a blind spot it had been given: it was told not to read the slice
log, so the `Fit` / `Hard to Kill` / `High Pain Threshold` precedent was not
available to it. **A review's reach is bounded by the corpus you hand it**, and
that bound is the reviewer's input rather than its judgement.

### The suite knew and production did not

`SelfControlTest` has recorded since 6am that `Grief-Stricken`'s offset "is
attached TO a roll ... so it is a modifier and `TraitEffects`' business", in a
test that lists it among four mechanics refused as self-control checks. It was
routed correctly, and `TraitEffects` **never took the business** — for four
milestones, on a row a player can buy.

That is 6bx's class, and it matters that 6bz ran exactly this sweep — *what
does the TEST suite know that production does not?* — **deliberately, and
closed it.** This is the third instance, found by accident again. A sweep
verdict expires (6ba); so does the sweep that was run to make sure none were
left.

### What shipped

`TraitEffects.WILL_CLAUSES` with the three rows quoted verbatim, plus
`willClauses` / `willClauseRows` / `willClauseNames` and an entry in `known()`.
`FrightBonus` / `frightBonus` become `ClauseBonus` / `clauseBonus`: the
filter-sum-join is behaviourally generic and only its NAME was scoped to the
Fright Check, so a second copy would have been the defect this file records
five times over. The chip row is extracted to one `ClauseChips` composable read
by three dialogs.

Three plumbing decisions worth inheriting:

- **`Concentration` takes its own parameter.** `fromTraits`, not folded into
  `hurt` — that one is named for reeling and fatigue and renders as "hurt or
  tired", so a trait bonus arriving through it would print under someone
  else's label. Its two call sites (`targetFor` for the caption, `attempt` for
  the roll) both take it, and `attempt` reaches it through `targetFor` rather
  than re-deriving.
- **The Fright Check takes both lists, concatenated.** It IS a bare Will roll,
  so refusing the Will rows there would be a qualifier the book does not print.
  `TraitClause.key` is `"$shown / $printed"` and no row appears in both lists,
  so no declaration can move two clauses.
- **`Incorruptible Will`'s exclusion is printed, not coded.** "Does not apply
  to mundane social pressure" is the GM's to honour; no code here can tell
  which pressure a scene is, and the chip quotes the cell.

### The review's four findings, two taken and two refused

Taken: `declared` is now keyed on `clauses` in both dialogs — a declaration is
a set of clause KEYS, and a changed trait list retires the key one names, which
is the stale-state family 6k, 6y and 6af each found once.

**Refused: recomputing the bonus inside `onClick`.** The reviewer's
stale-capture argument would create a SECOND call site for the number the
caption already prints — which is the drift the same review, in its own answer
to question two, certified absent. A LOW that reintroduces a MEDIUM is not a
LOW (6ch). The re-entrancy that IS reachable, two taps on the Roll button, was
already guarded inline (6p). The refusal is recorded where the value is
computed.

The review's other two findings were about the tests and both were right: a
test named "two of them are already read" never called the reader, and one
named "answers every bare will roll" proved two sites of three. Both now assert
what their names claim, the second through `FrightCheck.against`.

### Proof

1632 Kotlin tests and 300 Python, all green. RED-proved by neutering one
reading at a time and restoring from a copy, never `git checkout` (6ba):
`Incorruptible Will` +3 to +1 reddens the pin and the sum; `Concentration`
dropping `fromTraits` reddens the cross-site test; removing the
`Grief-Stricken` row reddens three; `FrightCheck.against` ignoring its modifier
reddens the third-site assertion the review asked for. The screens are
device-unverified, as every Compose change in this repo is.

**Next: no slice is named, and that is deliberate.** 6cp's lesson is that a
closing paragraph is the one part of this log nothing verifies. The sweep
directions already run each expire rather than stand — but one lead carries
evidence rather than memory.

**A lead in this paragraph was checked before it was written down, and it was
wrong.** `known()` named `FIT` alone where `HT_ROLL_TRAITS` holds three, which
looked like `Very Fit` and `Unfit` sitting outside the typo guard. Typo-ing
`VERY_FIT` reddens that guard under the OLD `known()` too: both are
`PARTLY_APPLIED` keys, which `known()` already reads. So there was no hole —
there was **coverage by a second route**, which is the accident this file's own
KDoc records against Outdoorsman. `known()` now derives from the map anyway, so
the first HT-roll trait with nothing left to report is covered by the route that
applies it; the comment says which of those two things it is. **RED-prove what
the OLD guard allowed, not only what the new one catches** — the difference
between a fix and a tidy-up is invisible without it.

And the census direction this
slice used — **every recorded COUNT re-run against a stated query** — has never
been run over this file, where counts are quoted constantly and filters almost
never are.

## 6de. Two flags, no reader — the rolls the HP table prints

6dd named a sweep: every rule delivered to one roll class while its printing
names a wider one. **The sweep came back closed, and the finding is what it
turned up on the way.**

### The sweep, and its verdict

Query: every `to all <X> rolls` clause in the content, against what the app
joins it to. 16 shapes across five files. The controlling-attribute joins are
already deliberate — `Alertness` on Per (6al), `Fit`/`Unfit` on HT (6bs),
`Ether Body Damage` on SPI (6ca) — and each has both paths, typed and bare.
The open class was **Will**: four rows name Will rolls, and this app makes
three bare Will rolls (self-control, Concentration, and the Fright Check).

All four are CONDITIONAL — `Incorruptible Will` is "+3 to all Will rolls **to
resist Beyonder abilities, evil god whispers, and ritual compulsion**",
`Grief-Stricken` is "in situations that echo a specific loss" — and **no
fixture carries any of them**. A conditional clause is a different feature
from an unconditional one (6bt), so the answer is that nothing joins, and
`SPI_ROLL_TRAITS`' KDoc sentence that would have made the next sweep skip this
("the app's other bare rolls are Will, IQ and Per, and nothing here names
those") was loose. It is corrected in place: Will IS named, four times, all
conditional, zero carriers. **A sweep that finds nothing still has a
deliverable — the sentence that would have stopped the next one.**

### What it found instead

`pool_thresholds.json` prints two rolls on the HP table:

| Row | Effect |
|---|---|
| `0 HP` | "Roll 3d6 <= HT or fall unconscious; roll each turn to remain conscious" |
| `-HP` | "Roll vs. HT or die; must roll vs. HT each turn while below this threshold" |

`Pools.hp` has computed `rollsToStayConscious` and `rollsToSurvive` **since
M0**, and a grep for readers returns `PoolsTest` and nothing else. The sheet's
`PoolRow` printed the sentence; no screen could roll it. That is 6cf's class
(tested, documented, called by nothing) sitting under 6dc's class (one screen
prints the rule, the next ignores it), on the same table 6dd had just fixed.

Reachability was checked before the slice was named, not assumed:
`BeyonderSession.spend` floors `hpLost` at zero and caps nothing, so current HP
goes arbitrarily negative and **both** rolls are reachable — not one.

### The scope, which is the whole slice

Three traits name an HT roll and none of them means the same thing:

| Trait | Cell | Reaches |
|---|---|---|
| `Fit` / `Very Fit` / `Unfit` | "to all HT rolls" | both checks, and the Major Wound's |
| `Hard to Kill` | "HT rolls **to avoid death**" | the `-HP` roll alone |
| `High Pain Threshold` | "to avoid knockdown" | neither |

`Hard to Kill` is refused the consciousness roll because dying starts one row
lower: widening a clause that names its own condition is the move 6ck refused
for facing. The design review put the same question the other way — is losing
consciousness part of a death spiral? — and answered it from the table's own
boundary rather than from the fiction.

**`VitalRolls.due` returns BOTH checks below `-HP`**, because `Pools` sets both
flags there and the dying row does not withdraw the row above it. Reporting one
would be a reading; reporting what the model already says is not.

### Very Fit, and a guard that could not see it

`HT_ROLL_TRAITS`' KDoc says it holds "every trait whose cell says 'to all HT
rolls'". It held `Fit` and `Unfit`. **`Very Fit` prints "+2 to all HT rolls"
and was not in it** — and `htRollNames()`, the accessor written for the guard
tests, returns the map's own keys, so every test built on it asserted the data
rather than the failure. The catalogue is the corpus that can disagree, and the
new test reads it: neutering the map entry reddens two tests, which is the RED
proof that it was never covered before.

Its consequence reaches further than this slice, which the diff review caught:
`Very Fit` now moves the **Major Wound's** HT roll too, through the same
`htRollBonus`. That is correct — "all HT rolls" includes the one this app
already made — but nothing asserted it, and a behaviour change nothing asserts
is one nobody chose. Pinned.

### Three refusals whose reason died

`TraitEffects.UNAPPLIED` said "this app models no death roll to avoid" of
`Hard to Kill`, and two more entries cited that refusal by name:

- **`Hard to Kill`** — now applied; the entry is gone and `deathRollBonus`
  carries the history in its KDoc.
- **`Uncanny Survivor`** — "once per campaign arc, when you would die on a
  death roll, succeed automatically". The death roll now exists, so the reason
  is re-stated on the half that survives: a once-per-arc budget needs a
  campaign this app does not hold, and the book hands the cost to the GM.
- **`Earth Mother`** — "revive from death" is not a modifier on a roll, and the
  HP table's rolls stop at "Dead — no roll required". The clock half of its
  reason was always the load-bearing one.

A refusal expires exactly like a sweep verdict (6ba, 6bl), and three of them
expiring on one commit is what a shipped roll does to a file that used its
absence as a reason.

### Deliberately not modelled

**The repetition.** Both rows say "each turn". This app holds no clock (6ad,
6ah, 6an, 6dc), so one roll is offered and the screen says the book asks for
one a turn — silence there would let a single roll read as the whole rule.

**The outcome.** Nothing latches. `Shock` latches because the app creates a
state it can then charge for; nothing in this app consumes unconsciousness, so
storing it would recreate the field-with-no-reader this slice exists to remove.
The design review's strongest counter is recorded rather than dismissed: a
failed consciousness roll IS a real state, and the day something reads it, this
decision is the one to revisit.

### One test caught its own author

`targetFor` was first asserted at HT 12 with `Fit` and a reeling `-1` — and
12 + 1 − 1 is 12, so **the assertion passed with both terms removed**. Fifth
vacuity in this file's recent history, and the same shape each time: the
expectation was written from the arithmetic rather than from the failure. It
now asserts three targets whose differences are the two terms.

### Two follow-ups the diff review and a second pass added

`VitalRolls.due` returns both checks below `-HP` and the screen rendered two
buttons reading `Roll HT n` — with **different** numbers, because `Hard to
Kill` lifts one of them and not the other. A player would have had to infer
which target belonged to which rule from two long sentences that start alike.
They are now named by the book's own row, `0 HP` and `-HP`, so no label is
invented (6cn: an unnamed label gets picked by whoever writes the screen, and
the default is the worse one).

And the FP reading is now stated rather than implied. These rolls are gated on
an **HP** threshold and take the FP penalty too, because "-1 to all rolls per 1
FP below 0" names ROLLS and not a pool; a character at -8 FP and 0 HP rolls at
-9, both rules at once. Scoping it to HP would add a qualifier the book does
not print, which 4.1 forbids in the same way it forbids dropping one.

**Next: the Will rolls, and the corpus the sweep should have used.** The four
conditional Will rows are carried by no fixture — but `PurchasableTraits.offered()`
takes the WHOLE advantages and disadvantages catalogue, minus Wealth, and none
of the four is excluded. **They are buyable today.** So "no carrier" was a
claim about the 23 sheets and not about the app, and every census in this file
that used the fixtures as its reachability corpus has the same blind spot. The
slice is a declared-condition chip on the three bare Will rolls, the shape
`socialClauses` and `frightClauses` already have — and the wider finding is the
corpus: a purchasable row is reachable whether or not a premade prints it.

## 6dd. One sentence, two reaches — and the bar it never had to clear

6dc named this next and named the wrong bar for it: *"whether it reaches a
defence VALUE on a screen that never rolls one needs the bar 6ck set for the
stun — a printing that says 'active defenseS'."* **That bar was already
cleared, four slices earlier, by a rule in production source.** Running the
inherited reason as a query is what found it (stage 1's rule), and the answer
was one grep away in `Shock.kt`.

### The finding

Three pool penalties print the same unqualified phrase:

| Book line | Printed |
|---|---|
| 2702 (p. 40) | `1/3 HP remaining` → `Reeling: -1 to all rolls` |
| 2852 (p. 42) | `At 1/3 FP or below` → `-1 to all rolls; Move and Dodge halved` |
| 2724 (p. 41) | `FP below 0: -1 to all rolls per 1 FP below 0` |

They reached `SkillKey` rolls and nothing else, through
`Conditions.forSkill`'s modifier ledger. **Line 2824, on the same page as the
second one, prints the identical phrase** — the Major Wound's success row,
`-4 to all rolls for 1 turn from shock and pain` — and `Shock` reaches all four
`RollKind`s with it, on a warrant its own KDoc records:

> **"All rolls" is taken at its word, and that is a reading.** GURPS 4e exempts
> active defences from its shock penalty; this book prints "all rolls"
> unqualified.

So one sentence had **two reaches in one app**, decided by which function the
wiring happened to land in. In play that meant a reeling, fatigued character:

- defended at **full Dodge, Parry and Block** (`ActiveDefenses.everyDefence`
  carried the stun's -4 and shock's -4 and nothing from the trackers),
- rolled their **Fright Check, self-control roll, Concentration and Detection**
  at full value (the four bare-attribute dialogs took `shockOnAttribute` alone),
- rolled the **Major Wound's own HT roll** at full value,

while their shock was applied to every one of those.

### The bar, and why 6ck's was the wrong one

6ck refused the facing penalty because `Attacked from side: -2 to defense` is
printed **singular** and needs a second printing to widen it to three rows.
That condition does not describe this rule at all. `-1 to all rolls` names a
**superset that already contains a defence** — nothing needs widening, and the
app had already decided, in `RollKind.ACTIVE_DEFENSE`'s own KDoc, that a
defence is *"a number the player rolls under"*. **A precedent travels with the
condition that produced it** (6cm), and so does a refusal's bar: inheriting
6ck's here would have refused a rule on a fact about a different sentence.

### What ships

`Conditions.penaltyFor(kind, hp, fp)` answers once for the three kinds the
ledger cannot see, and **refuses `RollKind.SKILL`** — that path takes them
through `forSkill`, and a caller taking both would charge a reeling character
twice with no other number on screen disagreeing. Its RED proof deleted the
`require` and reddened exactly one test of thirteen.

`spi` and `cor` are deliberately not in it. Spiritual Attrition prints "all
SPI-based **SKILL** rolls" and the CoR ladder "all **ritual** rolls"; both name
a scope, and a defence value has no skill to match against.

**Shock's own exclusion does not transfer, and that is the interesting half.**
`Shock.appliesTo` refuses `MAJOR_WOUND_HT` because that roll is what *creates*
the shock — an argument about WHEN, not about what the roll is. Nothing creates
reeling mid-roll: the character carried it in. So the two states answer
differently for the same kind, and `DamageDialog`'s call site names the kind so
the difference can be read rather than guessed.

`everyDefence` takes `poolPenalty` with **no default** (6ch: a literal at a
call site is a domain claim nobody argued for). Neutering the term reddened
2 of 27 `ActiveDefensesTest` cases and left the other 25 green.

### The composition order, which the book does not print

p. 42 prints two clauses for one state: `-1 to all rolls; Move and Dodge
halved`. 6dc's `Pools.halvedForFatigue` halves the BASE score, round up; the
boost, Dive!, Retreat and a shield's DB are additive whole numbers on top. The
-1 lands **on top**, where the stun's -4 and shock's -4 already do — halving is
a property of the Dodge SCORE and the -1 is a property of every ROLL. At base 8
the readings differ (`ceil(8/2)-1 = 3` against `ceil(7/2) = 4`), which is what
makes it a decision rather than a formatting detail. Both are pinned.

**The diff review's finding is about that test, and it is right.** The test
composes both readings itself, so it would stay green if `MainActivity` were
edited to halve `vitals.dodge + poolPenalty`. What actually stops that is the
**boundary**: `DefenseDialog` is handed a Dodge that is already halved and
never sees the raw score, so the dialog cannot express the refused order —
only the one site that owns the halving could, and no test in this repo can
reach a composable (6cq). The test now says which of those it is.

### Two process findings

**A reviewer can review the wrong target and exit clean.** `review --wait` with
no argument picked up `tools/extract_glossary.py` — untracked leftover from an
earlier session, not in this diff — reported two P2s about it, and dismissed
the actual change in one sentence. Re-asked with the target named and the
leftover excluded, the same reviewer returned the Medium above on its first
pass. **Read the reviewer's target list before reading its findings**; a
one-sentence "nothing found" over ten changed files is a non-answer. Its two
P2s are kept here rather than discarded, because that file is still untracked
and the next session would re-derive them: `tools/extract_glossary.py:128`'s
expected-count assertion always raises against today's
`build/extract/lines.json` (25 entries parsed), and once that is fixed, lines
104-106 fold book line 10213 (`Characters (4th Edition).`) into the `Will`
definition, because the closing note spans two lines and only the first is
skipped. Neither is this slice's work; both are checkable claims.

**`adversarial-review --wait` refused its own input**: `Input exceeds the
maximum length of 1048576 characters`. Not the prompt — the companion
discovers `CLAUDE.md` from the cwd the way Claude does, and this repo's
instruction file plus `docs/SLICE-LOG.md` are several hundred KB. The same
three questions through `task --effort high`, with an explicit *"do not read
CLAUDE.md or docs/SLICE-LOG.md"*, answered in full. Codex's usage limit had
reset (14:23, and the clock read 23:14 — 6am/6as's rule paying again).

### Two things a review AFTER the commit found

The diff applied a printed clause to Fright, Concentrate and Detection and gave
`DefenseDialog` **the number with no text** — a reeling character's Parry
dropping by 1 with nothing on screen saying why, which is the standard the same
diff's own `Detection` KDoc quotes ("a target that moves without the breakdown
saying why is how these numbers stopped reconciling", 6ag, 6ai). It now
announces itself beside the stun, inside the same `refusal.defends` block so a
withdrawn set of defences does not price a penalty on nothing (6cs).

The other was a claim, not a defect, and the check is the useful part. `hurt`
is re-read live on every recomposition, so a Major Wound HT roll made AFTER
Apply would charge the character for the very blow that triggered it — the
exact thing `Shock`'s own `MAJOR_WOUND_HT` exclusion exists to prevent, and the
opposite of what this slice's prose asserts. **Apply calls `onDismiss` in the
same handler**, so the panel is gone before that state exists; the tap order
cannot reach it. Latching would have been the wrong fix anyway (6ch: a live
pool must not be `remember`ed), and the reason now sits in the KDoc so the next
reader does not re-derive it.

### Left unapplied, deliberately

`Pools.thresholds(fp)` is still empty and FP's rows are still prose; nothing
here changed that. The **recovery and Regeneration RATES** stay unapplied for
6dc's mechanism reason — this app holds no clock — and 2899's Regeneration rule
still needs a reachability check before it can be named as a slice.

**The next slice: sweep the OTHER direction this one only half-ran.**
`Conditions.penaltyFor` now answers for three kinds; what has not been checked
is whether any *other* rule in this app is delivered to one roll class while
its printing names a wider one. The query is mechanical and the corpus is
small: every constant or clause that reaches `SkillKey` rolls alone
(`TraitEffects`' bonuses, `CommonModifiers`, the ritual and divination ladders),
asked whether its sentence names skills or names rolls. This slice found the
class by accident on one member; running it deliberately is the obligation
6ay's lesson sets.

## 6dc. The sentence one screen printed and the next screen ignored

6db named the recovery cluster and asked a precondition before any build:
`docs/HOW-TO-PLAY.md`'s *"FP recovery, stun duration and reload rates are yours
to run"* — is that a refusal with a mechanism reason, or a gap nobody looked
at? **It is both, and the split is the slice.** The sentence sits under the
bullet headed *"Track a clock it does not hold"*, so its reason is a mechanism
one and it covers the RATES. It never reached p. 42's other half — the
threshold rule, which needs no clock at all.

### The defect

Book line 2851-2852, in the same FP table:

```
At 1/3 FP or below | -1 to all rolls; Move and Dodge halved | Until above threshold
```

`Pools.fp` applied the -1 as `TIRED_PENALTY`, and `fpEffect` returned the whole
sentence verbatim, which `PoolRow` prints on the sheet screen. One tap away,
`DefenseDialog` was handed `vitals.dodge` — the derived score, never halved,
never FP-aware. **The screen that prints the rule and the screen that breaks it
are the same screen**, which is 6bl's class exactly.

### The census, re-run rather than inherited

6db's closing paragraph sized the cluster at "15 of the 33 newly visible
unclaimed lines". Re-running its own listing over 2842-2899 returns **16**, and
three of those are not unbuilt at all:

| Lines | State |
|---|---|
| 2847-2850 | Applied. `BeyonderSession.spend` charges 1 HP per FP spent below 0 |
| 2851-2852 | The -1 applied since 6h; **the halving reached nothing** |
| 2842-2846, 2861-2895 | Genuinely unread: rest, sleep, natural recovery, First Aid, Physician, Healing, five Regeneration rates |
| 2899 | Unread: Regeneration's interaction with the 0 HP consciousness roll |

The first two rows are unclaimed only because `coverage.py` builds its claimed
set from JSON `sourceLines`, and these rules live in Kotlin. **A count in a
handover is a claim about a query's output at a past moment** — re-running it
costs a minute and corrected both the arithmetic and what the number implied.
Chapter 5 stays at **73.9%** after this slice, which is the honest report: the
rule now applied claims no line, exactly as 6cy found for the attribute table.

### What the design review corrected before any code existed

Codex is still refusing (resets 2026-08-20), so the gate was
`ecc:kotlin-reviewer` on the DECOMPOSITION, scoped to three questions and three
files — the fallback 6cz cost two slices by walking past. It returned SHIP with
one required correction, and the correction was to my warrant:

- **CLAUDE.md 4.3 does not decide this.** I had cited it for rounding. Every
  `floorDiv` in `Pools` is a THRESHOLD COMPARISON, where the book states the
  fraction itself and the direction only matters for negatives. Halving a score
  to produce an output number is a different operation with no precedent in the
  file. **A rule cited from the right file can still be the wrong rule** — 4.3
  is about how this repo divides, not about what the book says to do here.
- So the direction is recorded as a CHOICE. The row prints "halved" bare, while
  the book prints "rounded down" (line 2450, the Deceptive Attack cap) and
  "round up" (line 6050, a halved FP maximum) where it cares — there is no
  house convention to fall back on. Rounding up ships on the one ground that
  survives: it cannot leave a character worse off than the printed sentence
  states. Both citations are pinned in `test_tools.py`, because an argument
  resting on a sentence needs the sentence guarded (6da).

The review also confirmed the placement by tracing the `remember` keys rather
than taking my word: `vitals` is `remember(sheet, drunk, session.edits)` and
`fpLost` is none of the three, so halving inside it would freeze the Dodge at
whatever the pool held when a potion or an edit last landed. It is a plain live
expression at the call site — `spiAvailable`'s precedent, in the same file.

### What shipped

- `Pools.isFatigued(fp)` — **one predicate, four readers.** `fp()`, `fpLevel`
  and `fpEffect` each re-derived `current <= floorDiv(max, 3)`; the fourth
  reader is the defence screen. The overload taking a `PoolStatus` refuses a
  non-FP pool: reeling is 1/3 HP and Spiritual Attrition is 1/3 SPI, the same
  fraction and neither halves anything.
- `Pools.halvedForFatigue(value, fp)` — ceiling, applied to the BASE score
  only. The boost, Acrobatic Dodge, Dive! and Retreat added afterwards print
  whole numbers by rules of their own, and halving the total would quietly
  halve a shield's DB too.
- `DefenseDialog` takes `fatigued` — the FACT, not the number — and prints the
  book's sentence under the row it moved, naming the rounding because the book
  does not.
- **`SheetComparison`'s Dodge row stays whole.** Found while checking for a
  second reader: that row audits the DERIVATION against the published sheet, so
  session state has no business in it. Two displays of one number, and only one
  of them is a table value.

### Not built, with the reason

The recovery and Regeneration rates stay unapplied: they are clocks, and this
app holds none — 6bf refused global round state and 6cp accepted per-round
values only because all six live in one composable. A daily or hourly tick is
further out than that. The player guide already refuses them for that reason,
which is why this slice leaves that file alone. Also unread and now recorded:
**"Very Rapid Healing" occurs once in the whole book** (line 2861) and appears
in no catalogue — `Rapid Recovery` (line 922, 5 pts) is a different rule, and
`Rapid Healing` (line 6928) is a potion grant that modifies the daily HT roll.
Three similar names, three different things; anything matching on name breaks
there. The one real join is line 6052, *"Grants Very Fast Regeneration for 10
seconds"* — a grant that names a level and prints no rate, where ch. 5's table
is the only place that rate lives.

### The review of the diff, and a fifth vacuity

The same reviewer on the diff: no CRITICAL or HIGH, and one MEDIUM that was
mine. My "the halving does not lift below zero" test asserted the effect text
of `fp(4, 12)` — the tired case, not the below-zero one its name and comment
were about. A regression that let `fpEffect`'s `current < 0` branch fall
through to the fatigued line would have passed it. **Fifth vacuity in four
slices, same cause: the assertion written from the shape of the DATA rather
than the shape of the FAILURE.** It now asserts both statuses as a pair, and is
RED-proved by deleting the below-zero branch.

**1604 Kotlin** (1118 `core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and **291
Python**, all green, counted from the JUnit XML and pytest rather than from
memory — and the count itself caught a miss of mine worth writing down: my
first glob read `*/build/test-results/test/*.xml` and reported **1138**,
because the `app` module writes to `testDebugUnitTest/` instead. The suite was
green either way; the NUMBER was wrong, and a per-module breakdown is what
showed it. **A total with no denominator per module cannot notice a whole
module missing.** Three readings RED-proved by mutating one at a
time and restoring from a `cp` copy: floor instead of ceiling (2 failures), the
wrong-pool guard deleted (1), the below-zero effect branch deleted (1). Not
device-verified — stated rather than skipped; the emulator run is what would
show a tired character's dialog reading `Dodge 5` with the sentence under it.

**The next slice is the OTHER half of the sentence this one applied.** Line
2852 reads "-1 to all rolls; Move and Dodge halved", and after this slice the
two clauses are treated differently on one screen: the halving reaches the
Dodge row, and the -1 reaches skill rolls only — `Conditions.forSkill` emits
it, and `DefenseDialog`'s three defence values take nothing from the pool
(`everyDefence` is built from `traits, stunned, shocked`). `Conditions` even
tags that modifier `ModTarget.AllRolls`, so the app's own model calls it
all-rolls and then never applies it to a defence number. **It is not obvious
that it should**: this app displays defences as target numbers and never rolls
them, so whether "all rolls" reaches a defence VALUE is exactly the question
6ck settled for the stun by finding a second printing that said "active
defenseS". Take it to a design review with that bar, not to an editor — and
note the asymmetry is live for every character who spends FP, where the
alternative below needs a reachability check first.

Behind it: chapter 5's 2899, "At 0 HP or below, a character with any level of
Regeneration still makes HT rolls to avoid unconsciousness".
`PoolStatus.rollsToStayConscious` already exists and already fires at 0 HP, so
this is a rule about a flag the app computes rather than a new table — but no
premade carries Regeneration and `advantages.json` prints only `Rapid
Recovery`, so check reachability first (6bv: an unreachable feature and a
missing one look identical in the source).

## 6db. A chapter reported 100% because the filter could not see it

The sweep that started this was the cheapest one available: `tools/coverage.py`
lists **chapter 7.5, Summoning Spiritual Creatures, pages 75-76, at 0.0%** — a
whole chapter nobody had read. It is two pages, so reading it costs nothing.

**It carried a recorded exclusion, and the exclusion had two halves that age
differently.** From an M3-era slice:

> Summoning (Ch. 7.5) was read and deliberately left unmodelled. It says "the
> GM must roll an additional 3d for the creature's response" and prints no
> response table; the creature's abilities, cost and attributes are a format
> for the GM to fill in. **Coverage agrees: one mechanical line in two pages.**

Run as a query rather than inherited, the **verdict survives and the evidence
expired**. The chapter really does print no response table — only a direction
("the better the response, the higher the chance they will peacefully arrive")
— and the Bookworm's abilities, contract cost and attributes are explicitly
"determined by the GM". Nothing to extract, still. But the last sentence is a
claim about an *instrument*, and the instrument was wrong. It is four
mechanical lines in two pages, not one.

**What the filter could not see is a cost that is not signed.** `MECHANICAL`
matched a die expression, a signed modifier, `N pts`, or an attribute offset.
Chapter 7.5 prices its example creature like this:

```
 Attributes: 4 HP
 Ability - Book Reading (1 SPI): The Bookworm can read through a novel-length
 Ability - Knowledge Transmission (1 SPI): By the contractor's request, ...
```

A bare integer followed by a pool. The filter **already admitted exactly that
shape** — `\d+\s*pts?\b` is a bare integer followed by the unit a rule reads —
and admitted no other unit, so every price this book quotes in SPI, HP, FP,
CoR or DR read as flavour prose. The widening is that same condition applied to
the rest of the pools, drawn from the filter's own definition rather than from
the lines I happened to find. The unit must follow the number, which is what
still keeps prose out: "around 5 cm in length" names no pool. There are no case
variants to worry about — the book never writes "Cor" or "hp".

**The important half is that the blind spot moved the DENOMINATOR.** A line the
filter cannot see is excluded from both sides of the ratio, and `main()` reads
an empty denominator as `pct = 100.0  # No mechanical lines to claim — chapter
is "complete"`. So invisibility rendered as completion, which is the worst
direction for an instrument whose only job is to report absence.

**Chapter 7.6, Spirit Vision Guide, is claimed by NO content file at all and
was reporting 100.0%.** Not "mostly done" — nothing in
`core/rules/src/main/resources/content/` names chapter `7.6` in its
`sourceLines`, and the chapter's mechanics are priced as "Activate by expending
1 SPI (1 SPI per minute to maintain)", so its mechanical-line count was zero
and the completion branch fired. It now reads **0.0%**, which is what it always
was.

**This was not a number nobody consulted.** 6cw's census — the one that found
chapter 8's equipment catalogue — opens "every chapter is at or near 100%
except four" and tabulates those four. 7.6 is not among them, and could not
have been: the instrument reported it complete. **An unread chapter was
filtered out of the sweep whose whole purpose is finding unread chapters.**
6cw's table stays as written; it was true of the instrument that produced it.

Census at the change: **286 lines book-wide became visible, 33 of them
unclaimed** (2144 -> 2430 matching lines). Six chapters moved:

| Ch | Before | After | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.6 Spirit Vision Guide | 100.0% | **0.0%** | claimed by nothing |
| 4 Spirituality | 100.0% | 66.7% | |
| 5 Combat | 80.8% | 73.9% | unclaimed 25 -> 40 |
| 6.5 Divination Arts | 89.3% | 81.2% | unclaimed 6 -> 13 |
| 7 Ritualistic Magic | 84.2% | 84.0% | unclaimed 25 -> 29 |
| 6 The Beyonder System | 85.4% | 89.7% | rose: newly visible, already claimed |
| 9 Sequence 9 Potion Effects | 94.8% | 95.1% | rose, same reason |

Two chapters going UP is the check that the widening is not simply pessimism:
where the newly visible lines were already claimed, the ratio improves.

**The 33 newly-unclaimed lines are two different findings, and the next reader
should not lump them.** 7.6 is an unread chapter: nothing names it in any
`sourceLines`, so every line it prints was always unclaimed and the filter was
the only thing hiding that. Chapter 4 is the other shape — it IS extracted
(`spi_affinity.json`, `spiritual_senses.json`) and went 100.0% -> 66.7%, so
its two lines are unclaimed lines in a chapter somebody finished and signed
off. Line 2309, "…their Ether Body (health), Spirit Body (emotions), and
auras. Cost: 1 SPI", is one of them: an extractor that stopped short of a
price, not a chapter nobody opened. Same 33, two causes, and they want
different slices.

**Every percentage recorded in this log before today was measured under the
narrower filter and is not comparable with one measured after it.** That
includes this session's own "chapter 8: 21.2% -> 81.7%" and "chapter 2: 30.8%
-> 76.9%". They are not retro-edited — they were true of the instrument that
produced them — but they must not be compared across the change.

**This does not touch what 4.6 pins.** That rule fixes the global line
numbering and the comparison of line *sets* rather than counts. `MECHANICAL`
is neither, and the docstring now says so where a reviewer will look.

### Checked rather than assumed

- **`4271` is not a defect.** "The caster burns HP in addition to or instead of
  SPI. Every 2 HP spent counts as 1 SPI toward the ritual cost" is an unclaimed
  line, and the obvious reading is a printed conversion nothing implements.
  `PowerSources.HP_PER_SPI = 2` implements it and quotes that exact sentence.
  So it is an unclaimed line for an *implemented* rule — an extractor gap, not
  a missing feature, and the difference decided whether this slice was one
  commit or two. `burned` elsewhere in the API is a red herring: in
  `Divination.spiFor` and `RitualResolution.spiFor` it means SPI spent to push
  a roll, not HP burned.

- **The RED proof failed silently the first time.** My mutation used a
  `str.replace` whose pattern did not match, so it rewrote nothing, printed
  `narrowed`, and both tests passed — which reads exactly like a test that
  cannot fail. The file was unchanged, not the tests vacuous. Deleting the
  regex line by index instead reddened both, on the real book line
  (`assert None ... 'Using Spirit Vision: Activate by expending 1 SPI'`).
  **A mutation that reports success is not a mutation that happened** — the
  same no-op blindness this log has already recorded once for a test runner,
  in a new place. Restored from a `cp` copy, never `git checkout`, because
  `coverage.py` held the uncommitted change under test.

- **`opencode` corrupted a file it was told not to touch.** Appending the two
  tests, it stripped four spaces from `for n in (2480, 2481):` inside an
  existing 6da test, moving that body to module scope and breaking collection
  of the whole suite. The same call reported "No existing line or other file
  changed". It had applied the `coverage.py` edit correctly minutes earlier, so
  this is not "opencode is down" — it is that its own report of what it changed
  is not evidence. Verify with a run, not with the tool's summary.

### The review, which found the test asserting the wrong thing

Codex is still refusing (limit resets 2026-08-20), and per the owner's
standing correction the fallback is `ecc:python-reviewer`, not the free panel.
Scoped to three questions and the two files. It returned a HIGH, a MEDIUM and
a LOW, and the HIGH was right:

- **HIGH — the test was named for a consequence and asserted a precondition.**
  `test_spirit_vision_chapter_no_longer_reports_itself_complete` checked that
  line 4840 matches `MECHANICAL` and is unclaimed, and never ran `coverage.py`
  or computed a percentage. Necessary, not sufficient: an off-by-one in the
  chapter page range, or the empty-denominator branch firing wrongly, would
  leave 7.6 claiming completion with every assertion still green. It now runs
  the tool and asserts the reported figure. **RED-proved with a mutation
  chosen to leave every precondition true** — `ch_start <= page <= ch_end`
  narrowed to `<`, which empties 7.6's line set — and the row came back
  `| 7.6 | Spirit Vision Guide | 77-78 | 100.0% | 0 |`. This is the fourth
  vacuity in three slices and the pattern has not changed: **the assertion was
  written from the shape of the DATA rather than the shape of the FAILURE.**

- **MEDIUM — "the old filter" was a hand-typed duplicate.** The negative half
  of the test compared against a retyped copy of the pre-change pattern, which
  stops representing the shipped filter the moment anyone edits one of the four
  shared alternatives. It is now derived by slicing the widening alternative
  off `coverage_tool.MECHANICAL.pattern`, guarded by an `endswith` assertion so
  a reordering says so instead of silently yielding a wrong `narrow`. That
  guard was RED-proved too, by moving the alternative to the front.

- **LOW — case sensitivity**, which the reviewer suggested documenting rather
  than fixing. Documented, and with a stronger claim than it had: the book
  contains **zero** occurrences of "5 cor", "5 hp" or any other rendering, so
  this is measured rather than assumed. A future unclaimed line priced that way
  is the signal to revisit.

### Left open, with the reason

- **7.5's second summoning method may be governed by chapter 7's table.** The
  chapter prints two methods: "one is by using one's own spirituality and
  authority, and the other is by **supplicating a higher being** for their
  assistance… the second requires a complex religious ritual." Chapter 7's
  `entity_response.json` (lines 4292-4312) is a 3d table for exactly that —
  an entity's response to supplication. Whether 7.5's "additional 3d for the
  creature's response" IS that table is unresolved: the consequences differ
  (ch 7's bands give a ritual modifier, 7.5's decide arrival and hostility),
  and mapping one onto the other would be authoring the mapping. Recorded here
  rather than settled, because an unwritten open question is how this file
  grows its next false absolute.

**The next slice is chapter 5's recovery cluster — 15 of the 33 newly visible
unclaimed lines, the largest group.** Lines 2842-2899: "1 HP per 12 hours",
"1 HP per hour", "Natural Recovery (20-29 HP)", "1 HP (2 HP w/ Very Rapid
Healing)", "2 HP (costs 1 FP)", FP thresholds at "0 FP" and "1/3 FP or below".
The evidence that makes it worth a slice rather than a shrug: **the only place
this repo records a decision about it is `docs/HOW-TO-PLAY.md`** — "FP
recovery, stun duration and reload rates are yours to run" — which is player
prose, in a file no sweep reads. That is 6cj's finding in a new location: a
refusal kept somewhere a sweep cannot iterate is invisible by construction, so
before building anything, decide whether that sentence is a refusal with a
mechanism reason or a gap nobody has looked at.

## 6da. Two careful exclusions, one hidden line

6cz's closing paragraph said Appendix A at 8.6% was "probably correct" and
nobody had read its 32 unclaimed lines one at a time. Reading them: **31 are
faithful restatements and one is not.**

| Lines | Content | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 9632-9633 | Core mechanic, criticals | Restates ch 2, claimed |
| 9635-9664 | Skill ladder | Agrees with ch 3 on all five overlapping columns |
| 9666 | Dodge/Parry/Block formulas, "-4 cumulative" | Modelled, incl. `ParryBlock.parryPenalty` |
| **9667** | **`Direction Penalties: Side -2 \| Rear -4`** | **The finding** |
| 9668 | Retreat, Aim | Applied by 6co and 6bm |
| 9669-9672 | Hit locations, wounding, major wound | Agree with ch 5 |

### Why two careful documents hid one line

`ActiveDefenses`' KDoc refused the facing penalty and justified it with **"the
facing rule has no second printing anywhere in the book -- checked, not
assumed"**. Line 9667 is a second printing. The claim had been checked by
sweeping the 59 content files — and `extract_appendix.py` had skipped this page
because it is "a summary of chapters already claimed", which is true of the
other 31 lines and **false of the one that summarises a rule nothing claims.**

Neither exclusion was careless. Each was correct about its own corpus, and the
line fell in the gap between them: invisible to a content-file sweep because
unextracted, and skipped by the extractor because it looked like a restatement.
**A sweep's blind spot can be another document's stated reason.**

### The design review said NO-SHIP, and the argument beat mine

I proposed treating 9667 as the second printing 6ck required and composing the
penalty into `everyDefence`. The review refused, on a sentence worth keeping:

> To widen the ch. 5 sentence, the second printing has to say something the
> first one didn't. This one says strictly less.

Line 9667 carries **no noun at all** — neither "defense" nor "defenses". The
stun precedent works because ch. 11 independently writes "active defenseS" in
its own right; there is nothing in 9667 to read a scope out of. A summary may
define, but not overrule.

It also killed my supporting argument, correctly. I had pointed out that
Retreat is applied to all three rows and the appendix prints it one line below
facing — but **Retreat's scope comes from ch. 5's own bullet**, which
enumerates "+3 Dodge/+1 Block/+1 Parry" before the appendix ever repeats it. The
appendix was never load-bearing for Retreat, so its proximity is evidence of
nothing. **A neighbour that was applied is not proof that the neighbourhood
grants authority.**

### What shipped

The refusal, on the right reason instead of the absent one — and the reason is
now falsifiable rather than absolute. `test_tools.py` pins 9667's exact wording
AND its nounlessness, because the KDoc now cites it: **an argument resting on a
sentence needs that sentence guarded, or the correction becomes the next stale
claim.** RED-proved against a pluralised ch. 5 and an appendix line that
acquires a noun.

`extract_appendix.py`'s exclusion is corrected in the same commit, so the two
documents no longer disagree about what this page contains.

### Notes

- **The census is the deliverable, not the finding.** Appendix A is 8.6%
  claimed and that number is right: it restates. Recording WHICH lines were
  read and cleared is what stops the next agent re-running this.
- Nothing was extracted. Raising the appendix's coverage would mean claiming
  lines whose content is already claimed elsewhere, and 6ae's rule stands: a
  summary is authoritative only for what it alone prints.

### What is next

Nothing named. Appendix A is now read rather than assumed, which was the only
outstanding item 6cz left.

## 6cz. What the free panel's silence was hiding

6cx and 6cy both shipped recording the same gap: Codex is out, the free panel
answered with empty bodies, so neither diff got an independent review. The
owner's instruction was one line — use the ECC reviewer instead of the free one
— and it is the documented Codex-exhausted fallback that both slices had walked
straight past. **It returned BLOCK on two HIGHs and a MEDIUM.**

**The lesson is about what a self-check cannot reach.** 6cx's design review was
thorough and correct, and it argued entirely about whether the feature should
exist: ownership, stacking, direction. Nobody asked the smaller question of what
`forSkill` does when the key carries a specialization. A reviewer with no stake
in the design argument asked it first.

### The defect: strict identity hid gear from the one character who wanted it

`Equipment.forSkill` matched name AND specialization exactly. The catalogue
draws a distinction the matcher did not:

| Skill | `specializable` | Rows printed | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Navigation` | false | 3 (bare, Sea, Land) | Different skills. Strict match is right — the compass names Land. |
| `Survival` | true | 1, "specify terrain" | `Survival (Woodlands)` is an INSTANCE. A bare bonus reaches it. |

`fixtures/hunter_tracker.json:85` buys `Survival (Woodlands)`, and the bedroll
prints a bare "+1 to Survival when rested". So **the one character in the corpus
who would use the bedroll was the one who could not see it** — the false-negation
failure 6cx's own design review had named in the abstract, shipped in the
concrete.

The fix asks the catalogue rather than hardcoding a list: a bare clause reaches
any instance of a `specializable` row, and a clause naming a specialization
still matches only that one. Blast radius measured before writing it —
`Survival` is the only bare-named gear skill that is `specializable`, and the
other 23 keep strict matching.

**The reviewer was right about the defect and wrong about its reach**, and the
difference mattered: it rated the finding latent, "not reachable through today's
23 fixtures", having grepped and found no specialized Survival. One parse of the
fixtures finds it. A reviewer's reachability claim is a claim about the data and
gets checked like any other (6au, 6av, 6bv) — checking it moved the finding from
latent to live.

### Two vacuous assertions, in a test file written to prevent vacuity

Both in 6cy's own `SecondaryCostPinTest`, which exists to stop a value drifting
unnoticed:

- **`the derivations agree with the printed column` never called the engine.**
  It compared a JSON string to a literal in the test. Deriving HP from DX would
  have left it green. It now asks `SecondaryCharacteristics.of` with four
  distinct attribute values, so no two derivations can agree by coincidence.
- **`step == null || step == "level"`** was satisfied by all five rows
  regressing to `null` — exactly the corruption the comment above it warns
  about. Now an equality over the five priced rows.

That is the third vacuity in two slices, after 6cy's unreachable guard. The
pattern across all three: **the assertion was written from the shape of the DATA
rather than from the shape of the FAILURE.** "null or level" describes what the
field currently holds; "level" describes what would be wrong.

### Notes

- All three fixes are RED-proved: reverting the matcher fails the new Survival
  test, deriving HP from DX fails the derivation test, nulling the steps fails
  the unit test.
- The reviewer's third question (Android runtime deserialization) found nothing,
  and its reasoning is worth keeping: `core:rules` is a plain JVM module, the
  loader is the same `getResourceAsStream` path as 76 other files, and the JVM
  tests already decode the same bytes. It named one PRE-EXISTING repo-wide risk
  — no visible R8/ProGuard keep rules for `kotlinx.serialization` generated
  serializers — true of every content file and not this diff's.
- 1599 Kotlin tests (was 1597), 285 Python, all green.

### The Python side, reviewed after the Kotlin

The Kotlin reviewer never saw the two extractors — ~470 lines that had also
shipped unreviewed. `ecc:python-reviewer` returned **no CRITICAL and no HIGH**:
it confirmed the slice arithmetic is correct at both edges and that both clause
regexes fail CLOSED (a mangled capture produces a compound string that matches
no skill). Its three findings were all **guards that could not fire**:

- **A floor instead of an exact row count.** The failure that matters ADDS a
  row — a note cell whose text fullmatches a price form becomes a new row's
  cost, steals the rest of the real note, and fabricates a row named after its
  last cell. Proved on a MIDDLE cell of a three-line note, where the existing
  adjacent-cost guard is blind: 78 rows, and `len(rows) < 60` stays false.
- **A modulo instead of an exact cell count.** Three cells wrapping at once
  leaves the total a multiple of three. Proved at 30 cells, where `% 3` is
  silent and the exact check fires.
- **The `&`/`or` splitter had no bound.** It is the book's two-skill shorthand
  in three clauses and ordinary prose in a fourth, so splitting is safe only
  while that holds; a new `"-1 to Lockpicking or Acting"` would hand the player
  a skill the sentence never meant.

**Two corrections to myself, both worth more than the findings.** The reviewer
proposed testing the whole trimmed target before splitting. I wrote it — then
checked whether it could ever fire, and **no skill name in the catalogue
contains `" or "` or `" & "`**, so it could not. A no-op that reads as
protection is worse than no guard, because the next reader believes the case is
handled. It was reverted for the closed set above, which does fire on exactly
the case the reviewer described. **Take a reviewer's diagnosis over its
prescription**: the hole was real and the proposed patch did not reach it.

And that closed set was hand-written with three members. **The guard found the
fourth on its first run** — `"+1 to First Aid on burns & rashes"`, the prose
case my own docstring uses as its worked example. A census hand-counted while
writing the thing it describes is still a hand count (6cb).

All three RED-proved, and both extractors regenerate byte-identical content, so
these are guard-strength changes with no data movement.

### What is next

Nothing named. But the honest read of this slice is a process finding rather
than a code one: **two slices in a row recorded "no review available" and
shipped, when a documented fallback existed and took six minutes.** An
unavailable gate is a reason to reach for the next gate, not a reason to record
its absence and carry on.

## 6cy. Two things wearing the same words

6cx closed naming nothing, so this slice began with a sweep and ended by
overturning a recorded exclusion. Chapter 2 goes from **30.8% to 76.9%**,
unclaimed mechanical lines from 9 to 3.

### The sweep that mostly found nothing, which is the useful part

`tools/coverage.py` after 6cx leaves four chapters short. Reading their
unclaimed lines one cluster at a time:

| Cluster | Lines | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Ch 3 p10-11, p32 | 40 | The attribute-cost doubling and the skill ladder — implemented as RULES in `AttributeCosts` and `SkillLadder`, so no `sourceLines` will ever claim them |
| Ch 3 p11 Point Budget | 5 | `STARTING_TOTAL = 70` and `MAX_DISADVANTAGES = 40` both exist |
| Ch 2 p8-9 | 6 | **The finding** |
| Appendix A | 32 | A summary that restates other chapters (6ae's rule) |

Four of five clusters are the documented coverage-proxy artefact: a table
implemented as arithmetic reads 0% forever. **Saying which cluster was
checked and cleared is the deliverable**, because the next agent to run
coverage will see the same numbers and needs to know they were read.

### The exclusion, and why its reason was believable

`extract_core_rules.py` left the Secondary Characteristics table out with a
recorded reason: *"`SecondaryCharacteristics` implements every formula and ch
3 prints the costs, which are already extracted. A second span here would
double-claim."*

Run as a query — this repo's rule that a recorded reason is a claim with an
expiry date — **every clause is false**:

- Chapter 3 prints no cost-to-modify for any secondary. Its `pts/level` lines
  are **advantage rows**: Hard to Kill 2/level, Charisma 5/level, Acute Senses
  5/level. Two different things wearing the same words, which is exactly the
  resemblance the exclusion was built on.
- `"Cost to Modify"` occurs **once in the entire book**, line 357 on page 8.
  Appendix A names the characteristics in its glossary and prices none.
- Nothing extracted them, so there was nothing to double-claim. The claimed
  chapter 2 spans stop at 285 and resume at 387; the table sits at 353-386,
  in the gap between them.

**The most reusable finding is the first: `pts/level` is not a unit, it is a
coincidence of phrasing between two unrelated tables.** 6by's spelling seam and
6ce's slash were the same shape — two printings that look like one thing until
you ask which table each belongs to. Here the resemblance survived long enough
to become a written reason and then to justify skipping a page.

### What the gap actually was, measured

The six constants `PointBudget` bills every character with — `COST_HP = 2`,
`COST_FP = 3`, `COST_WILL = 5`, `COST_PER = 5`, `COST_SPEED_QUARTER = 5`,
`COST_MOVE = 5` — had no tie to any printed line.

They were not unpinned in every direction, and the distinction matters. Change
a constant and `SecondaryCharacteristicsTest` reddens, because it asserts
`assertEquals(10, costOf(basicSpeedQuarters = 2))` against a hand-typed 10.
What nothing pinned was the **book**: the chain ran book → *nothing* → constant
→ test literal. A re-extraction that moved a price would have left the engine
billing the old one.

**Measured rather than argued.** With the extracted HP price moved from 2 to
4, exactly **one test in 1597 fails**, and it is the new one.
`PointBudgetTest`, `SecondaryCharacteristicsTest` and `GoldenSheetTest` all
stay green while the book and the engine disagree about what every character
paid. That is 6cx's lesson applied deliberately one slice later: know which
test is the guard, and prove the others cannot see it.

### Three details the table settles by printing them

- **Three of nine rows are unbuyable at any price** — Spirituality "Fixed at
  0", CoR "Tracked in play; never bought", Digestion "Tracked through acting".
  They carry `null`, never `0`, because a zero reads as a free purchase. This
  is section 4.4's rule about SPI printed a second, independent time one
  chapter over — corroboration nobody had noticed was available.
- **Basic Speed is the only row priced per 0.25** rather than per level, which
  is why `SecondaryDelta` counts quarters. A parser that kept the number and
  dropped the unit would price a whole point of Speed at 5 instead of 20.
- The printed name → key map is **pinned rather than slugified**: a renamed row
  stops the run instead of producing a key no consumer joins on.

### A guard that could not fire

The first version checked the priced set before checking the unbuyable rows,
so `if row["pointsPerStep"] is not None: raise` in the unbuyable loop was
**unreachable** — pricing Spirituality made the priced-set comparison fail
first. A Python test written to prove that guard fires is what exposed it,
by matching on the wrong message.

Reordering the two blocks makes both reachable and gives the specific row in
the error. This is the "prove the second assertion can fail" class, and the
thing that caught it was writing the RED test for the guard rather than for
the feature.

### Notes

- The diff review was attempted twice through the free panel; both runs
  exited 0 with empty response bodies. **`ecc:kotlin-reviewer` then reviewed
  this slice together with 6cx and returned BLOCK on two HIGHs** — one of them
  in this slice's own new test file. Recorded in 6cz.
- 1597 Kotlin tests (was 1592) and 285 Python (was 278), all green.
- Regenerating `secondary_costs.json` after the mutation produced a
  byte-identical file, which is the cheap check that the RED-proof left
  nothing behind.

### What is next

Nothing is named. Chapter 2's three remaining unclaimed lines are prose about
the play loop. **Appendix A at 8.6% is the largest raw number left and is
probably correct** — it restates other chapters and 6ae's rule says a summary
is authoritative only for what it alone prints — but "probably" is the word
that hid this slice's finding for four milestones, and nobody has read its 32
lines one at a time.

## 6cx. A precedent that travels by role, not by shape

6cw named chapter 8 and built nothing, asking for its own decomposition and
design review. This is that slice. Chapter 8 goes from **21.2% to 81.7%** and
its unclaimed mechanical lines from **82 to 19**, and the 19 that remain are
four tables refused in production source rather than overlooked.

### 6cw's own census was too narrow, and re-running it found the taxonomy

6cw wrote "34 signed clauses name 30 distinct skills". Run as a query over
pages 79-84: **47 signed clauses, 29 resolving on a naive head-match and 18
not** — and the 18 are six shapes, of which 6cw named two.

| Shape | N | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Names no skill the book prints | 7 | `-2 to spot`, `-5 to fool officials`, `+1 to infection-resistance rolls` |
| Conjunction `&`, one bonus two skills | 2 | `+2 to First Aid & Surgery` |
| Disjunction `or` / `/`, a choice | 2 | `+1 to Fortune-Telling or Psychology` |
| Specialisation in parentheses | 3 | `Navigation (Land)`, `Connoisseur (Books)` |
| Hyphenation seam | 2 | `Fortune-Telling` vs `Fortune Telling` |
| Absent from chapter 3 (4.1) | 2 | `Forced Entry`, `Gather Information` |

The disjunction row settles a question 6ce answered by argument: **the same
page uses `&` for "both" and `or` for "either"**, so a slash between two skill
names is disjunction here, on the book's own evidence rather than on a reading.

The census instrument's blind spots, stated because a filter's false negatives
are invisible by construction (6ba, 6bt): it matches `±N to X` and `X ±N` only.
It cannot see `DR 1 on torso`, `Move ×½ when pushing`, `1d-2 cr`, or the
hired-ally skill LEVELS (`Research-13`, `Brawling-12`) — a seventh shape
carrying no sign at all.

And the 47 span **three subjects**: `+1 to reaction rolls per Status level` is
page 80's Status paragraph, already `wealth.json`'s; two more are page 84's
hired allies, a service rented rather than an item owned. Quoting 47 as one
number reproduces 6cw's error in the other direction.

### Three checks that each changed the shape before any code

- **Specialisation has three answers in one table, not two.** `skills.json`
  stores specialisations in a separate field, never in the name.
  `Navigation (Land)` **resolves** as an enumerated row; `Connoisseur (Books)`
  and `Savoir-Faire (High Society)` are `specializable: true` with open
  instances, which is 6cc's `InstantiableTrait` shape one domain over. The
  design question was posed as a yes/no and the data answered it three ways.
- **The Fortune seam is the BOOK's, not the extractor's.** `book.txt:1963`
  prints `Fortune Telling` (ch. 3) and `:5252/5255/5258` print
  `Fortune-Telling` (ch. 8). 6by's rule holds — evidence per spelling, never a
  normaliser — so both tarot decks join nothing and the crystal ball joins only
  the `or Psychology` half.
- **A clause has a DIRECTION, and it is orthogonal to whether the target
  resolves.** `-1 to spot at night` (dark clothing) penalises whoever is
  looking FOR the wearer. Stored as `{target, value}` and rendered on the
  owner's dialog it inverts — section 5's measured class, base -4 landing
  on +2. Both known instances are already excluded by the resolve condition,
  which is worth saying rather than leaving implied (6cs, 6co).

### The design review said NO-SHIP, and the warrant it killed was mine

The decomposition proposed nine unconditional single-skill rows as selectable
chips in `RollDialog`, modelled on `AttackDialog`'s weapon picker. Three
independent refusals, all verified against source before being accepted:

1. **The precedent does not transfer.** `Weapons.forSkill(skillKey)` is
   ungated and offers chapter 8's own catalogue — but it **re-parameterises**
   the roll (which attack, which damage, which parry, melee or ranged). An
   equipment chip **adds to** it. Same control on screen, opposite role.
2. **`RollDialog`'s own possession control is double-gated.** `socialClauses`
   is filtered on the skill's category AND on `TraitEffects.socialClauses(traits)`
   — a list of what this character actually carries (`MainActivity.kt:782-790`).
   The ungated precedent lives in a different dialog; the gated one lives in
   the dialog being edited. 6cs's "gated on an owned list the CALLER resolves"
   was about *this screen* after all.
3. **Both stacking pairs sit inside the proposed nine.** Disguise kit (basic)
   +1 with (advanced) +2 reads +3; Camera (simple) -2 with (folding) +1 reads
   -1. Mutual exclusion is a property of the ITEM, and no printed field says
   two rows are alternatives — inventing a `functionalClass` taxonomy would be
   authoring content to make a feature safe.

**The most reusable finding is the first: a precedent travels with its ROLE,
not its shape.** 6cm found that a precedent travels with the condition that
produced it; this is the same lesson one level down. Two controls can be
pixel-identical and mechanically opposite, and "the app already does this"
is a claim about the screen when it needs to be a claim about the semantics.

### What shipped instead, and its precedent is in the same function

`conditionalBurnNote` — four lines above where the new block landed — carries
the principle in its own KDoc: *"A push the book allows on part of what this
skill covers, which the engine cannot test for itself. **Shown, never
applied.**"* Its comment argues the case exactly: *"granting it would push
rolls the book does not, and withholding it in silence would hide a printed
rule."*

So the whole table ships as reference. `Equipment.referenceFor(key)` returns
the item, its price and the book's sentence **unedited**, and the dialog
prints them under "Gear that names this skill (not applied):". Every one of
the three refusals dissolves: nothing asserts ownership, nothing stacks
because nothing is a number, and a penalty aimed at an observer is a sentence
the GM reads rather than a modifier on the wrong roll.

It also dissolves the review's second finding, which was about the BOUNDARY:
shipping nine of seventy-seven rows as chips would teach a player that a skill
with no chip has no gear — false exactly in the conditional band, which is most
of the table. Showing **every** row that names the skill, conditions intact,
makes no such promise.

### The join is a discovery index, and a mention is not a clause

`skills` on each row exists to answer "which rows should a Search roll put in
front of the player", and is built only from SIGNED clauses. `Lock picks (set)`
says "Required for Lockpicking skill" and joins nothing; `Lockpick set (basic)`
one line below says "-1 to Lockpicking" and joins. A substring matcher would
have offered the lock picks on every Lockpicking roll as though they helped —
the unhardened predicate 6cj caught 6ci using.

The target is **trimmed, then split**, in that order: `+1 to First Aid on
burns & rashes` is one skill, and splitting first would claim a skill called
"rashes". Splitting is a claim about which rows to SHOW and never about what
to add, which is what makes it safe to reach both halves of a conjunction.

### The RED-proof found something about the tests, not the code

Neutering the signed-clause predicate into a bare mention makes the extractor
**refuse to run** — `verify()` raises on the first pinned row it reaches. But
only ONE of the eleven Kotlin tests and one of the ten Python tests can see it:
the rest read `equipment.json`, and **a failing extractor never rewrites the
file**, so they re-read the old good data and pass.

That is this repo's own recorded class (a failure filter cannot see a no-op)
appearing in test DESIGN rather than in a grep. The data tests pin the data;
only `verify()` pins the parser. Worth knowing which of your tests is the
guard, because ten green ones next to it prove nothing about the code you just
changed.

### Refused in the same commit, in production source

`Equipment.UNMODELLED` carries a reason per table, to the
`ActiveDefenses.UNPAYABLE` / `Divination.UNAPPLIED` standard — discoverable by
a sweep over Kotlin, not buried in this journal (6cj). Armour's three DR rows
(nothing here models DR, and `Damage.kt:20`'s KDoc already says DR sits on the
target's side); both currency systems and the exchange rate (`startingMoney` is
a printed STRING and no arithmetic anywhere touches money); Legal Licenses &
Permits and Hired Allies (different subjects, neither reaching a roll). Each
would otherwise be 6cf's loader with no caller.

### Notes

- `tools/extract_equipment.py` reads 77 rows, which matches a hand count of the
  four printed categories (27 + 15 + 11 + 24). 235 cells, 77 cost matches, no
  two adjacent — so no note line can fullmatch `COST_CELL` and split a row.
- **The 19 unclaimed lines were checked one by one, not inferred from the
  total.** All 19 fall in the four refused tables — currency 6, armour 2,
  licences 2, hired allies 9 — and **nothing inside the claimed span
  5062-5310 is unclaimed**, so the parser skipped no row of its own table.
- **Which gate ran, corrected after the fact:** the DECOMPOSITION got a full
  design review before any code, and it returned NO-SHIP on three counts,
  which reshaped the slice. The diff review was attempted through the free
  panel, which ran sixteen minutes and **exited 0 with two empty response
  bodies** — a silent no-answer, and 6ba's lesson about instruments: the run
  succeeded and the review did not happen. This note originally stopped there,
  recording the diff as self-checked. **The owner then asked for
  `ecc:kotlin-reviewer`, the documented Codex-exhausted fallback, and it
  returned BLOCK.** It found a real defect in `forSkill` that neither the
  design review nor the self-check reached. See 6cz.
- The opencode round-trip produced 13k tokens of (correct) analysis and wrote
  no file. The built-in editor was the fallback, per the documented rule.
- 1592 Kotlin tests (was 1581) and 278 Python (was 268), all green, counted
  from the JUnit XML rather than from a BUILD SUCCESSFUL line — the Android
  module reports under `testDebugUnitTest` and a naive glob misses its 466.
  `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` also hid two unused imports, which warn rather than error.

### What is next

Nothing is named. The four refusals above are refusals, not deferrals: each
would need a consumer to exist first (a DR model, a money model, a
character-creation surface for licences). The conditional band inside the
equipment table is the nearest real feature and it needs what the chips
needed — a record of what a character owns.

## 6cw. The chapter that is 21% read

With no slice named, the sweep went back to the instrument this repo built for
exactly this and had not run in a long while: `tools/coverage.py`. Every
chapter is at or near 100% except four, and one of them is not a rounding
error.

| Ch | Title | Claimed | Unclaimed mechanical lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | Equipment & Starting Wealth | **21.2%** | **82** |
| A | Quick Reference Tables | 8.6% | 32 |
| 2 | Core Rules | 30.8% | 9 |
| 7.5 | Summoning Spiritual Creatures | 0.0% | 1 |

**Chapter 8 holds an equipment catalogue this app has never seen.** Reading its
unclaimed lines: armour with DR values, a three-tier currency system with an
exchange rate, and item after item carrying a mechanical clause — "-1 to
Lockpicking", "+1 to First Aid; 10 uses before restock", "+2 to First Aid &
Surgery; 50 doses", "+1 to Ritualistic Magic & Religious Ritual", "DR 1 on
torso", "-1 to spot at night". `weapons.json` (9 rows) and `wealth.json` (7)
claim their parts of that chapter; the gear does not exist here at all.

**The join was checked before the slice was named** (6bv's rule). 34 signed
clauses name 30 distinct skills, and the catalogue already holds nearly all of
them — `Research`, `Carousing`, `Accounting`, `Administration`, `Engineering`,
`Connoisseur`, `Savoir-Faire`, `Chemistry`, `Cogitation`, `Diagnosis`,
`Disguise`, `First Aid`, `Lifting`, `Lockpicking`, `Merchant`, `Photography`,
`Physician`, `Religious Ritual`, `Ritualistic Magic`, `Streetwise`, `Survival`,
`Theology`. So this is reachable rather than aspirational: an item's bonus has
a skill row to land on and a roll that already exists.

Three seams are worth naming now, because they are the parts that will decide
the shape rather than the size:

- **`Forced Entry` and `Gather Information` are absent from `skills.json`.**
  Chapter 8 grants bonuses to skills chapter 3 never prints. That is a
  chapter-versus-chapter disagreement of the kind 4.1 governs, and it must be
  recorded rather than resolved by inventing rows.
- **`Fortune-Telling` here, `Fortune Telling` in the catalogue** — a
  hyphenation seam, the same class 6bx and 6by worked through for trait names,
  where the answer was evidence per spelling rather than a normaliser.
- **Most clauses are conditional**: "+1 to Search for fine details", "+1 to
  Hiking in rain", "Merchant +1 when appraising unknown items". 6bt already
  found that a conditional row and an unconditional one are different features
  — a naive extractor that keeps only the number would ship a permanent bonus
  the book scopes to a circumstance.

Nothing is built here. This slice is the census and the evidence for the next
one, which is large enough to deserve its own decomposition and design review:
an extractor for the gear table, a content file, and a decision about where a
conditional item bonus reaches a roll (the modifier ledger, or a chip on the
skill dialog beside the circumstance rows that already exist).

## 6cv. The field with nowhere to go

One grep closes the `published` block. `cor` is the last of its fields with no
reader anywhere — and unlike `spi`, which has a test asserting `toCharacter`
carries it, **there is nothing to carry it into**: `Character` declares no
corruption at all, because CoR is session state (`SavedSession.cor`). All 23
sheets print 0, so nothing is wrong today; a sheet that printed 5 would have it
dropped in silence and start the table clean.

So the artefact is a guard whose failure message says what the silence would
mean, and the slice is one test.

**Its first draft was tightened for a wrong reason, and the review caught it.**
I replaced `(cor ?: 0) == 0` with a strict `== 0`, arguing an elvis would
swallow a null the guard exists to hear. `Premades.kt:80` settles it one field
over: *"Mortals print 0; four of the 23 sheets print 9. **Absent means
mortal**"*, and `spiOf()` is `published.spi ?: 0`. Under this file's own
convention a null CoR IS zero, so the strict version would have failed on a
state the repo already calls correct — a guard reporting a non-finding. The
elvis is back with the citation beside it.

**The lesson is 6cl's, one level down.** There the refusal survived because
reading the content produced a real reason where the cited defect could not.
Here the tightening did NOT survive, because the convention it needed to
respect was written eleven lines above the function it was mirroring, on the
sibling field, and I had not read it. **A predicate is a claim about what a
null means, and that meaning is usually already decided somewhere in the same
file.**

**A second finding, and it is about this session rather than the code.**
Bumping the slice range with a PowerShell `Get-Content -Raw | Set-Content`
round-trip corrupted both `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/SLICE-LOG.md` — 129 and 1279
mangled sequences — because PS 5.1's `Get-Content` reads UTF-8 as ANSI and
writes it back re-encoded. Every em-dash in two of this repo's largest prose
files became `â€"`. Recovered with `git checkout` of exactly those two files,
which was safe **only** because their sole uncommitted content was this
slice's own paragraphs, reproducible verbatim, and the file holding real work
(`GoldenSheetTest.kt`) was not in the checkout. Use the editing tools for
prose; a shell round-trip is a re-encode.

## 6cu. Two errors, six columns, and the sign that carries the finding

6ct named the sibling column, and said to start with the question that needs no
engine: does `totalSpent + unspent == bpTotal` hold as published? **21 of 23
do.** Two carry nulls, and one of those is the interesting one — Beat Cop has
every POINT BREAKDOWN field null *except* `unspent: 0`, and the extractor reads
that field with a different helper (`value_right_of`) than the two beside it
(`points_after`). That is the shape of an invented zero.

**It is not one, and the repo could settle it.** The source spreadsheets are on
this machine, so the question was answerable rather than arguable: `Beat
Cop.xlsx` prints "Unspent" at row 1 with `0.0` two cells to its right, and
contains no "Budget (BP)" or "Total spent" label at all. The zero is published
and the nulls beside it are correct. **A suspicion about extracted data is a
question for the source, not for the extractor's code** — and the answer here
inverted the suspicion.

Running both reconciliations with no exclusions returned five failures, and
every one is an error already recorded here, resurfacing in a column nobody had
checked:

| Sheet | Column | Published | Computed | Cause |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| University Librarian | budget | 100 | 95 | its disadvantages gap (30 printed, 25 listed) |
| University Librarian | unspent | 9 | 4 | the same five points |
| Monastery Scholar | unspent | 1 | 11 | its advantages gap, inverted |
| Beat Cop | unspent | 0 | 4 | its own, with nothing to check it against |
| LOTM Blank Character Sheet | budget | 0 | 70 | a template, not a character |

**The sign is the finding.** The librarian's gaps are +5 and the scholar's is
−10, and the reason is structural: the budget IS 70 plus capped disadvantages,
so an over-stated DISADVANTAGE raises the sheet's budget and its unspent
together, while an over-stated ADVANTAGE raises what the sheet thinks it SPENT
and therefore lowers its unspent. A guard asserting magnitude would pass under
either sign — the defect class section 5 measured once (base -4 landing on +2)
and 6cg measured again (a substring guard blind to a minus). Both guards assert
the signed difference, and the scholar's was RED-proved by dropping the minus:
1 of 223 fails.

**The diff review verified both signs with the published arithmetic and got a
third number wrong** — it computed Beat Cop's surplus as 64 where the failing
run printed 4. The verdict it supported (pin the SIGN, not the magnitude, since
that sheet has no per-category subtotal to anchor a number to) survives its own
bad arithmetic, and the reminder is 6cq's one level up: **a review's numbers
are evidence to check, not facts to copy.** Every figure in the table above
came from a test run, not from the review.

**The blank sheet needed no exclusion at all.** Switching both factories to
`playable()` drops it, which is what the file's older budget test already does,
and it is the honest filter: a template with no skills is not a character whose
budget disagrees. An exclusion is a claim someone has to maintain; not needing
one is better than recording one.

So the two known spreadsheet errors are now pinned in every column they touch —
three each. `tools/test_tools.py`'s `test_beat_cop_has_no_point_breakdown`
enumerated six fields of that block and stopped one short of the seventh, the
only one that is not null; it now asserts the published zero with the source
reference beside it, so the Python and Kotlin suites agree about the same odd
sheet. 1580 Kotlin green, 268 Python green.

**Next, with evidence.** Nothing is named. The fixture sweep that opened 6ct is
now exhausted for the `published` block, but it only ever asked "does a Kotlin
reader exist" — it never asked whether a reader **reconciles** the value or
merely displays it. `hp`, `fp`, `will`, `per`, `basicSpeed`, `basicMove` and
`dodge` are all reconciled by `derived secondaries match on the trusted field
set`; `spi` and `cor` are not, and `spi` has a test asserting only that
`toCharacter` carries it. Whether `cor` is checked anywhere is the next
question, and it is one grep.

6cs closed its direction with no successor, so this one starts from a corpus
rather than a category: **the 23 fixtures.** Every sweep this repo has run
iterates the book's content or its Kotlin — 6ai swept extracted content fields
for a reader, and nothing has ever asked the same question of the *character
sheets*. One grep gives 32 distinct keys across `fixtures/*.json`; every one of
them occurs in Kotlin, which is where 6ai's lesson bites, because an occurrence
can be the data-class declaration itself. Counting readers **outside the model
declarations** leaves five, and four of those are reconciled by
`GoldenSheetTest` already.

The fifth is `totalSpent`: **prod=1 (its own declaration), test=0.** The
sheet's own printed TOTAL SPENT — extracted, stored, documented in
`Premades.kt`'s KDoc — and never once compared against what the rules compute,
while every other POINT BREAKDOWN row is.

Wiring it up took one `@TestFactory` and produced exactly one disagreement:
