**Monastery Scholar, published 99 against a computed 89.** Section 4.1 has
recorded that sheet since M0 for printing "Advantages: 15 pts" over a single
5-point advantage — the same ten points. So the exclusion is not a second
disagreement to record, and the slice says so with a test rather than a
sentence: `the excluded total spent is short by exactly its advantage gap`
asserts both gaps are ten and equal. **If they ever diverge, one spreadsheet
error has become two, and that is the finding.** RED-proved by emptying
`totalSpentExclusions` — 1 of 180 fails — and restored from a copy.

**The count guard is where this slice went wrong, and it is the most useful
part.** Following the file's own idiom (`every fixture but Beat Cop carries an
attribute subtotal` exists to stop a filter degrading to zero cases), I added
one asserting 23 — measured by `grep -l '"totalSpent"' fixtures/*.json`, which
returns 23. It fails: the answer is 22. Beat Cop's file *contains the key* and
its value is `null`, which `Premades.kt` has documented all along ("Null on
every field for Beat Cop, which has no such block at all"). **A grep for a key
is not a count of a value**, and the comment I wrote around the wrong number
asserted the opposite of the truth — that this filter and the attribute one
cover different sets, when they cover the same 22. The guard caught its
author's own claim within a minute, which is the argument for writing it at
all.

**The diff review then found the condition the whole reconciliation rests on**,
which neither the test nor its KDoc had named: `budget.spent` adds
`SecondaryCharacteristics.costOf(secondaryDelta)`, and the POINT BREAKDOWN the
extractor reads has four rows with no secondary among them. Today every fixture
carries a default `SecondaryDelta`, so the two quantities measure the same
thing; a fixture that bought a secondary would diverge **for a reason that is
not a sheet error**, and someone would record a disagreement that is really an
apples-to-oranges comparison. Pinned rather than commented, because a comment
is not a pin (6cq): a test asserts no fixture buys one, and its failure message
says what the divergence would mean.

Suite 1538 green: 21 reconciliations (23 fixtures, less Beat Cop's null, less
the one exclusion) and three guards.

**Next, with evidence.** The same census left `unspent` unexamined — it is
carried by every fixture and has more than one production reader, so it did not
surface, but nothing yet checks a sheet's printed unspent points against
`BudgetReport.surplus`. That is the sibling column of the one this slice wired
up, and the cheap question to ask first is whether `spent + unspent == bpTotal`
holds on all 23 as published, because a sheet that fails its OWN arithmetic
needs no engine to prove it.

## 6ct. The fixtures nobody had swept

**Recovered from `CLAUDE.md`'s lead paragraph in 6eb, and that is the point of
recording it here.** This slice never had a section in this file — the
sections run 6cv, then 6cu, with nothing between — so for however many slices
that has been true, its only surviving account was the summary paragraph in
the handover. 6eb cut that stack of paragraphs to get `CLAUDE.md` back under
its size limit, checked each cut section against this file first, and found
this one missing. **A lead paragraph can be the only copy**; the check that
catches it is one `grep -c "^## <slice>\."` per name, and it costs a second.

What the paragraph said, verbatim:

> **6ct is next**, and it sweeps a corpus nobody had swept: **the 23
> fixtures.** 32 keys, all occurring in Kotlin; counting readers outside the
> model declarations leaves five, four already reconciled, and one —
> `totalSpent` — with its declaration and nothing else. The sheet's printed
> TOTAL SPENT had never been compared with what the rules compute. Wiring it
> up found exactly one disagreement, Monastery Scholar's 99 against 89, and
> that is 4.1's existing advantages error surfacing in a second column: a
> test now asserts both gaps are ten and EQUAL, so if they diverge one
> spreadsheet error has become two. Read it for the count guard that caught
> its own author — `grep -l` says 23 fixtures carry the field and the loaded
> answer is 22, because Beat Cop's file has the key with a `null` value. **A
> grep for a key is not a count of a value.**

Its successor's own opening confirms the subject: 6cu begins *"6ct named the
sibling column, and said to start with the question that needs no engine"*.
Nothing here is reconstructed beyond that paragraph — the slice's commits are
in `git log`, and this section is a pointer to them rather than a rewritten
account of work it did not witness.

## 6cs. The slice that ships a refusal

6cr's census found one constant in 96 that occurs once in the repository:
`Divination.SPECIALISATION_BONUS`, whose KDoc quotes book line 3653 — "A
Beyonder may specialise in one method, gaining +1 when using it." A printed
rule reaching no roll is this project's oldest defect class, so the obvious
slice was a declaration chip on the divination screen.

**The design review returned NO-SHIP, and the evidence was already in the
repo.** The same book sentence prices it: *"This counts as a technique (see
GURPS Techniques, p. B229)"* — a points purchase under a rule this book does
not reprint and this app's builder cannot buy. And nothing in the corpus
records WHICH method a diviner trained in: all 23 premades are mortals and not
one carries a divination skill, no potion grant records a specialisation, and
no saved edit has a field for one. Meanwhile every other bonus on that screen
is gated on ownership — `ownedSupportSkills` is resolved by the CALLER, and its
KDoc says the screen must not decide membership itself. The GM call those chips
carry is about **relevance of an owned skill**, never about ownership.

**The sharpest finding was against my own state design.** I proposed the chip
reset when the method changes, by analogy with `spiChoice by remember(method)`.
The reviewer took that apart: `spiChoice` resets because it is *re-derived* from
the new method's printed cost — the reset loads a fresh value. Specialisation
has nothing to load, so "resetting" it only offers the tick again, and a
per-method boolean lets a player specialise in a different method every
question. **One permanent point-bought technique would have become a free +1 on
whatever method was picked** — the entitlement defect in state form, and
invisible in a diff. The book says "one method", singular; the honest shape is
a single nullable method, which is exactly the field this repo has nowhere to
store.

So what shipped is the refusal. `Divination.UNAPPLIED` holds the rule beside
its reason, in production source where a sweep over Kotlin reaches it — the
`ActiveDefenses.UNPAYABLE` standard, with the same honest caveat in its KDoc:
**discoverability, not strength.** Removing an entry turns nothing red. The
screen now says it out loud too, reading the reason from the map rather than
paraphrasing it, so the note and the rule cannot drift the way 6bl's disclaimer
did.

**Writing that value taught the small lesson of the slice.** The first draft was
developer prose — "…which is the one thing every other bonus on this screen is
gated against" — and it rendered verbatim into the dialog. A string with two
readers must be written for the harsher one: the player got one sentence, and
the argument moved up into the KDoc, where the maintainer was going to look
anyway.

**And the note shipped in the wrong branch.** It was first written directly
under the support-skill cap line, which lives in the `else` of
`if (ownedSupportSkills.isEmpty())` — so the only diviners who would ever have
read "Specialisation +1 is not applied here" were the ones who own Occultism,
Hidden Lore, Psychology or Cogitation. **A refusal that renders beside an
unrelated condition is a refusal most readers never see**, and the placement is
invisible to every test in this repo, because none of them reach a composable.
It sits outside the branch now, with the reason for the placement in a comment
beside it. Caught by asking the diff review to quote the branch condition the
block sits in — a question worth asking of any block added next to existing
code rather than at a boundary.

The test is deliberately weak and says so: it pins the key set, the constant's
value, and that the reason still names what the book prices it as. RED-proved
by rewriting "technique" to "trained knack" — 1 of 51 fails, restored from the
copy. Suite 1514 green (measured per module: 1028 `core:rules`, 466 `app`, 20
`core:model` — the filtered RED-proof run overwrites one module's XML, so a
per-module count taken straight after it is wrong).

**The corrected census ran in the same session, and it is clean.** 6cr's
version counted occurrences repo-wide, tests included, so a constant *pinned by
a test and applied by nothing* scored the same as one in daily use; its second
column ("no reader outside the declaring file") matched 52 healthy constants
and was worse than useless. The query that actually answers the question is
**production readers excluding the declaration LINE, against test readers** —
excluding the whole declaring file was the earlier bug, because a constant used
once inside its own object is normal.

Over 100 constants in `core/rules` and `core/model` it returns **one hit, and
that hit is a false positive**: `SpiritualSenses.SEER` has no production reader
because it exists to LOCATE a row in a test — `perception.modifiers.single {
it.situation == SEER }`. The rule itself is applied: `MainActivity` passes
`SpiritualSenses.forSkill(skill.key)` into the roll dialog, which renders the
sense's rows by loop, so "+6 Seer" is on screen without any code naming it.
**That is 6ci's finding restated at the level of a constant** — a table
consumed by loop correctly names none of its rows, so "no reader" and "not
applied" are different claims and only the second one is a defect.

So this direction is exhausted rather than deferred, and there is **no named
successor**. The next slice needs a fresh sweep; the directions already run
(fields with no reader, functions with no caller, rows with no consumer,
literals restating a computed value, constants with no production reader, seams
between claimed spans, rules the app contradicts, what the tests know that
production does not) have each returned their findings and expire rather than
standing.

## 6cr. Three of the four hits were quotations

6cq named its own successor: the ritual screens' HP↔SPI strings, checked for
which are *quotations of a printed cell* and which are *restatements of a value
the rules compute*. Running it, **three of the four were quotations and one was
a duplicate** — and two of the three were not even user-visible.
`ArtifactDialog`'s `"1 SPI/turn"`, `DivinationDialog`'s `"1-2 SPI"` and
`RitualDialog`'s KDoc `"every 2 HP spent counts as 1 SPI"` are code comments
citing the page. Deriving any of them would make the source stop saying what
the book says.

The one real hit is `RitualDialog`'s user-visible `"Paid in HP (2 HP = 1 SPI,
no bonus to the roll)"`, which restates `PowerSources.HP_PER_SPI`.

**The discriminator is not the string.** A grep cannot tell the two apart —
both are literals holding a number the rules also hold. The test is: *would a
rules value have to move for this sentence to become false?* A quotation stays
true when the code changes, because it is a claim about the book. A restatement
does not.

Widening past HP/SPI to any literal carrying a signed number found two more,
and one of them is a correction to the slice before it:

- **A fifth `+2` in `DefenseDialog`.** 6cq fixed four and this one sat in
  `NewRoundControl`'s "Free actions, parries and any paid +2 are spent for this
  round." Two patterns had already searched that file. **A widened query is not
  a finished query** — the third pattern found what the second missed, in a
  file the first had cleared (6ba, again).
- **`DivinationDialog`'s support line was half-derived already**:
  `"+1 each, capped at +${Divination.MAX_SUPPORT_BONUS} — … not ch. 7's +3."`
  One number read from the rules, two typed, in one sentence. That is 6cq's
  `DefenseDialog` shape at the level of a single string.

**`"+1 each"` was deleted rather than derived.** The chips underneath render
`"${option.skill} ${signed(option.bonus)}"` for every supporting skill, so the
header was a third copy of a number already on screen — and the per-skill value
is not a constant at all, it is each row's own `bonus` field. Deriving it would
have meant inventing a rendering for the case where the rows disagree; deleting
it costs the player nothing, because the rows already speak. Where a value is
already visible, deletion beats derivation.

The `"ch. 7's +3"` half is `RitualMode.SUPPORT_CAP`, and it is the more
interesting one: that sentence exists **to say two chapters disagree**. It is
the kind of sentence that breaks silently, because it is only true while both
numbers stay where they were.

**A data check ran before the deletion, and it found nothing wrong** — all four
rows in `divination_support.json` print `bonus: 1`, so the sentence was true.
That is the state this whole defect class lives in: **true, on screen, and
unpinned.** Nothing was wrong; nothing would have gone red.

Full suite green at 1513; no new test, and the reason is 6cq's — no test in
this repo can reach a Compose label, and all three changes remove a copy rather
than guard one.

**Next, with evidence.** The reverse direction of this sweep has never been
run: **a rules constant with no reader.** 6cf swept public functions for a
caller and 6ai swept extracted fields; a `const val` is neither. One grep says
`Divination.SPECIALISATION_BONUS` occurs **exactly once in the repository — its
own declaration.** Its KDoc quotes the book ("A Beyonder may specialise in one
method, gaining +1 when using it"), and nothing reads it, no test names it, and
no screen offers the choice. A printed rule that reaches no roll, which is this
project's oldest defect class.

**The census ran before this slice closed, because one grep hit is not a
census.** 96 `const val`s in `core/rules`, each counted repo-wide: **exactly
one — `SPECIALISATION_BONUS` — occurs once.** Every other constant is read
somewhere, and the 52 that showed no reader *outside their own file* are not
suspects: that column counts production readers only, so a constant used once
in its own object and pinned by a test in another module scores zero and is
perfectly healthy. **The instrument's useful signal was the total, not the
outside count** — a second column that looks like a finding and is not is worth
saying out loud, because the next reader of this paragraph will otherwise
inherit 52 false leads.

## 6cq. The pins stop at the UI

A seventh sweep direction, and one this repo had never run: **numbers a screen
types in English that production already reads from content.** The six before
it all iterate declarations — extracted fields with no reader (6ai), public
functions with no caller (6cf), content rows with no consumer (6ci), seams
between claimed spans (6ba), rules the app contradicts, what the tests know
that production does not (6bz). None of them can see a *string literal*, which
is not a declaration at all.

The query is one grep over `app/src/main`: string literals containing a digit,
then each one asked "does the rules layer already own this number?". Six sites
answered yes.

- Three `FilterChip` labels in `AttackDialog` printed the extra-effort prices —
  `"Strong Blow (1 FP, +2 damage)"`, `"Heroic Charge (2 FP)"`, `"Giant Step
  (1 FP)"` — while `Attacks.fpCost` charges what `extra_effort.json` prints.
  Two copies, and only one of them pinned.
- Three literals in `DefenseDialog` said `+2` beside a line already reading
  `ActiveDefenses.fpCostOf(boost)`: **one number derived and its sibling typed,
  inside one composable.** A fourth turned up only after the first pattern was
  widened past `Text("…digit…")` to any literal mentioning FP/CoR/HP/SPI — the
  "lands on nothing" note 350 lines up the same file. An instrument's false
  negatives are invisible by construction (6ba), so the second query is not
  optional.
- `PathwayScreen` printed `"advancing now also costs 10+ CoR"`.

**The CoR one is where the slice changed shape.** Chasing that label found
`PotionConsumption.attempt` charging `if (state.isFullyDigested) 0 else 10` — a
Kotlin literal — while `cor_gained.json` carries the row `"Advancing sequence
without full digestion"` with `minimum: 10`. That looked like a third unpinned
copy, and it was not: `CorruptionTest` has a test named *the advancement floor
in the content matches what the PCR charges*, which asserts the row says 10.
Reading it settled the candidate and raised a better one. The test pinned the
DATA. What joined the data to the charge was its comment — *"PotionConsumption
.attempt states the same 10; both must come from the same book row"* — and a
comment is not a pin. Change the JSON to 12 and the test goes red, correctly;
change the Kotlin to 12 and nothing anywhere notices.

So the fix is the same in all three places and it is not a refactor: **make the
number unreachable except through the row that prints it.**
`Attacks.effortFp(option)` is now public (it was `private effortCost`), which
mirrors `ActiveDefenses.fpCostOf(boost)` — the function the same
`DefenseDialog` was already calling one line above the literal it typed. And
`PotionConsumption.earlyAdvancementCor()` reads the CoR floor from
`cor_gained.json`, so `attempt` states no number of its own.

**The design review ran before any code** (free panel via `qa.mjs`; Codex is
still refusing until 2026-08-20). It agreed on the seam and refused two
alternatives with reasons worth keeping: the dialog reading
`ContentLoader.extraEffort()` itself forks the lookup and re-creates the
duplication (4.1), and building the label from the row's printed effect string
is 6f's parser nobody tests — `ActiveDefenses.printedBoost()` survives only
because its row prints a clean sentence that a test pins, and the extra-effort
rows are not held to that standard. It also answered the proof question
honestly rather than inventing a check: **no test in this repo can reach a
Compose label.** Deriving does not catch the drift, it removes the place drift
could happen.

That leaves exactly one runnable check, on the CoR half, and it was RED-proved
the way this file requires: copy the file, mutate the reading to
`?.minimum?.plus(1)`, run — `CorruptionTest` fails 1 of 11 — restore from the
copy, never `git checkout` (a file holding uncommitted work). Full suite green
at 1513.

**The most reusable finding is that a comment is not a pin.** A test that
asserts the data and a comment that asserts the join look identical in a diff
and are not the same artefact: only one of them fails. This is 6bl's expiring
disclaimer one level up — there the prose contradicted the code, here the prose
was the *only thing holding two correct numbers together*, and it would have
gone on being true-looking after either side moved.

**Next, with evidence.** The widened query returns rows this slice did not
touch, and they are a different question rather than more of the same: the
ritual screens print conversions — `RitualDialog`'s `"every 2 HP spent counts
as 1 SPI"` and `"Paid in HP (2 HP = 1 SPI, no bonus to the roll)"`,
`ArtifactDialog`'s `"1 SPI/turn"`, `DivinationDialog`'s `"1-2 SPI"`. Before
deriving any of them, check which are *quotations of a printed cell* (which
must stay verbatim, like `printedBoost`) and which are *restatements of a value
the rules compute*. Only the second kind is this slice's defect, and calling a
quotation a duplicate is how a screen stops saying what the book says.

## 6cp. The refusal that was about reach, not about global state

The round boundary p. 36 names exists on the defence screen: one `New round`
control clears the three free actions, the parry count, the paid boost and the
three refusals, and `RoundState` is the unit it operates on. 6co named this as
the honest next candidate and said to run it as a query rather than inherit it.
Run as a query, the recorded ruling expired -- and the interesting part is
*which half* of it expired.

**6bf refused a round tracker on the grounds that it would be global state for
a payoff of one rule.** That reading survives: four of the five rules 6bd
ranked behind a tracker still need a declaration rather than a clock, and the
fifth (reload rate) is still double-blocked by weapons not being editable.
Nothing here is global. What shipped is a `data class` inside one composable.

**6co refused it on a different ground, and that is the one that expired: a
latch on ONE control would claim a boundary the others could not honour.** That
is a claim about REACH, and reach is what changed while nobody re-read the
sentence. When it was written, one free action existed. Today `declared`,
`acrobatic`, `dived`, `retreated`, `priorParries` and `boost` are all `remember`
vars in `DefenseDialog`, so a single assignment honours the paragraph for every
control it governs. **A refusal can survive its own author's reason and die of
a fact none of its words mention** -- the count of things it had to reach.

### Membership is the rule, and the guard is a reflection test

A field on `RoundState` IS a value a new round clears, so the test asserts the
field set exactly:

- `stunned` must never join it. The book gives stun its own clock -- "Stunned
  for 1d6 seconds (roll HT each turn to recover early)" (line 2826) -- so a
  round boundary is not what ends it, and a later "tidy-up" folding it in is
  precisely what the assertion exists to redden.
- The shield carried, the facing and the incoming attack are excluded for a
  SECOND reason rather than the same one: they are not per-round facts at all.
  6co's own lesson about a borrowed warrant, applied to an exclusion.

Every refusal's printed scope was checked at its own line before it was
included, because they are three rules and not one clock: surprise is "their
first turn" (2377), the All-Out Attack is the turn it was taken (2453), and an
unaware shot is one ATTACK (2686-2687) -- shorter than a round, so clearing it
at the boundary can never leave it stale.

### Two RED proofs, one reading each

`newRound()` returning `this` reddens the value test alone; adding `stunned` to
the class reddens the membership test alone. The second is the one worth
having: an assertion that only checks "these six became defaults" is vacuous
about the values that must NOT reset (6bu's hole, on this screen).

### What the design review changed before any of it shipped

Codex still refuses (2026-08-20 14:23) and `pi-qa`'s gateway was saturated by
this session's own long-running job, so the gate was the stronger-model advisor
on the decomposition and again on the diff. Three findings, all taken:

- **`LaunchedEffect(acrobatics)` is not the guard `remember(acrobatics)` was.**
  The remember key re-initialises DURING composition; a LaunchedEffect fires
  after the pass commits, so the row would render one frame carrying a roll
  made against a level that had already moved. Restored as a composition-time
  compare. And the obvious alternative is worse: keying the whole holder would
  discard the boost `onSpendFp` has already charged for.
- **Three comment blocks were left orphaned above the wrong declarations** --
  "Parries already made THIS ROUND" sitting over `var incoming`, and so on. In
  a file whose entire style is "the comment names the control below it", that
  is 6bl's defect in its documentation form. Each is now the matching field's
  own KDoc.
- **The control was in the button bar beside "Close"**, where it reads as
  Cancel and a mis-tap drops FP already spent. Moved into the content above the
  rows it clears -- this screen's own placement rule, the one `StunPicker`
  follows -- and hidden entirely while `isSpent()` is false, so a control that
  clears nothing never invites the tap that later clears something.

**1139 Kotlin** (1027 `core:rules`, 92 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and 268 Python,
green, counted from the JUnit XML rather than from a silent console. Not
device-verified: the state and its boundary are unit-covered, the control is
Compose, which this repo does not test.

### The closing paragraph this slice got wrong, and caught the same hour

This section first ended by naming 6cb's successor -- "one record shape for an
instantiated trait, which offers all nineteen withheld rows at once" -- copied
forward rather than re-derived. **6cc built it**, five review passes deep, and
the tree says so in four places: `InstancedTraitDialog.kt`, `InstantiableTrait`,
`PurchasableTraits.instantiableIn`, and the picker's own "The book prints a
range, or asks you to name the instance." The two items filed *behind* it are
closed too -- `TraitEffects.QUOTED_INSTANCE_ROWS` resolves the six
`Sense of Duty` instances on the verbatim-quotation warrant, and `Secret` stays
unmatched with its reason written down.

That is 6ci's finding reproduced by the slice that cites 6ci, which is the
useful part: **a closing paragraph is the one piece of a slice log nothing
verifies.** Every other claim here has a test or a book line behind it; the
"next slice" line has only the last author's memory, and it survives being
copied because it reads like a conclusion rather than a claim. One grep per
named artefact is what it costs to check, and the check is what turned this
paragraph over.

**So the honest state is: no named successor is outstanding, and this slice
does not invent one.** What the next slice needs is a fresh sweep rather than
an inherited name -- the directions this repo has already run are fields with
no reader (6ai), functions with no caller (6cf), rows with no consumer (6ci),
seams between claimed spans (6ay, 6ba), rules the app contradicts, and what the
TEST suite knows that production does not (6bz). Each expires; none is a
standing answer.

## 6co. Three numbers on three rows, and a disclaimer whose trigger had drifted

The last `defense_modifiers.json` bullet with a number is applied: "[Free
Action] [Retreat] Step back 1 hex: +3 Dodge / +1 Block / +1 Parry vs. 1 melee
attack per round". `ActiveDefenses.Retreat` is an enum of the three rows, each
carrying its own figure, and `retreat(taken, isMelee, row)` is the one predicate
that allows or refuses all of them. With this the file is closed: three bullets
applied, and the two facing bullets refused by 6ck with a test that pins their
"to defense" singular.

**The refusal to route it through `everyDefence` needed its OWN warrant, and
that is the most reusable thing here.** `dive` and `acrobaticDodge` stay out of
that helper because each *names Dodge and no other row* — the bar the stun
clears only by a second printing that says "active defenseS". The obvious move
was to write that sentence a third time. It would have been false: this bullet
names all three rows. What keeps it out is a different fact entirely — **its
three numbers differ**, so no single all-rows value can carry it. Same
conclusion, different reason, and copying the sibling's is exactly 6ck's
one-excuse-in-three-files, where the copies read as corroboration and were
evidence of nothing.

**A disclaimer's trigger had quietly stopped being its stated reason.** The
Block row prints "Against ranged attacks: N" under `if (shot != melee)`, and the
comment above it says why that note exists: a light shield is "-1 to Block vs.
ranged" and one number cannot say both. That condition was a correct proxy while
every term on the two sides was identical. The moment a **melee-only** bonus
landed on `melee` and not on `shot`, the two could differ for a reason the
comment does not cover, and the note would fire announcing the shield's penalty
when the shield had none. The trigger now asks the shield's own rule —
`Shields.blockPenalty(held, isRanged = true) != blockPenalty(held, isRanged =
false)` — which is a pure refactor today (verified row by row against
`shields.json`: Light differs, Improvised's -2 names no scope and so does not,
Medium and Heavy carry none) and is no longer perturbable by any term a later
slice adds to either side. **6bl's defect class reached one step earlier than
usual**: not a disclaimer that outlived its rule, but a *condition* that outlived
the question it was standing in for.

**One fact, one spelling.** The Dive! is "vs. ranged only" and the Retreat is
"vs. 1 melee attack" — one declaration read in opposite directions. The dialog
derives `val isRanged` once and hands `dive` that and `retreat` its negation, so
the two free actions cannot disagree about what a shot is. Writing
`incoming == Incoming.SHOT` at one site and `incoming != Incoming.SHOT` at
another is 6cn's defect, not the drift it would eventually produce.

**Two printed warrants were used instead of two arguments.** The Dodge row now
carries the acrobatic swing, the Dive!'s +3 and the Retreat's +3 at once, and the
justification is no longer p. 36's general "alongside any active defense": the
Acrobatic Dodge's own cell ends **"Stacks with Retreat."**, which names the other
bullet. That sentence is now pinned by an assertion in the acrobatic bullet's
test, so losing it is a finding rather than a silent return to the general line.
And the fair objection to showing a one-attack bonus on five rows at once is
answered by text this repo already wrote down: `ActiveDefenses.UNPAYABLE` says
this dialog "reports what every row WOULD be and never asks the GM to pick one".
A screen that allocates no defence cannot be spending one Retreat five times.

**"Each can be used once per round" is still not enforced, and here that stops
being an omission.** All three free actions now exist as controls, so the
sentence finally governs three things this app has. It stays the GM's for the
reason the parry stepper does: this screen keeps no round, `priorParries` is a
number the GM sets and a paid boost never clears either, so a latch on one chip
would claim a boundary the other two cannot honour. Written into
`ActiveDefenses.retreat`'s KDoc rather than left in a transcript — the split 6cj
made when it moved a refusal out of the journal and into production source, where
a sweep can find it.

**Placement was a design finding, not a layout preference.** The first plan put
the control beside `StunPicker` at the top, reasoning correctly that it is the
first free action to move Dodge *and* Parry *and* Block and so belongs above all
of them. But its number depends on `IncomingPicker`, and its refusal note has to
say where to go and fix it — above that picker the note would point at a control
further down. It sits between the two: after the attack pickers, before the
shield picker and every row.

**1136 Kotlin** (1027 `core:rules`, 89 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and 268 Python,
green — counted from the JUnit XML, because an empty console on success cannot
tell a pass from a suite that never ran. Three RED proofs, one reading each,
restored from a copy rather than by `git checkout`: dropping `isMelee` reddens
the value test; collapsing the three figures into one reddens the value test AND
the bullet test (the enumeration compares each row only against its own number,
so the second assertion is what catches it); leaving the bullet out of
`APPLIED_ROWS` reddens the applied/unapplied census.

**Both free reviewers were unavailable and the fallback chain ran to its end.**
Codex still refuses until 2026-08-20 14:23. `pi-qa probe` reported **1 of 20
live** where the same day's earlier record says four — three of the four are now
429 rather than dead, so the catalogue moved *within a single day*, which is
sharper than 6cd's "a catalogue is a claim about the past". The one live model
then 429'd through the whole failover chain, so the gate was the documented
single `ecc:kotlin-reviewer`, scoped to three questions and four files. It
returned no findings and independently derived the algebra behind the Block
trigger (`shot - melee` reduces to the penalty difference, every other term being
common), which is the half worth keeping: a clean review is worth what its
questions were worth, and this one confirmed a rewrite rather than clearing a
diff it was never asked about.

Not device-verified: the arithmetic and the scope are unit-covered, the chip, the
note and the row totals are Compose, which this repo does not test.

**A tidy-up was refused.** The obvious follow-up is to extract the Block note's
new predicate into an `internal` helper so `DefenseDialogTest` can pin it, the
shape `shieldForDb` and `boostOn` already take. Refused: those two exist because
the same predicate had **two** call sites and this one has one, and the reason
the old trigger was fragile — a comparison of totals that later terms can
perturb — is structurally gone rather than guarded. A guard against a failure
mode the rewrite removed is scaffolding.

**The next slice is not in this file, because this file is finished.** The
honest candidate with evidence behind it is the round boundary itself: three free
actions, a parry stepper and a boost that lasts "until next turn" now all sit on
one screen with no clock, and 6bf's decision that a round tracker is not worth
global state was taken when only ONE of them existed. That is a claim about the
data and it has changed — re-run it as a query before inheriting it (6au, 6av,
6bv). Behind it, unchanged: the nineteen withheld trait rows, one record shape.

## 6cn. The number the test suite knew and production did not

6cm named this one with evidence and it held: `ranged_modifiers.json` stores the
prone row as `{"condition": "Target is prone", "printed": "-2 ranged (but -4 in
melee)", "modifier": -2, "melee": -4}`, and `RangedModifier.melee` had exactly
**one reader in the tree** — `RangedTest.kt:112`, asserting it is -4. No
production caller. `Ranged.meleeConditions()` and `Ranged.meleeModifiers()` now
apply it, and the attack dialog's in-reach branch offers the chip that selects
it.

**The finding is 6bz's sweep shape, and this is the second time it has paid.**
What does the TEST suite know that production does not? Here the test knew the
melee value existed and was -4, had known since the row was extracted, and
nothing on any screen could reach it. A melee attack on a prone target was
modified by nothing — on a state **the app itself hands out**, since 6cm's Dive!
chip puts a character down. That pairing is 6bl's shape exactly: a rule this app
creates the conditions for and then does not charge.

**The scope was checked before it was chosen, and the check is one grep.** The
filter is `melee != null` — drawn from the data's own definition rather than
from a list of row names, the shape `AIM_ROWS` and the darkness row already
take. But that predicate encodes a claim: *in reach, this table has exactly one
row*. The table is global lines 2665-2685; grepping all 10252 lines of
`build/extract/lines.json` for "melee" returns exactly one hit inside that span,
line 2681. The other eight rows are distance, cover, movement and light — priced
for a shot and for nothing else — and no other page prices them in reach. So one
row is the whole scope, recorded in the KDoc, and `RangedTest` pins the list
**whole** rather than asserting prone is in it: a re-extraction that gave a
second row a melee value would then be a finding rather than a silent widening.

**The guard is the whole slice, and it is the one thing that was RED-proved.**
`rangedModifiers` opens `if (!plan.isRanged) return emptyList()`; the new
`meleeModifiers` opens with its mirror. Both are called from one expression
against one `plan`, so exactly one can speak. Without the mirror the two-tap path
— tick the chip in reach, tap "At range" — sums them: `onPlan` clears
`circumstances` only when going the OTHER way, so the selection survives, and the
roll would take **-6**, a number the book prints nowhere. That is 6bx's live
double count, and deleting the guard turns `a prone target is priced once, on
whichever side of the toggle the plan is` red. The helper is `internal` for
exactly that reason: a content-only test would have added a second reader of the
melee value and left the slice's actual finding — no production caller —
standing.

**A tidy-up was refused, and the refusal is checkable rather than argued.** The
obvious next move is a `surviving(circumstances, isRanged)` filter deciding which
rows outlive the toggle. Refused: the chips offered in reach come only from
`meleeConditions()`, a strict subset, so nothing selectable in reach is ever a
ranged-only row and there is nothing to strip; the other direction already clears
explicitly. The predicate would have one member and two call sites, and adding it
at one and not the other is the third-copy divergence the comment at
`AttackDialog.kt:436` already warns about — the one that shipped an unscoped
option.

**That refusal needed one qualification, found after the commit.** "The other
direction already clears explicitly" is true and now slightly too broad:
`onArmed`'s clear fires on `!held.isFired`, so picking up a sword **while already
in reach** drops a ticked prone chip too, and the stated reason for that clear
("carrying either into reach asks for a number nothing can supply") does not
cover that path — the plan was melee and stays melee. Recorded rather than
narrowed, for the same reason the filter was refused: narrowing it puts
`meleeConditions`' predicate at a second call site. The cost is a lost
declaration the player watches deselect, not a wrong number. **A justification
written one paragraph after fixing an expired comment can expire in the same
diff.**

**A sign direction was stated backwards in prose, and nothing could contradict
it.** `tools/extract_ranged.py`'s docstring explained the two-scope row by saying
"a prone target is easier to hit in reach and harder at distance" — which the
numbers reverse. Every row of that table modifies the ATTACKER's to-hit roll
("Target running: -2", "Shooter moved this turn: -2"), and 6cm had already
recorded this line as the attacker's rather than the defender's, so -4 in reach
is the HARDER case. The sentence survived since the row was extracted **because
the melee value had no reader**: no code could disagree with it. That is the
other half of this slice's own finding — an unread field does not merely leave a
rule unapplied, it leaves the prose about that rule unfalsifiable. Corrected in
the extractor and stated in `meleeConditions`' KDoc, where the direction is now
load-bearing.

**The design review's finding was about a LABEL, and it was right.** It cleared
the guard and the refusal, then caught what the decomposition had left
unspecified: step 4 never said what the melee chip's text was. The ranged side
renders `"${option.condition} ${option.printed}"` — the whole clause, both
numbers, whichever one currently applies — and a melee chip labelled with the
bare condition would have shown no magnitude at all in reach. Reusing the ranged
pattern also answers the one thing the refusal above leaves open: crossing the
toggle silently changes the applied number from -4 to -2, and the chip says both,
so the change is visible rather than silent. **A spec that omits the label is not
a spec that has no label** — the implementer picks one, and the default is the
worse one.

**A comment expired in this slice's own diff.** `AttackDialog.kt:120-122` read
"they describe the TARGET and the scene ... and only a ranged attack reads them".
True when written, false the moment the melee helper existed. That is 6bl's
disclaimer class, caught here only because the sentence sat three lines above the
declaration being changed — no test reads it, and none can.

**1134 Kotlin** (1025 `core:rules`, 89 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and 268 Python,
green — counted from the JUnit XML. Codex is still refusing (its own error text
says 2026-08-20 14:23). `pi-qa` was tried first, as the free widener it is meant
to be, and **produced zero bytes in ten minutes**, so it was abandoned under the
scoping budget's own rule rather than waited out; both gates were then the
documented `ecc:kotlin-reviewer` fallback, scoped to three questions and the
files needed to answer them. The decomposition review returned SHIP with one
MEDIUM (the label above); the diff review returned SHIP with no findings, and
independently traced the fifth test to confirm it is not vacuous. Not
device-verified: the arithmetic and the guard are unit-covered, the chip and the
breakdown line are Compose, which this repo does not test.

**The next slice is Retreat**, the last `defense_modifiers.json` bullet, whose
three numbers are scoped per defence row (+3 Dodge / +1 Block / +1 Parry vs. 1
melee attack per round) — the shape 6cl ranked second and 6ck's shield-arc half
already has a precedent for. Book lines 2456-2457 ("Each can be used once per
round") stay unclaimed on purpose: that sentence governs all three free actions,
so the slice that enforces it enforces all three.

## 6cm. A scope the sentence names itself, and a cost the book charges the other side

6cl closed the Acrobatic Dodge and ranked the two remaining
`defense_modifiers.json` bullets, putting **Dive!** first because both of its
conditions are already declared on the defence screen. That ranking held, and
this is the slice that took it:

> "[Free Action] [Dive!] +3 Dodge vs. ranged only. Spend 1 turn getting back up
> (Change Posture)."

`ActiveDefenses.dive(taken, isRanged)` composes both scopes and the dialog
supplies the two declared facts — `dived`, a new chip, and `incoming ==
Incoming.SHOT`, the declaration the unarmed parries have read since 6bg. The +3
joins the acrobatic ±2 and the bought +2 on the Dodge row and nowhere else.

**The reusable finding is about a BAR rather than a rule.** 6ck refused the
facing penalty because "Attacked from side: -2 to defense" is bare and SINGULAR,
and the stun only reaches every row on the strength of a second printing saying
"active defenseS". Dive! is a bullet in the very same list, so the obvious move
was to ask whether it too has a second printing — and it does not. A sweep of
the whole book finds "Dive"/"diving" on twelve lines and only two are this rule:
the bullet itself (2485) and the free-actions paragraph that names it (2456).

Applying 6ck's bar there would have refused this rule, and it would have been
wrong. **The bar attaches to the CONDITION that made it necessary, not to the
category of thing it was first applied to.** What the facing bullets lack is not
corroboration but a stated scope: "to defense" does not say which row, so a
second printing is the only thing that can settle it. Dive!'s sentence says
"+3 **Dodge**" and "vs. **ranged** only" — it names its row and it names its
condition, so there is nothing left for a corroborating printing to decide. This
is 6cl's lesson pointed the other way: 6cl found a cited DEFECT whose measured
scope did not cover the case it was cited for, and here a cited REFUSAL's
warrant does not cover the case it would have been extended to. **A precedent
travels with the condition that produced it, not with the shelf it was found
on.**

**The cost was checked rather than assumed, and the book charges the other
side.** Diving leaves you prone, and a rule that hands out a bonus while
silently skipping its own drawback is the class 6bl found. So: what does being
prone cost? The book prints "prone" on five lines. One is unrelated ("prone to
debt", a Wealth row), three CREATE the state (a Takedown, a crippling blow, a
failed ritual), and the only line that PRICES it is p. 39's ranged modifiers —
*"Target is prone: -2 ranged (but -4 in melee)"*, which is the **attacker's**
to-hit roll, not the defender's defence. No page prices a prone character's own
defences. So Dive! costs the defender nothing but the turn, and a slice that had
lowered the Dodge row to "balance" the +3 would have authored a rule from a
resemblance (4.1). The check is recorded in `dive`'s KDoc, so the next reader
inherits the evidence rather than the conclusion — the standard 6ck set after
finding one excuse copied into three files.

**The sentence that settled the design question lives OUTSIDE the span the table
claims.** Does Dive! stack with the Acrobatic Dodge? The Acrobatic bullet ends
"Stacks with Retreat.", naming one sibling and staying silent about the other,
and silence is exactly the shape that invites an invented rule. The answer is on
p. 36, lines 2456-2457: *"Free Actions: Retreat, Acrobatic Dodge, and Dive! are
free actions — they do not cost your maneuver and can be taken alongside any
active defense. Each can be used once per round unless stated otherwise."*
`defense_modifiers.json` claims 2480-2485; that paragraph is in neither its span
nor anyone else's. 6ba's seam lesson has so far been about RULES falling between
two claimed spans — this is the same seam holding the REASON a design needs,
which no coverage number can report as missing, because nothing was ever meant
to be extracted from it. The "once per round" half stays unenforced on purpose,
as CLAUDE.md says: it governs all three free actions, so the slice that enforces
it enforces all three.

**Three neuterings, three reds, one per direction.** Dropping `isRanged` from
`dive` fails the four-cell truth table; dropping `[Dive!]` from `APPLIED_ROWS`
fails the partition test, which is 6bl's disclaimer guard now reading two
applied bullets instead of one; and replacing "vs. ranged only" with "vs. any
attack" in the content fails `extract_defenses.PINNED`, which is 6cg's
book→JSON direction. The rule, the screen's honesty about it, and the sentence
underneath it each have their own guard.

**The verification method failed once, and that is worth writing down.** A test
run piped through `grep -E "FAILED|BUILD"` came back completely empty, which
reads as "nothing failed". The shell's working directory had been moved by an
earlier compound command and the build tool was never found — the error text
matched neither filter term. **A filter tuned to detect failure cannot tell "no
failures" from "the command never ran"**, and the optimistic reading is the
default. Any filtered output used as evidence needs a positive token that only a
completed run can emit.

**1129 Kotlin** (1022 `core:rules`, 87 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and 268 Python,
green. Codex is still refusing — its own error text now says **2026-08-20
14:23** — so both gates were the documented `ecc:kotlin-reviewer` fallback,
scoped to three questions and the three files needed to answer them: the
decomposition before any code (SHIP, and it corrected a fallback I was
weighing, that the `taken && isRanged` AND belongs in the dialog rather than in
the rules module), and the diff before commit (SHIP, no findings). Not
device-verified: the arithmetic and the partition are unit-covered, and the chip
with its two notes is Compose, which this repo does not test.

**The next slice is a -4 nobody applies, and this slice is what makes it sharp.**
Verifying the prone claim above meant reading `ranged_modifiers.json`, which
stores that row as `{"condition": "Target is prone", "printed": "-2 ranged (but
-4 in melee)", "modifier": -2, "melee": -4}`. `RangedModifier.melee` has exactly
one reader in the whole tree — `RangedTest.kt:112`, a test asserting it is -4.
**No production caller.** The attack dialog offers the row as a circumstance chip
and `Ranged.modifiers` applies the -2; a melee attack on a prone target gets
nothing. That is 6bz's sweep shape (what does the TEST suite know that
production does not), and the row is now not merely printed but *reachable*:
this slice gives the app a control that puts a character prone, so the state the
row prices is one the app itself hands out — 6bl's shape exactly. Behind it, the
last `defense_modifiers.json` bullet: **Retreat**, whose three numbers are
scoped per defence row.

## 6cl. The bullet with a die behind it, and a caveat borrowed from the wrong table

6ck named three display-only `defense_modifiers.json` bullets and ranked
**Acrobatic Dodge** first, on the grounds that it is not a modifier at all but a
ROLL this app can make: *"[Free Action] [Acrobatic Dodge] Roll vs. Acrobatics:
success gives +2 Dodge; failure gives -2 Dodge. Stacks with Retreat."*
Extracted since 6g, applied by nothing. That ranking held, and the slice shipped
it. Two of the 23 premades carry Acrobatics (Street Acrobat, Underground
Courier), so the control is reachable rather than merely correct (6bs).

### The design review was right to say NO-SHIP, and its best finding was about a REASON

Four findings before any code existed. The sharpest one did not attack the
decision — it attacked the argument for it, and the decision survived on a
different reason.

**I withheld the roll from a character without the skill, citing 6aw**:
`SkillLadder.defaultFor` has no production caller and cannot express the
per-skill overrides p. 39 prints (Brawling DX-2, Wrestling **no default**). The
review's answer: **those three rows are the unarmed-parry skills, and Acrobatics
is not among them.** The cited defect could not have produced a wrong answer for
this skill at all. I had imported a caveat from a table this case does not sit
in and let it stand in for a reason.

The refusal survives on the reason that actually does the work, found by reading
the content rather than the precedent: `common_modifiers.json` stores the
untrained row as **"Using untrained skill (default): Attribute -4 to -6" with no
`modifier` number at all** — the book prints a RANGE, so there is no target to
roll against without choosing a policy for 158 skills. **A recorded defect is
evidence about the inputs it was measured on**; reusing it for a different input
is an unchecked generalisation, and it hides the fact that no reason has been
given.

### The once-per-round latch, refused for the shape 6ck had just refused

The plan latched the roll and offered a **"New round"** button to clear it. Two
answers killed it:

- **`ParriesThisRound` is the precedent and it runs the other way.** The GM sets
  it, the app never increments it. A latch has the app assert "the round has not
  ended" on a screen whose every other round-scoped fact is a declaration — and
  a button clearing only this roll while `priorParries` still reads 3 and a paid
  boost still says "this turn" is **false by omission**.
- **The warrant is plural and the enforcement was singular.** Lines 2456-2457
  read "Retreat, Acrobatic Dodge, and Dive! are free actions … **Each** can be
  used once per round". Enforcing that on one of the three is the mirror image
  of 6ck's refusal, which turned on a rule being printed *singular*. So the
  limit is the GM's, the roll is re-rollable, and the paragraph stays unclaimed
  for the slice that enforces it for all three.

### The finding that changed a number: a roll is not a `SuccessRoll`

The plan rolled `SuccessRoll.against(level, dice)`. Every other skill roll in
this app goes through `SkillRoll.at` carrying `Conditions.forSkill`, whose HP
and FP penalties are **unscoped — they reach every skill**. So a reeling
character would have rolled Acrobatics at one target in this dialog and another
on the sheet screen: one rule, two sites, the class that has broken this
codebase's numbers three times (6ag, 6ai, 6be), reachable in the exact state a
defence dialog is opened in. `DefenseDialog` now takes the same
`conditions: (SkillKey) -> List<Modifier>` ledger `AttackDialog` does.

### What shipped

`ActiveDefenses.acrobaticDodge(Outcome?)` — null (not rolled) is 0, a success is
`+ACROBATIC_SWING`, a failure is `-ACROBATIC_SWING`. **One constant, not a +2 and
a -2**: the bullet prints one magnitude twice and a pair could drift. A critical
counts as its plain sibling, because the bullet prints two outcomes and only two.

The ±2 joins the bought boost on the **Dodge row alone** and stays out of
`everyDefence`, which is reserved for rules printed plural — the same bar 6ck
held the facing penalty to, answered the other way because this bullet names
Dodge twice.

`ActiveDefenses.unappliedModifiers()` is new and is the 6bl guard in structural
form. The dialog printed all five bullets as bare notes while all five were
display-only; one now reaches a number, and printing it beside the four that do
not — with neither marked — is precisely the disclaimer-outlives-its-rule defect
6bl found **on this same screen**. The partition lives in rules so a test can
read both halves, and its last assertion is deliberately asymmetric:
`all - applied` drops the FIRST match while `filterNot` drops every one, so a
second bullet carrying the tag fails loudly instead of vanishing from the UI.

`extract_defenses.PINNED` gains the three phrases the app now applies, **sign-
anchored** — `"success gives +2 Dodge"`, not `"2 Dodge"`, because 6cg measured
that a magnitude guard is satisfied by a sign flip. A pytest case feeds `verify()`
a bullet with both signs reversed and asserts it raises.

**Two more files carried the same false excuse**, one slice after 6ck found the
last set: `Content.kt`'s `DefenseModifier` KDoc and `extract_defenses.py`'s
docstring both said there is "no single figure to extract" because Acrobatic
Dodge carries a bonus and a penalty — an excuse drawn from ONE row and
generalised to a table whose first two bullets print exactly one number each.
Both now say what is true and narrower.

### Verified

**1127 Kotlin** (1020 `core:rules`, 87 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and **268
Python**, green. Three RED-proofs: flipping the failure branch's sign fails 5
rules tests; removing the partition's filter fails 1; and the Python sign-flip
guard is a live test rather than a manual proof. `extract_defenses.py` re-run
against the PDF wrote both JSON files byte-identical, so the pinned phrases are
really there. The Dodge row's composition is not unit-testable (this repo tests
no composables) and is **unverified on device** — stated, not skipped.

**Codex still refuses** (resets 2026-08-20 14:23). Two `ecc:kotlin-reviewer`
passes, decomposition then diff. The diff pass returned SHIP with three LOWs:
two taken (the roll state is now keyed on the skill, so a level change cannot
leave a stale ±2 on the row, and the skill is carried as a `Pair` rather than a
live `Map.Entry`, which is unstable and can never skip recomposition), one
refused with its reason recorded in the KDoc — `printedAcrobaticDodge()` throws
on a content drop, exactly as `printedStun()` already does on this screen.

**Next, with evidence.** Two `defense_modifiers.json` bullets are still
display-only and each still fails its own test: **Retreat** prints three numbers
scoped per defence row (+3 Dodge / +1 Block / +1 Parry) and "vs. 1 melee attack
per round", so it needs the per-row shape this slice did not; **Dive!** prints
one number scoped to Dodge AND to ranged attacks, which this screen can express
(`Incoming.SHOT` is already declared) but which costs a turn getting back up —
a Change Posture this app has nothing to spend. Take Dive! next: its scope is
two conditions the dialog already holds. And note that lines 2456-2457 remain
**unclaimed on purpose** — the slice that enforces "once per round" must enforce
it for all three bullets, which is what makes it one slice rather than three.

## 6ck. One excuse in three files, and the arc the book does print

6cj closed by naming chapter 5's lines 2456-2457 as "unclaimed and unread".
**Unread was false** — 6ba's widened seam sweep had triaged line 2457 at
`docs/SLICE-LOG.md:3957`, with a reason. I made 6ci's mistake one slice after
writing the lesson about it and shipping a memory file for it, which is the more
useful half of this entry: **a lesson learned at the end of one slice is applied
at the start of the next, when it is least available.** Bind it to the artifact
that must satisfy it — the closing paragraph itself — or it gets documented and
skipped in the same session.

Checking that reason ("needs a round tracker this app does not hold") turned up
something bigger than the clause it defends. The tracker excuse had already
expired: `ParriesThisRound` is a per-round counter the GM steps, and four rules
(6bm, 6bn, 6bo, 6bh) became buildable as declarations rather than through the
tracker 6bd ranked first.

### The same false sentence, in three files

`defense_modifiers.json`'s five bullets are rendered as bare Notes at the bottom
of the defence dialog and applied by nothing. Three separate KDocs explained
why, and all three said a version of the same thing:

| Where | The claim |
|---|---|
| `Content.kt:753` | "Prose, not signed numbers: 'Acrobatic Dodge' grants +2 on a success and -2 on a failure, so there is no single figure to extract" |
| `Shields.kt:20` | "facing is the GM's to adjudicate and **the book prints no arc to test against**" |
| `DefenseDialog.kt:56` | "this app does not model facing — **the book prints no arc to test against**" |

The book prints the arc. Two hundred lines above the shield table, in the very
list that dialog renders: "Attacked from side: -2 to defense", "Attacked from
rear: -4 to defense". And the model's excuse is drawn from **one row** — true of
Acrobatic Dodge's ±2, generalised to a table whose first two bullets each print
exactly one number (6cb's lesson: a safety rationale is a hypothesis about which
condition does the work).

### The design review inverted the slice, and was right to

**NO-SHIP, two HIGH and two MEDIUM.** The plan was to apply the -2/-4 through
`everyDefence`, the function every rendered defence already calls, on the
grounds that "-2 to defense" is unscoped exactly as the stun's "-4 to Active
Defense" is.

The review answered with this repo's own history: that warrant is the stun's
*insufficient-alone* reading. `ActiveDefenses.everyDefence`'s KDoc says the stun
reaches every row because a **second** printing says "active defenseS" — "that
second printing is load-bearing twice". Facing was being handed the first kind
of evidence and none of the second.

**So it was checked rather than argued.** Every occurrence of "active defense"
in the book, and every printing of the facing rule: `-2 to defense` and `-4 to
defense` appear **once each, singular, with no companion anywhere**. The diff
reviewer independently re-ran that grep across all 59 content files and
confirmed it, and also located the stun's second printing (`pathways.json`, an
ability text reading "-4 to active defenses"). The bar is the same bar. The
penalty is refused.

**And the same check found the half that ships.** The shield's Defense Bonus is
conditional on that identical arc, in a sentence printed in exactly the form
this repo requires — plural and enumerated: *"its DB (Defense Bonus) adds to all
active defenses (Dodge, Parry, and Block) **against attacks from the front or
shield side**."* No inference needed. That inverted the slice: not "apply the
penalty and incidentally handle the shield", but "the only facing rule printed
in an acceptable form is the shield's own, so apply that and record the penalty
with the bar it fails".

### What shipped

`Facing` (FRONT/SIDE/REAR) and `ShieldCoverage` (COUNTS/GM_DECIDES/WITHHELD),
with `Shields.coverageAt`. **Three states rather than two**, because the clause
draws two lines and this app can see one: the front and the rear are decided by
the sentence, and the side is not — "shield side" names a hand this book never
assigns to a character. A Boolean would have to answer it, and both answers are
wrong half the time.

The review's second HIGH was the implementation risk, and it was real: **the
Block row builds its arrow by hand** rather than through `shielded()`, so gating
the shared helper alone would have left the DB standing on exactly the row the
change exists for — reachable by any character with the Shield skill and a
shield Readied. Both sites now consume one `shieldForDb(carried, facing)`, which
is also what made the rule testable at all, since this repo tests no composables.

`extract_shields.PINNED` gains the clause. It already pinned what the DB
*reaches* ("adds to all active defenses (Dodge, Parry, and Block)") and did not
pin what it is *conditional on* — so the sentence the app now withholds on had
no guard.

The penalty's refusal is recorded on `everyDefence`, where someone would add it,
and **pinned by its own wording**: a test asserts the two bullets still end "to
defense". The reason expires the day the book reads plural, which is the only
way a recorded "not applied" can expire on its own rather than quietly outliving
its reason (6bl).

One MEDIUM from the diff review, taken: the FRONT and SIDE notes opened with the
same sentence ("Arrow shows the DB applied"), so a GM who stops after the first
clause reads the app as having decided the side. The verb now carries the
difference where a skimmer reaches it.

### Verified

**1124 Kotlin** (1017 `core:rules`, 87 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and **267
Python**, green. Three readings RED-proved by neutering one at a time and
restoring from copies (6bu): `coverageAt(REAR) -> COUNTS` fails the rules test
AND the app test; `shieldForDb` ignoring facing fails the app test; flipping the
singular pin to "defenses" fails the wording test. `extract_shields.py` re-run
against the PDF with the new pin and the committed JSON came back byte-identical
— the phrase is really there.

**Codex still refuses** (resets 2026-08-20 14:23). Two `ecc:kotlin-reviewer`
passes, decomposition then diff. The design pass returned NO-SHIP and rewrote
the slice; the diff pass returned SHIP with one MEDIUM.

**Next, with evidence.** The three remaining `defense_modifiers.json` bullets —
Retreat, Acrobatic Dodge, Dive! — are still display-only, and each fails a
different test, which is why they are three slices and not one: Retreat prints
three numbers scoped per defence row (+3 Dodge / +1 Block / +1 Parry), Dive!
prints one scoped to Dodge and to ranged attacks, and Acrobatic Dodge is not a
modifier at all but **a roll against Acrobatics** this app could make, with +2
on a success and -2 on a failure. Line 2457's "once per round" governs all three
from twenty-five lines above them. The Acrobatic Dodge roll is the one with a
die behind it; take that first, and note that the "needs a round tracker" excuse
above it has now expired twice.

## 6cj. The slice that did not ship, and the journal no grep can read

6ci closed by naming `All-Out Defense (Double)` as the next slice, with what
looked like decisive evidence: it is priced at 2 FP, this app charges the other
eight priced rows, and it has "no code, a test, a comment, or a recorded
reason". **That last clause was false, and finding out why is the slice.**

### 6bl refused this row four slices earlier, in the journal

`docs/SLICE-LOG.md:4954`, from 6bl's maneuver clause sweep:

> **All-Out Defense (Double) is a permission with nothing to permit.** Line
> 2453 prints the rule it lifts — "you may attempt one active defense" — and
> this dialog does not allocate defences: it is a reference sheet saying what
> each one WOULD be... paying 2 FP to lift a limit the app never imposed would
> charge for nothing.

6ci's sweep iterates content rows against Kotlin source. A rationale recorded in
a prose journal is not a row, a field, a function or a comment, so **the
instrument was structurally incapable of seeing it** — and its author read the
absence of an in-source comment as the absence of a decision. That is a fifth
distinct unit rationale has hidden in here, and the first outside the compiler's
reach entirely.

### The reason is a claim about the data, so it was re-run as a query

6bl's sentence has two halves. The PROVENANCE half — that line 2453 is a rule
the app does not hold — **expired**. `defense_refusals.json` claims `[2453,
2453]` and stores the whole sentence as the `ALL_OUT_ATTACK` row; `printedFor`
reads it, `state()` returns it as `narrower`, and `DefenseDialog.kt:236` prints
it on screen today. One cell, two rules: the PARENTHETICAL ("unless you took an
All-Out Attack maneuver") is a refusal this app applies, and the MAIN CLAUSE is
the one-defence limit, read by nothing. Both sweeps pass it — the field has a
reader (6ai), the row has a consumer (6ci).

The MECHANISM half survived intact, and a design review said so before any code
existed. **NO-SHIP, three HIGH findings**, each worth more than the build:

1. **Provenance is not mechanism.** That the sentence is extracted, stored and
   displayed says nothing about whether the dialog gates the GM to one defence.
   It does not: every row renders its own value at once and nobody is ever asked
   to pick. So the cap this row buys would have to be **invented in the same
   commit that charges for lifting it** — authoring a mechanic to justify a
   price, which is the inverse of 4.1.
2. **The FP trigger I copied was wrong.** I took `BoostPicker`'s charge-on-first-
   selection, itself a rule fixed after a review found double-charging. It is
   correct there because +2-on-one-row is delivered by the FIRST pick; Double's
   effect is delivered at the SECOND, so charging at the first bills the GM for
   the ordinary free case. **A pattern transfers by meaning, not by shape.**
3. **A standing limit Note would contradict the screen.** `narrowerFor` exists
   precisely to stop that sentence being cited as general, and `DefenseDialog`
   frames it as narrow. A permanent second printing of the same string, beside
   the first, overturns the codebase's own documented reading through a UI
   addition nobody re-decided.

### What shipped instead

`ActiveDefenses.UNPAYABLE` — one entry, name beside reason, in this repo's own
`TraitEffects.UNAPPLIED` shape — and the census test reads its expected set from
there instead of a literal. The reason moves out of the journal into the file a
reader of the defence rules will open.

**That move buys discoverability, not strength** — the diff review's finding,
recorded rather than smoothed. An entry added to that map turns the census green
without touching `AttacksTest`, exactly as editing the literal used to. Claiming
it was a stronger pin would have been a disclaimer that lies (6bl, again).

Three more findings from the same review. `ORDINARY_DEFENCES = 1` was deleted:
no caller, and the "one" is a number the book prints, so restating it in Kotlin
is the copy 4.1 forbids — a constant wearing a KDoc as justification. The
mechanism reason was written twice, in the value and in the KDoc above it; it is
now written once, in the value, with the KDoc carrying only how the entry got
there. And I removed **my own vacuous assertion** before the review saw it: a
second check that every excuse names a priced row cannot fail, because the
equality above it forces the sets identical and the gap is a subset of `priced`
by construction. It is 6ci's vacuous-filter finding in a new disguise, and what
caught it was trying to write its RED case.

### 6ci's other three deferrals are artefacts of its own instrument

6ci left `hit_locations.json` ('Leg'), `divination_support.json` ('Cogitation')
and `ritual_support.json` ('Professional Skill (Astrology etc)') as untriaged
single-miss tables, "one grep to classify". All three are closed here, none real:

| Table | Consumer | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `hit_locations` | `Wounds.locationNamed` matches any target by name | Loop-consumed. 4 of 9 rows appear in Kotlin, not 8 — and Neck/Vitals/Skull/Torso appear because they carry multipliers, not because the table is enumerated. |
| `divination_support` | `Divination.supportBonus` sums whatever rows are passed | Loop-consumed. `Occultism` reads as "modelled" because the string occurs 25 times as a skill elsewhere. |
| `ritual_support` | `RitualMode.supportBonus` matches by bare name | Loop-consumed, same reason. |

**The sweep's "modelled" predicate is a substring search over Kotlin**, so its
sibling ratio is only trustworthy for a table the code models row-by-row. 6ci
hardened its own *test* against that predicate after a reviewer showed `Move`
and `Wait` were "covered" by this file's prose — and then left its *shortlist*
built on the unhardened one. An instrument fixed in one place is not an
instrument fixed.

### Verified

**1121 Kotlin** (1015 `core:rules`, 86 `app`, 20 `core:model`) and **267
Python**, green. RED-proved by neutering the one reading and restoring from a
copy (6bu): emptying `UNPAYABLE` fails the census at `AttacksTest.kt:492` and
only it — 39 tests run, 1 failed. No behaviour changed, so there is nothing to
device-verify; stated rather than skipped.

**Codex still refuses**, confirmed by calling rather than by reading the date
(resets 2026-08-20 14:23; today is 2026-08-15). Two `ecc:kotlin-reviewer`
passes, decomposition then diff, each scoped to three questions and the files
needed to answer them. Both came back NO-SHIP; the design one cancelled the

**Next, with evidence.** Nothing in the two FP tables is outstanding — the

one**, which is what makes All-Out Defense (Double), the Feint's Quick Contest

decision, not a rule-shaped one, and it must be argued before it is built — 6bl

## 6ci. Nine priced rows, seven charged

Both slices before this one closed by naming the same next step — "6ca's
`Ether Body Damage`, which wants purchasable traits, is the largest thing
outstanding". **Both were false when written.** 6cc shipped purchasable
traits three slices earlier and device-verified an `Ether Body Damage`
purchase surviving a reload; `TraitEffects.spiRollBonus` has production
callers at `MainActivity.kt:366`, `DivinationDialog.kt:455` and
`Detection.kt:160`. The second item behind it — "the Sense of Duty
resolution" — is `TraitEffects.QUOTED_INSTANCE_ROWS`, also already shipped.

Two closing paragraphs copied forward instead of re-derived, and the queue
they described had been empty for four slices. **A handover's own "what is
left" is a claim about the tree and expires exactly like a sweep verdict**
(6au, 6av, 6ba, 6bv). Two greps settled both.

### The sweep this repo had never run

Every audit here has iterated one of two units. 6ai swept extracted FIELDS
for a reader. 6cf swept public FUNCTIONS for a caller. Neither can see a
table that is loaded, whose fields are all read, and one of whose **rows**
reaches nothing — a row is not a field and not a function.

So: every content JSON, every row's identifier, grepped against all Kotlin.
The raw output is mostly noise, and **the noise is the instrument working
correctly**: `appearance.json` names 2 rows of 8 in source and `skills.json`
52 of 158, because those tables are consumed by loop, which is the right
design. The signal is the SIBLING RATIO inside one table — where the code
models rows individually and skipped some:

| Table | Modelled | Named nowhere |
|---|---|---|
| `maneuvers.json` | 13 of 14 | **All-Out Defense (Double)** |
| `extra_effort.json` | 3 of 4 | **Giant Step** |

Neither has code, a test, a comment, or a recorded reason. This repo's own
standard (`TraitEffects.UNAPPLIED`) is that a printed rule reaching nothing
says so with its reason, "so the omission stays a decision rather than
becoming an accident".

### The design review was right to refuse, and wrong about why

Reviewed as a decomposition, no diff. Verdict **NO-SHIP**, and its first
finding was a correction to me: my hazard argument named
`ActiveDefenses.boostFor`, **which does not exist** — line 191 is
`const val BOOST_BONUS` and I had read its KDoc as a function's.
`boostOn` is real but lives in `DefenseDialog.kt:421`, outside the rules.
A design document is an argument made of claims about code, and one grep
per symbol is what those claims cost.

Its substantive counter-case: `(Increased)` already ships with its own
"Cannot attack" clause unenforced, so Double's unmodelled middle clause is
not categorically different. That argument is inconclusive from inside
itself — either side could be argued from the same evidence. **A census
settled it in one command.** Take the attribute both rows share, and count
how the corpus treats it:

```
YES  maneuvers     2 FP  All-Out Attack (Determined) / (Strong) / (Double)
YES  maneuvers     2 FP  All-Out Defense (Increased)
NO   maneuvers     2 FP  All-Out Defense (Double)
NO   extra_effort  1 FP  Giant Step
YES  extra_effort  1 FP  Strong Blow / 2 FP Heroic Charge / 1 FP Feverish
```

Nine priced rows, seven charged. **The price is the half this app does
model** — it holds no map, no opponent and no round, but it holds the FP
pool. So neither row is out of scope: they are *unpayable*, which is a gap.
That inverts my own proposal, which was to record both as unapplied with a
reason. Recording a reason for something the app can in fact do is how a
disclaimer starts lying (6bl).

### What shipped, and what is pinned instead

`Attacks.GIANT_STEP`, `AttackPlan.giantStep`, one addend in `fpCost`, one
chip. **No `require` guards it**, and that absence is pinned by a test:
its two neighbours in the same bullet list each print a scope ("Regular
melee attacks only", "Ignore **Charge Attack** penalties") and this cell
prints none, so refusing it anywhere would be this app inventing a limit
(4.1). "No require" is invisible in a diff, so it is a test.

The census is now the guard, anchored to `AttackManeuver.printed`,
`DefenseBoost.printed` and the option constants — **never to a text search
of the source**, which the reviewer showed would call `Move` and `Wait`
covered because this file's own prose contains those words (6cg's
sign-blind guard, one class over). It asserts the remaining gap by NAME:
All-Out Defense (Double). That line fails the day it ships, which makes it
a pin rather than a comment (4.2).

### The diff review found the transition I did not know existed

**SHIP with one MEDIUM.** `atRange` and `withAttack` centralise what
survives a plan transition, and both KDocs say why: a caller doing its own
is a second copy of the rule, which stopped this codebase's numbers
reconciling three times (6ag, 6ai, 6be). There was a **third** transition —
the maneuver chip rebuilt `AttackPlan` inline — and it went unnoticed
because everything it dropped deserved dropping. Giant Step is what exposed
it: no maneuver scopes it, and the rebuild dropped it anyway, so a player
comparing to-hit numbers across maneuvers silently lost a paid option.
`Attacks.withManeuver` now owns it, RED-proved.

One LOW taken: `.filter { it.fp != null }` on the extra-effort side is
vacuous — `ExtraEffort.fp` is a non-nullable `Int`, so it read as the
maneuver side's condition while testing nothing.

**One LOW refused, with evidence.** The reviewer notes the census cannot
see an `fp` VALUE drifting on an already-payable row. There is no second
copy to drift: `fpCost` reads `maneuver.fp` and `effortCost(...)` reads
`row.fp`, both from the JSON at call time. Every FP number this app charges
already comes from the row it is printed in.
